description: Crocus minimus, a dwarf saffron rarely reaching ten centimetres, its narrow almost thread-like leaves overtopping the small flower. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804) and places the plant in the iris family of the Jussieu arrangement.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Dianella Cœrulea
description: Plate 79 shows Dianella coerulea, set apart from the sword-leaved species by its azure-blue flowers borne in a loose panicle on a tall stalk, the wheel-shaped corolla of six reflexed lobes contrasting with yellow anthers. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Dolley Madison
description: Dolley Madison faces the viewer in a low-cut white Empire-waisted gown with a gold chain at her throat and dark hair dressed close to the head. Gilbert Stuart painted this portrait in 1804, when Madison was wife of the Secretary of State, four years before James Madison became president. The work is associated with the White House Historical Association.
credit: White House Historical Association [1]

title: Dracœna Reflexa
description: Plate 92 shows Dracaena reflexa, a shrub with spirally set lance-shaped leaves that bend and arch toward the ground, topped by a large panicle of seven or eight simple racemes of whitish flowers. The plate sits in the Asparagaceae of Jussieu and appears in the second volume (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Dracœna Terminalis
description: Dracaena terminalis, a small shrub whose foliage shifts from dark green to reddish, drawn with its ringed stem and a branching panicle of pale flowers. Redoute placed it among the asparagus family (Asperges) for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the cultivated specimens reddened in the glasshouse much as wild ones do in the Moluccas.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Epidendrum Aloifolium
description: Epidendrum aloifolium, a stiff-leaved orchid with a spike of seven or eight white flowers banded in reddish bronze, the lip ridged and three-lobed. Despite the work's title, Les Liliacees covers many monocot families beyond true lilies, here an orchid as the Jussieu classification line shows.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Epidendrum Bifidum
description: Epidendrum bifidum, an orchid with jointed stems carrying two sheathing leaves and a terminal raceme of purple-red flowers, the corolla split into six segments. The plate appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804). Enlarged dissection figures at the foot of the sheet show the flower's parts.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Epidendrum Ciliare
description: Epidendrum ciliare, a large white-flowered orchid named for the long fringe on the side lobes of its lip, set above firm dark green leaves on noded stems. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used throughout the eight folio volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Epidendrum Sinense
description: Epidendrum sinense, with linear leathery leaves and a stiff scape of five or six erect flowers, the outer segments dull yellow marked with seven red lines. A.P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text accompanying Redoute's plates, here for the second volume (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Fritillaria Persica
description: Fritillaria persica, set apart by its oblique spiralled leaves and a long raceme of many small bractless flowers in dull green-tinged purple. The plate appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804). A callous tubercle replaces the bract at the base of each pedicel.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Cardinalis
description: Gladiolus cardinalis rises from a small tuberous bulb on a stiff stalk topped by five or six bright red flowers, their lower three segments each marked with a white central patch, above sword-shaped glaucous leaves nearly as long as the stem. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacées (1804), drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Carneus
description: A flesh-pink Gladiolus carneus, its four blooms in a leaning spike above glaive-shaped leaves, the flower colour likened to apple blossom. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method Redoute used through all eight folio volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: gladiolus strictus
description: Gladiolus strictus, long confused with the plaited gladiolus, its whole surface covered in soft bristling hairs and its pleated leaves topped by a spike of blue-lilac flowers. The bottle-shaped bulb is shown below. This plate is from the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Hemerocallis Cærulea
description: Hemerocallis caerulea, broad stalked leaves and a bare scape ending in a raceme of bell-shaped flowers in pale blue tinged with lilac, the tube grooved with six furrows. The dissection figures show the enlarged stamens and style, a botanical convention of Redoute's day.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Anemonæflora
description: Plate 85 shows Ixia anemonaeflora from a whitish ovoid bulb, its slender stem leafy nearly to the top and carrying two or three spaced white flowers tinged yellow at the throat. Despite the title, Les Liliacees covers many monocot families; this Ixia belongs to the Iridaceae, as the classification line records.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Bulbocodium
description: Plate 88 shows Ixia bulbocodium, set apart by a simple scape shorter than the leaves and bearing a single flower, with a stigma so deeply split it appears six-parted. The text notes wide variation, the small-flowered race shown here under a decimetre tall with white, bluish or violet blooms.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Cepacea
description: Plate 96 shows Ixia cepacea, named for hollow cylindrical leaves like an onion's, with a simple stem ending in a flat two-ranked spike of pale grey-blue flowers. Each funnel-shaped bloom sits between two opposite membranous bracts; Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees in 1804.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Dubia
description: Ixia dubia carries a dense, nearly globular spike of golden-yellow saucer-shaped flowers, each segment marked with a purple blotch at its base. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1804. The slim leaves are folded sword-fashion along the lower stem.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Fusco-Citrina
description: Ixia fusco-citrina carries a short head of jonquil-yellow flowers, each division stained with a brown lustrous blotch at its inner base. The plate belongs to the iris family in the Linnaean class Triandria monogynia. Below, the dissection figures enlarge the flower's stamens in the period's botanical convention.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Hyalina
description: Ixia hyalina is distinguished at first glance by its large crimson-rose flowers, the spatula-shaped lobes edged with white transparent bands along their lower half. A fairly dense spike of four to eight blooms sits atop a glabrous stem, the sword-shaped leaves slightly shorter in the lower part of the plant. Redouté included it in Les Liliacées, dated between 1804 and 1806.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Liliago
description: Ixia liliago carries two or three large flowers resembling those of the white lily, whitish outside and yellowish within, with a dark violet spot at the inner base of each segment. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804). Enlarged stamen figures sit at the foot of the sheet.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Minata
description: Ixia miniata carries its flowers in alternating two-ranked spikes, the corolla lobes opaque at their lower margins rather than transparent. The classification line places it in the iris family, Triandria monogynia. The glaucous-green leaves are folded sword-fashion along the lower stem.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Jérôme Bonaparte by Gilbert Stuart 1804
description: Napoleon's youngest brother sits for an American portraitist while honeymooning in Baltimore with his first wife, Elizabeth Patterson. Stuart painted the 19-year-old Jérôme on canvas at 28 1/4 inches, the loose brushwork of the unfinished collar typical of his late Boston manner.
credit: The Athenaeum [1]

title: Lilium Penduliflorum
description: Lilium penduliflorum, rising to five or six decimetres with whorled three-veined leaves and a single nodding orange flower spotted brown within. Its six funnel-formed petals end in fleshy callused points. Stamen and pistil figures sit below, following the botanical convention of the period.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lilium Philadelphicum
description: Lilium philadelphicum, the wood lily, with whorled ovate-oblong leaves and a single erect orange-red flower, yellow within at the base and spotted dark toward the clawed petals. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804), one of the North American lilies in the work.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lilium Superbum
description: Lilium superbum, the swamp lily, tall with three-veined lance-shaped leaves whorled below and numerous nodding orange-yellow flowers spotted dark, the petals reflexed as in the martagon. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the club-shaped seed capsule appears alongside.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Limodorum Purpureum
description: Limodorum purpureum, an orchid rising from a whitish tuber to a loose raceme of purple-red flowers, each corolla split into six deep segments on two ranks. Despite the work's title, Les Liliacees ranges across many monocot families, including the orchids shown here.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Moræa Sordescens
description: Moraea sordescens, a low iris-family plant under three decimetres, with spathes of two flowers some three to four centimetres across, dull reddish and marked by three red-edged yellow blotches. De Candolle worked from an unpublished L'Heritier drawing in describing it.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Newton
description: Blake's monoprint shows the natural philosopher hunched naked on a sea-floor rock, drawing geometric figures with a compass. The image reads as a critique of pure reason: Newton, absorbed in measurement, becomes blind to the imaginative cosmos beyond his diagram.
credit: The William Blake Archive

title: Ornitho­galum Longibrac­teatum
description: Ornithogalum longibracteatum, recognised by its huge apple-sized bulb sitting half above the soil, with a tall scape carrying a long raceme of white flowers each crossed by a broad green stripe. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method Redoute used across all eight folio volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ornithogalum Arabicum
description: Ornithogalum arabicum, the Arabian star-of-Bethlehem, a tall cylindrical scape carrying a short corymb-like raceme of broad white bell-shaped flowers, each centred on a glossy near-black ovary. The text calls this contrast its true distinguishing mark; Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pitcairnia Angustifolia
description: Pitcairnia angustifolia, its narrow stiff leaves rising in a tuft and edged the whole length with brown horny spines, below a loose raceme on a woolly stem. The work places it in the pineapple family on the Jussieu line. The plate appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pitcairnia Bromeliæfolia
description: Pitcairnia bromeliaefolia, a tuft of leaves spined with short hooked teeth only on the lower half, below a simple loose raceme of flowers on short bracted pedicels. The work places the genus in the pineapple family on the Jussieu line. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pitcairnia Latifolia
description: Pitcairnia latifolia, broad lanceolate leaves bearing spines only near the base, below a firm white-downy stem carrying a dense cylindrical spike of crowded red flowers. The plate, from the second volume of Les Liliacées (1804), places the genus in the pineapple family.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pontederia Cordata
description: Pontederia cordata, an aquatic plant of still waters with long-petioled heart-shaped leaves and a spike of blue almost two-lipped flowers held above the surface. The text notes a variety gathered by Fraser in South Carolina. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Portrait of Anna Payne Cutts
description: Dolley Madison's younger sister Anna Payne Cutts, wife of Massachusetts congressman Richard Cutts, sits in a soft white gown against a neutral ground. Stuart painted her in Washington shortly after her marriage, working in the bust-length format he reserved for society wives of the early Republic.
credit: The Athenaeum: Home - info - pic

title: Scilla Maritima
description: Plate 116 shows Scilla maritima, the sea squill, recognised by its spherical bulb larger than a fist that often sits half out of the ground, sending up a tall scape with a long raceme of white star-opening flowers. Its bracts carry a basal appendage found in no other squill.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Sisyrinchium Striatum
description: Sisyrinchium striatum, its cylindrical iris-like stems carrying a long spike of pale yellowish flowers veined in brown or purple. Printed as a stipple engraving in colour and finished by hand, the plate appeared in Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Strelitzia Reginæ
description: Strelitzia reginae, its long leathery leaves on cylindrical petioles set beside the spathe from which the brilliant crested flower emerges. The text records it as a Cape of Good Hope introduction much admired in European gardens; Redoute drew it for Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: The Young Harpist
description: A young woman seated at a pedal harp, her gaze turned toward the viewer. Oil on canvas catalogued 1977.152 at the Yale University Art Gallery and dated about 1804 to 1806. The harp signals the musical accomplishment expected of women in this period.

title: Tradescantia Rosea
description: Tradescantia rosea, a small species with narrow channelled leaves and a simple umbel of pink flowers on stalks longer than the floral leaves. The work places it among the rushes of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: tradescantia virginica
description: Tradescantia virginica, its grassy leaves below clustered flowers of rich violet-purple, the colour for which the plant was sought in gardens. The accompanying text notes pale-violet and white-flowered variants as well as hairy forms; the plate appeared in Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Tulipa Suaveolens
description: Tulipa suaveolens, the scented tulip, its single fragrant bloom of six pointed petals in vivid red shading to yellow at the margins. The stem and upper leaf surfaces are downy, a trait the French text uses to separate it from the garden tulip. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Wachendorfia Thyrsiflora
description: Wachendorfia thyrsiflora, its golden-yellow flowers gathered into an upright oblong raceme above pleated lance-shaped leaves arranged like those of an iris. The French text places it near the iris family on an ovoid tuber whose flesh turns red when cut. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Allium Globosum
description: Allium globosum, its slender stems each ending in a globular umbel of bright pink bell-shaped flowers above thread-like leaves. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the enlarged figures show the brick-coloured anthers and the three-angled seed capsule.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Amaryllis Belladonna
description: Amaryllis belladonna, its umbel of large rose-pink funnel flowers carried on a firm scape dusted grey-green, the broad strap leaves appearing here alongside the bloom. Each flower opens into six segments with six stamens shorter than the perianth. This plate belongs to the first volumes of Les Liliacées, published by Pierre-Joseph Redouté between 1805 and 1807.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Amaryllis Lutea
description: Amaryllis lutea, recalling the colchicum and crocus in habit, its solitary yellow bell-shaped flower seated in a membranous spathe above narrow two-ranked leaves. The stamens stand upright here, unusual among the amaryllis, the three outer ones nearly twice as long. Plate 148 belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ancient city at the foot of a mountain
description: An imagined Greek polis spreads along a rocky promontory, temples and stoa stacked up the slope toward a fortified acropolis. Schinkel painted the canvas in Berlin around 1806, years before his architectural career began, channelling his early training as a stage and panorama painter into archaeological reverie.

title: Anigosanthos Flavida
description: Anigosanthos flavida, the kangaroo paw, with sword-shaped leaves and branching stems ending in clusters of tubular flowers, the outside bristling with thick yellowish wool. Despite the title of Les Liliacées, Redouté's volumes ranged across many monocot families; this species is included from the family Haemodoraceae, native to Australia.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Asophodelus Fistulosus
description: Asphodelus fistulosus, with fibrous roots, slender awl-shaped hollow leaves, and a bare branching stem carrying loose racemes of white flowers, each segment crossed by a russet midrib. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), stipple-engraved and coloured by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Belamcanda Chinensis
description: Belamcanda chinensis, the blackberry lily, its fan of sword-shaped leaves rising to branched spikes of spotted orange flowers. The plate places it in the iris family (Iridaceae); Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees in 1805.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Coronation of Emperor Napoleon I and Coronation of the Empress Josephine in Notre-Dame de Paris
description: Joséphine kneels before Napoleon at Notre-Dame as he raises the crown to place it on her head, Pope Pius VII seated in the background. David's monumental canvas, painted between 1805 and 1807 and now in the Louvre, recasts the coronation as a spectacle of dynastic legitimacy, famously including Napoleon's mother Letizia in the gallery despite her absence from the actual ceremony — her presence a posthumous addition at Napoleon's request.

title: Crocus Sativus
description: Crocus sativus, the cultivated saffron, its corm raising narrow grassy leaves and a large purple flower with prominent orange-red stigmas — the source of the spice saffron. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées, the plate dating between 1805 and 1807.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Diasia Graminifolia
description: Plate 163 shows Diasia graminifolia, reaching three or four decimetres, with grass-like leaves sheathing iris-fashion and a loose panicle of slender divergent branches. The flowers, whitish and often marked with a red line on the midrib, sit in the iris family of the classification line.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Eucomis Regia
description: Eucomis regia rising from a bulb nearly the size of a fist, its broad green leaves crisped and lightly crinkled at the edges and a dense spike of sessile greenish flowers crowned with a pineapple-like tuft of leafy bracts. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805); Redouté, who served as flower painter to Empress Joséphine, drew numerous bulbous plants from living specimens for the series.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Fall of the Rhine at Schaffhausen
description: The thundering Rheinfall in Switzerland, its spray rising into a churning sky encountered on Turner's first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens. The painting marks his early engagement with the Alpine sublime that would shape his Romantic vocabulary.

title: Fritillaria Imperialis
description: Fritillaria imperialis, the crown imperial, its tall leafy stem topped by a ring of pendent saffron flowers beneath a tuft of crowning leaves, each petal cupping a silvery nectar drop at its base. The lily-family plant was familiar even to non-botanists; Redoute drew it for the third volume (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Cuspidatus
description: Gladiolus cuspidatus, a tall plant rising well over a metre, carries five or six large pale-yellowish-white flowers with long, wavy, lance-shaped segments and three dark lance-shaped basal spots on the lower divisions. The plate comes from the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805), drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Junceus
description: Gladiolus junceus carries bright rose flowers in loose spikes along branching stems, the lowest segment marked half yellow and half purple at its base. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand. It appears in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Mucronatus
description: Gladiolus mucronatus, its whole surface clothed in soft whitish hairs, bears four or five purplish-red flowers whose outer segments end in a small mucronulate point. The pleated lance-shaped leaves and the rounded bulb with its white inner tunics are shown in full. From the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Orobanche
description: Gladiolus orobanche, leafless at flowering with a slender scaly stem like a broomrape, ending in a spike of seven or eight white flowers spotted yellow and edged blue. The leaves appear only after the blooms. This plate comes from the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Ringens
description: Gladiolus ringens bears blue-violet flowers with yellow markings in the throat, arranged in a loose arching spike, with sheathing leaves that exceed the stem in length. The species is distinguished by its violet-scented flowers, and the two-lipped, funnel-shaped corolla is shown in the botanical dissections at the foot of the sheet. This plate belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Undulatus
description: Gladiolus undulatus, from a white irregular tuber, carries four or five erect scentless flowers with wavy, half-reflexed segments and a slender purple-red tube. The lower segments are streaked purple in one variety. This plate appears in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Gladiolus Xanthospilus
description: Gladiolus xanthospilus, a plant with numerous lance-shaped leaves arising from an ovoid bulb, its flexed stem bearing a spike of white flowers marked with sulphur-yellow blotches at the throat and on the petal margins. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Globba Erecta
description: Globba erecta sends up erect herbaceous stems with lanceolate leaves and a terminal raceme of small flowers mottled white, yellow and red. The plate places it among the Balisiers (canna family) in Jussieu's order; the enlarged floral parts below follow the botanical convention of the day.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Heliconia Psittacorum
description: Heliconia psittacorum, a smooth banana-like stem ending in an erect spike with an orange bract tipped in black, the seven or eight orange flowers marked with black and clear yellow. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), printed in colour and hand-finished.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Hypoxis Sobolifera
description: Hypoxis sobolifera, its hairy linear-lanceolate leaves rising from a thick knotted rootstock to scapes bearing two to four yellow six-parted flowers. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), where Jussieu placed it among the Narcissus family.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Hypoxis Stellata
description: Hypoxis stellata, a single bright yellow star-shaped flower on a stiff scape, each segment marked with a brown spot at its base, above narrow leaves spread along the ground. The plate is a stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all eight folio volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Fimbriata
description: Iris fimbriata is distinguished by the fringed and shredded tips of its stigma segments, its pale blue flowers washed with white and bearing yellow spots on the larger outer lobes. The branched stem rises from a horizontal tuberous rootstock and carries several blooms in an irregular panicle. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées (1805–1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Martinicensis
description: Iris martinicensis, a solid tuber sending up a bare stem topped by a cluster of bright yellow flowers spotted with black, the segments opening in succession. The enlarged figures at the foot of the sheet show the three stamens and the short style with its yellow stigmas.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Bulbifera
description: Ixia bulbifera, distinguished by its torn scarious bracts, pale funnel-shaped flowers and small bulbs in the leaf axils of an often-branched stem. The blooms range from yellowish white to citron yellow, sometimes spotted purple at the base. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees, 1805.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Conica
description: Plate 138 shows Ixia conica, its orange flowers marked with black spots at the base of the segments and gathered into a dense rounded spike, the corolla conical before opening. The style divides into three stigmas only near the anther tips. From the third volume of Les Liliacees, 1805.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Grandiflora
description: Ixia grandiflora bears large, erect, violet-purple flowers from membranous spathes torn into narrow reflexed strips. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees, published in 1805. A white spot marks the base of each funnel-shaped lobe.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Maculata
description: Ixia maculata shows a tightly packed, nearly head-like spike of star-spread flowers, each division darker at its base than above. The text notes its countless garden varieties, a collection of which Jacquin gathered at Schonbrunn. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees in 1805.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Patens
description: Ixia patens shows a dense terminal spike of carmine-red flowers, the bell-shaped limb divided into six oblong segments white at the base. Long grown by Dutch gardeners, it was known by the common name Ixia Kermes. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Polystachia
description: Ixia polystachia bears a branched spike of bell-shaped flowers, white in one variety and red-striped in another, the three outer segments slightly longer. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees in 1805. Enlarged stamen and pistil figures sit at the foot of the sheet.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Scillaris
description: Ixia scillaris bears small rose-coloured flowers in loose elongated spikes along the stem and branches, resembling those of a squill in form and arrangement. The iris-like leaves are folded and slightly notched along their inner edge, distinguishing this species within the genus. The plate was drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté for the first volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Tricolor
description: Ixia tricolor carries three or four large flowers in a loose spike, each lobe citron-yellow at the base, brown-purple at the middle, and bright vermilion-red at the tip. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805). Below, the enlarged anthers shed a yellow pollen in the dissection figures.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Kim Hong-do
englishTitle: Ode to the Sounds of Autumn (Chuseongbudo)
description: Kim Hongdo's 1805 illustration of Ouyang Xiu's prose poem on the sounds of autumn presents a horizontal scroll pairing extensive calligraphic text on the left with a landscape at right — bare trees, a pavilion, and misty mountains rendered in delicate ink wash. Painted late in his career as Joseon Korea's leading court painter, the work fuses Chinese literary subject matter with Hongdo's characteristic atmospheric ink technique.

title: Kœmpferia Galanga
description: Kaempferia galanga, its broad ovate leaves spread flat and its white six-parted flower rising from bracts at the rootstock, with one inner segment deeply cleft. The aromatic rhizome places it in the Zingiberaceae; Redoute drew the plate for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lachenalia Angustifolia
description: Lachenalia angustifolia, the smallest of its genus, with long narrow half-cylindrical leaves and a raceme of bell-shaped flowers, dull white tipped green, on a purple-flecked stalk. Enlarged stamen and ovary figures sit at the foot of the sheet, following the botanical convention of the day.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Leucoium Æstivum
description: Leucoium aestivum, the summer snowflake, its umbel of four to six nodding white bells hung from triangular pedicels above a winged hollow stalk, each segment tipped with a green callus. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); stamen and ovary figures appear below.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Leucoium Autumnale
description: Leucoium autumnale, the autumn snowflake, its slender threadlike leaves and one or two small white nodding bells on a fine stalk. The plate belongs to the Narcissus family in the Jussieu classification line and was drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Leucoium Trichophyllum
description: Leucoium trichophyllum, with three or four very fine linear leaves and a slender stalk carrying one or two small flowers, white in one variety and rose in another. The pointed segments lack the apical callus of related snowflakes. The plate was drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lilium Martagon
description: Lilium martagon, the Turk's-cap lily, shown here in a pink-purple cultivated form, its many nodding flowers carried on a tall stem with broad ovate-lanceolate whorled leaves bearing five prominent veins. The reflexed petals and pendant posture are characteristic of the species, which ranges in colour from the typical orange-red through pink to near-white variants. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805); a seed-capsule detail appears at lower left.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lilium Pyrenaicum
description: Lilium pyrenaicum, the Pyrenean lily, its firm stem hung with one to three nodding yellow flowers whose six recurved petals carry dark inner spotting above narrow lance-shaped leaves. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the cultivated form bears more blooms than the wild plant.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Muscari Ambrosiacum
description: Muscari ambrosiacum, the musk grape hyacinth that named the genus, its ovoid white bulb sending up a dense raceme of small urn-shaped flowers in a dull greyish-yellow that turns russet after fertilisation. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Calathinus
description: Narcissus calathinus, the large-cup daffodil, a rounded bulb giving two flat linear leaves and a tall scape ending in two large yellow flowers, each with a broad petaloid cup as long as the spreading perianth lobes. From the family of Narcisses in Jussieu's classification; Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Jonquilla
description: Narcissus jonquilla, the jonquil, recognisable by its rush-like semi-cylindrical leaves and short bell-shaped cup, with two to seven small sweetly scented flowers turned to one side. The botanical text supplied with Redoute's plates notes its leaves resemble those of the rushes, the source of its name; this plate came in the third volume (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Odorus
description: Narcissus odorus, the scented daffodil, set apart by a bell-shaped cup half the length of the perianth lobes and divided into six rounded segments, carrying one to three yellow flowers twice the size of the tazetta's. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Poeticus
description: Narcissus poeticus, the poet's narcissus, a single nodding white flower on a flattened scape, its very short lemon-yellow cup crenate and rimmed with red. The plate notes some forms carry a scarlet margin and others an orange or near-yellow one; Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Pseudo-Narcissus
description: Narcissus pseudo-narcissus, the wild daffodil, its trumpet flower rising on a single scape above strap-shaped leaves from a tunicate bulb. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the stipple engraving was printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Neottia Elata
description: Neottia elata, a tall slender orchid bearing a one-sided spike of small greenish flowers above oval half-fleshy leaves, the lip pale yellow-green with a faint rose tint. From the orchid family in Jussieu's system; the enlarged figures below detail the column and its sexual parts after the convention of the period.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ornithogalum Umbellatum
description: Ornithogalum umbellatum, the common star-of-Bethlehem, with narrow channelled leaves rising from an ovoid bulb ringed with offsets, and a scape bearing white flowers whose petals are banded green on the reverse and arranged in a loose corymb-like false umbel. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pamcratium Speciosum
description: Pancratium speciosum, an umbel of five to seven large white flowers above broad lanceolate leaves, the stamens joined by a bell-shaped petal-like membrane bearing sharp pointed teeth between the filaments. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pancratium Disciforme
description: Pancratium disciforme, named for the flared membrane joining the stamen filaments, which spreads almost into a disc, above linear leaves and a scape of three white flowers in a short spathe. The Amaryllis-family plant shows its long perianth tube and orange-yellow pollen in figures below, drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pancratium Illyricum
description: Pancratium illyricum, its two-ranked blunt leaves below a flattened scape bearing an umbel of seven or eight nearly stalkless white flowers from a membranous spathe. The crown between the filaments opens star-like and splits into two-pointed lobes, a feature unique to this species. Drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pancratium Littorale
description: Pancratium littorale, with two-ranked pointed leaves and a flattened scape carrying five or six large faintly scented white flowers in an umbel. The bell-shaped membrane joining the long divergent filaments has nearly entire margins, distinguishing it within the genus. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Philipp Otto Runge
description: A close study of a hound's head in chalk and lead, the breed's soft fur and alert eye observed with quiet precision. The drawing belongs to Runge's wider effort to ground his Romantic symbolism in patient natural observation.

title: Polianthes Tuberosa
description: Polianthes tuberosa, the tuberose, a tall firm stem carrying alternate linear leaves and a long spike of fragrant white funnel-shaped flowers, often paired and wrapped in spathes. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Portrait of Pope Pius VII
description: Pope Pius VII sits three-quarter length before the viewer, clothed in richly embroidered red papal vestments over a white rochet, his hand resting on the gilded arm of a throne-like chair. Inscribed 'PARISIIS 1805', the portrait was painted by Jacques-Louis David in Paris while the pontiff remained in the city following Napoleon's coronation. A restrained and penetrating characterisation, it shows the measured authority that made David the pre-eminent portraitist of the Napoleonic era.
credit: gallerix.org

title: Scilla Amœna
description: Scilla amoena, with channelled basal leaves and angular scapes each ending in one to three amethyst-blue flowers larger than those of other squills. The source describes the flowers as bell-shaped in bud, opening to six spreading segments with a longitudinal nerve and two small white spots at the base. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805), drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Scilla Peruviana
description: Plate 167 shows Scilla peruviana, with linear leaves spread in a wide rosette and a stout scape ending in a dense conical raceme of many blue-violet flowers. The lower dissection figures show the stamens and the three-angled, three-celled capsule typical of the squills.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Scilla Umbellata
description: Scilla umbellata, set apart by its low habit and few pale-blue flowers arranged in a false umbel, with linear channelled leaves shorter than the scape. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the dissection figures show the stamens and three-celled capsule.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Self portrait of Louis-Leopold Boilly
description: A self-portrait of Boilly in middle age, bust-length and turned slightly toward the viewer. Oil on canvas, about 1805, in the collection of the Château de Versailles. The painter renders his own features with the close finish he applied to his commissioned heads.

title: Sisyrinchium Bermudiana
description: Sisyrinchium bermudiana, with a flattened two-edged stem, iris-like fan of sheathing leaves, and wheel-shaped flowers of blue mixed with yellow clustered within spathes. Jussieu's line places it among the Iridaceae; the three stamens are joined by their filaments into a cylindrical tube.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Sisyrinchium Elegans
description: Sisyrinchium elegans, growing from a small ovoid bulb to a slender stem bearing a long sword-shaped leaf and a single large six-segmented flower with a yellow centre, the segments marked with a longitudinal greenish blotch. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805–1807); the plate includes a dissection showing the flattened open perianth and the pistil.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Sunset on the River
description: An English river caught at the end of the day, with rushes and a low bank silhouetted against burning sky. The work belongs to the loose Thames oil sketches Turner made from his boat around Walton and Windsor.

title: The Deluge
description: An early biblical disaster scene depicting the universal flood, with massed bodies struggling against rising water beneath churning storm clouds. Turner builds the composition from a baroque diagonal of light, a precedent for his later sublime catastrophes.

title: The Hülsenbeck Children
dateCreated: between 1805 and 1806 Romanticism (second half of 18 th century –first half of 19 th century )
description: Three young children of the Hülsenbeck family are depicted in a Hamburg garden dominated by tall sunflowers: the eldest stands to the right holding a hoop, the middle child brandishes a whip, and the youngest sits in a small wooden cart at left. Runge invests the scene with symbolic weight, treating childhood as a metaphysical state within his broader Romantic vision. The painting, dated 1805–06, is held at the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

title: The Shipwreck
description: Survivors clinging to lifeboats amid mountainous green seas, the doomed vessel rolling beyond. Engraved by Charles Turner, this was the first of the artist's canvases reproduced as a mezzotint, spreading his fame as a painter of catastrophe.
credit: Google Arts & Culture — LwFch0SXuzBAIw Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N00476&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

title: Tradescantia Discolor
description: Tradescantia discolor, recognised by leaves green above and deep red-purple beneath, with a head of small whitish flowers cradled in two reddish boat-shaped bracts. The work places it among the rushes of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 3 of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Trillium Rhomboideum
description: Trillium rhomboideum, growing from a thick rhizome to a whorl of three rhomboidal leaves from which a single stalked flower rises on a short scape. The work places it among the Asparagaceae of Jussieu and distinguishes it from Trillium sessile by its stalked bloom; the plate appeared in Volume 3 of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Trillum Sessile
description: Trillium sessile, growing from a thick horizontal rhizome, its whorl of three broad mottled leaves — marked with dark and glaucous green — bearing a single erect flower of deep crimson-red above them on a visible peduncle. The text distinguishes it from related trilliums by its variegated foliage, likened in colour to that of the dog's-tooth violet. Redouté drew it for Volume 3 of Les Liliacées (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Tritoma Media
description: Tritoma media, its long drooping keeled leaves below a stout scape ending in a dense raceme of tubular flowers shading from pale yellow to orange-red. The text notes the colour varies with season, redder in spring blooms; the plate appeared in Volume 3 of Les Liliacees (1805).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Tulipa Sylvestris
description: Tulipa sylvestris, the wild tulip, its single yellow flower held upright when fully open, the six oblong segments slightly bearded at their tips; the three outer segments carry a greenish tinge on their exterior face. A small engraving of the stamens and pistil appears to the lower right. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805), the accompanying text noting that the bud nods before opening but the flower stands erect once in bloom.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Willows beside a Stream
description: A screen of willows leans over still water in an unforced piece of Thames-side observation. It belongs to the group of Thames oil sketches on canvas that Turner kept in his studio rather than exhibiting; it entered the nation with the Turner Bequest in 1856.

title: Windsor Castle from the Thames
description: The royal castle rides above the river on its chalk bluff, painted from Turner's boat on one of his summer Thames campaigns. Sky and water are set down in long, wet sweeps that leave the paint visibly mobile.

title: Linlithgow Palace
description: Linlithgow Palace rises through a warm golden haze above a wooded landscape, with bathers in the foreground pool and figures resting on the bank. The oil painting, dated circa 1806, translates a motif Turner drew on his Scottish tours into a richly atmospheric composition. It is held at the Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool.

title: Newark Abbey
description: The ruined arches of Newark Priory on the River Wey in Surrey appear as a faint silhouette through riverside trees at dusk, the foreground occupied by moored barges — one glowing with an interior fire — and quietly reflective water. Dated between 1806 and 1807, the canvas is held at the Yale Center for British Art, and exemplifies Turner's picturesque treatment of Gothic ruins in the English landscape.

title: Peter on the sea
description: Christ stretches out his hand to a sinking Peter on the Sea of Galilee, the figures reduced to clear, near-archaic outlines. Runge's interpretation of the Gospel episode reflects his ambition to fuse landscape, religion, and Romantic symbolism.
credit: 1st-art-gallery.com

title: Shipping at the Mouth of the Thames
description: Working vessels labouring in the Thames estuary chop, sails braced against a low, weather-laden sky. The painting belongs to Turner's productive run of estuary subjects answering his rivalry with the marine tradition of van de Velde.
credit: Google Arts & Culture — qgGcWeWQCxwJMQ Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N02702&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

title: The Card Sharp on the Boulevard
description: A card game at a makeshift table on a sunlit Parisian boulevard, a sharper at work among a mixed crowd of players and onlookers. Oil on panel, 24 by 33 cm, in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. Boilly showed it in 1808 with a pendant of young Savoyards displaying their marmot, among his first street scenes of everyday Paris.

title: The Death of Nelson
description: Vice-Admiral Nelson collapses on the quarterdeck of HMS Victory at Trafalgar, surrounded by officers and ratings in a tightly compressed crowd. West composed the 1806 canvas, now at the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool, in deliberate echo of his own Death of General Wolfe, applying his epic modern-history formula to a second imperial martyr.

title: The Victory Returning from Trafalgar
description: Nelson's flagship shown in three rotated views entering Sheerness with the admiral's body aboard, after Turner sketched her at anchor. The triple study reflects his marine fascination and the national mourning that followed Trafalgar.

title: Walton bridges
description: Sheep and shepherds gather on the riverbank below two bridges at Walton, one a timber lock structure in the foreground and the other a broad stone bridge spanning the Thames beyond. Turner painted the scene around 1806 during his sketching tours along the river, and the work is held by the National Gallery of Victoria.

title: Washington at Dorchester Heights
description: George Washington in Continental uniform stands beside his horse on the Boston-area hill where his artillery emplacement forced the British evacuation in March 1776. Stuart painted the full-length composition in 1806 for the Boston town fathers; it now hangs at the Museum of Fine Arts and remains the city's official Washington portrait.
credit: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, online database

title: Weir and Cattle
description: Cattle wade in the slow water below a country weir in one of Turner's pastoral Thames-valley sketches. The thin oil handling and silvery palette recall his admiration for Cuyp.

title: Abama Ossifraga
description: Abama ossifraga, the bog asphodel, its narrow iris-like leaves rising to a cylindrical spike of six-parted yellowish-green flowers. The supplied text places it in the rush family (Joncées); the enlarged stamen and seed figures at the foot follow the botanical convention of the period.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Albuca Abyssinica
description: Albuca abyssinica, distinguished by nearly stalkless flowers arranged in an elongated spike above narrow channelled leaves. The text records its Abyssinian origin; the plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1807.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Allium Foliosum
description: Allium foliosum, close to the chive but carrying one leaf near the base of its stem, ending in a tight rounded head of pale violet flowers. The plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); a white-flowered variety was found on the high Pyrenean summits.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Allium Mutabile
description: Allium mutabile, its loose umbel mixing small red star-shaped flowers with little white bulbils among the slender pedicels. The plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), the basal leaves channelled below and rolled bristle-like toward the tip.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Allium Nutans
description: Allium nutans, its flattened two-angled scape bearing a tight head-like umbel that nods in bud before straightening, the flowers pale lilac flushed rose. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the species is close to Allium senescens.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Allium Roseum
description: Allium roseum, its bulb shedding stalked offsets, the scape topped by a flat fifteen- to twenty-rayed umbel of pink flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the figures below show the yellow anthers and the rounded seed capsule.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Asphodelus Luteus
description: Asphodelus luteus, the yellow asphodel, rising from a cluster of fleshy yellow roots, its stem nearly hidden by numerous linear leaves and topped by a long dense raceme of large yellow flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the round three-celled capsule is shown below.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Bulbocodium Vernum
description: Bulbocodium vernum, the spring meadow saffron, two or three lilac flowers sitting almost on the bulb among lance-shaped leaves, each bloom split to the base into six narrow segments. Redoute placed it near the colchicums and crocuses; the work was issued in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Butomus Umbellatus
description: Butomus umbellatus, the flowering rush, its triangular basal leaves below a tall scape ending in an umbel of fifteen to twenty rose-coloured flowers. The text notes it as the only known plant whose flower carries nine stamens and six styles, both shown enlarged in the dissection figures below.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Canna Indica
description: Canna indica, the Indian shot, with thick creeping roots, ovate pointed leaves, and red flowers washed with yellow in a loose terminal spike. The plate places it in the canna family (Cannaceae); the enlarged stamen and style figures below follow the botanical convention of the period.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Cassiobury Park: Reaping
description: Harvesters work an open field on the Earl of Essex's estate at Cassiobury in Hertfordshire. The painting was a private commission produced alongside a series of watercolours of the park. It shows Turner extending his Claudean pastoral mode to a contemporary English country-house setting.

title: Cliveden on Thames
description: A pastoral prospect along the Thames at Cliveden in Buckinghamshire, with cattle near the water's edge and trees softening the middle distance. Turner treats the open landscape with a warm, suffused light that dissolves firm outlines into haze. Painted in 1807, the oil sketch is held at Tate Britain (N01180).
credit: Google Arts & Culture — AAF7MnUg-TIdUQ Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N01180&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

title: Colchicum Autumnale
description: Colchicum autumnale, the autumn crocus, its pale lilac flowers rising in autumn on long tubes that serve as stalks, the leaves and capsule following in spring. The plate shows the six stamens and three long styles enlarged below, a botanical convention of the period.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Colchicum Variegatum
description: Colchicum variegatum, the wavy-leaved meadow saffron, its flower segments marked with small white and lilac squares set like a chequerboard. The text likens this tessellated colouring to that of the snake's head fritillary; flowers appear in autumn, the wavy leaves in spring.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Commelina Africana
description: Commelina africana, its lance-shaped leaves on a glabrous jointed stem and its flowers held within a folded heart-shaped bract, the three inner segments a soft matt yellow. Redouté drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), the source text noting the similarities and differences between the outer calyx-like lobes and the larger, delicate inner segments.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Commelina Communis
description: Commelina communis, the Asiatic dayflower, its lance-shaped leaves on a hollow ascending stem and its flowers enclosed in a heart-shaped spathe, the two upper inner segments a clear blue. The text describes six unequal stamens, three of them bearing fertile anthers, shown enlarged at the foot of the sheet.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Commelina Zanonia
description: Commelina zanonia, a dayflower with broad lance-shaped leaves clasping jointed, sheathed stems and small three-petalled white flowers opening at the upper nodes. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées, the plate dating from between 1807 and 1809.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Convallaria Majalis
description: Convallaria majalis, lily of the valley, its two glossy lance-shaped leaves beside a leafless arching scape hung with five or six nodding white bells. The plate notes the fruit as a red three-celled berry. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and the work appeared in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Crinum Giganteum
description: Crinum giganteum drawn for Les Liliacées, its large bulb sending up broad leaves and an umbel of wide white trumpet flowers with open, spreading lobes. The plate dates from between 1807 and 1809 and appears in the fourth volume of the series.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Crocus Luteus
description: Plate 196 shows Crocus luteus, its flattened corm sending up tufts of grassy leaves and a yellow bell of six lobes streaked outside with brown or violet lines, the three style branches enlarged below. Each plate was stipple-engraved, printed in colour, and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Cross in the Mountains
description: A wayside crucifix stands atop a fir-clad alpine peak, gilded by rays of an unseen setting sun. Originally an altarpiece for the Tetschen chapel, the work provoked the so-called Ramdohr controversy by daring to treat pure landscape as a vehicle of religious revelation.

title: Cyrtanthus Vittatus
description: Cyrtanthus vittatus, drawn for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), showing a bulb with strap leaves and a scape of flowers whose open white petals are striped pink-red on the reverse, alongside slender pink-flushed buds. The plate belongs to the amaryllis family of the Jussieu classification.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Erythronium Dens Canis
description: Erythronium dens-canis, the dog's-tooth violet, named for its tooth-shaped bulb segments, with two mottled basal leaves and a solitary nodding flower whose six segments reflex sharply upward. Redouté depicted two specimens for the fourth volume (1807), both in the pink-purple range; the source text also notes a yellow variety C among the colour forms known for this lily-family plant.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Eucomis Punctata
description: Eucomis punctata, its long wavy leaves spotted beneath with small black points and a cylindrical raceme topped by a tuft of leafy bracts. The plate notes its close resemblance to the royal eucomis figured in the third volume; this one appeared in the fourth (1807) of Les Liliacees.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Fritillaria Melegris
description: Fritillaria meleagris, the snake's-head fritillary, rising from a solid bulb on a slender stem with narrow glaucous leaves and a nodding bell-shaped flower marked in a purple-and-white chequer. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume (1807); colour variants run from pure white to almost wholly purple.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Galanthus Nivalis
description: Galanthus nivalis, the common snowdrop, with an ovoid bulb sending up two narrow leaves and a slender scape bearing a single nodding white flower. Its three outer segments are shorter, notched, and green-tipped, while the three inner segments are milky white and oblong. Redouté placed it among the narcissus family (Narcisses); the plate appeared in the fourth volume (1807) of Les Liliacées.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Game of Billiards
description: A billiard room crowded with players and spectators, a woman taking her shot at the centre of the table. Oil on canvas, 56 by 81 cm, in the Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg, dated 1807. The presence of women at the game reflects the looser social manners of the First Empire.
credit: This file was derived from: Louis-Léopold Boilly - Game of Billiards - WGA02350.jpg :

title: Hæmanthus Multiflorus
description: Haemanthus multiflorus, a spotted scape bearing a globe-like umbel of bright red flowers with long projecting filaments, set beside an erect tuft of ribbed leaves. The plate belongs to the Narcisses family in Jussieu's order; Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Hyacinthus Serotinus
description: Hyacinthus serotinus, an ash-red scape carrying a one-sided raceme of dingy greenish-yellow flowers, the bell-shaped perigone in two ranks of lobes. A three-celled capsule figure sits below; the plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Hyacinthus Viridis
description: Hyacinthus viridis, a slender scape with a loose raceme of six or seven green flowers whose outer segments taper almost to threads, set above narrow linear leaves. The plate was drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Monnieri
description: Iris monnieri, a tall species reaching one or two metres, its sword-shaped leaves sheathing the stem below three or four large yellow flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the inner segments run longer than the stigmas, setting it apart from the yellow flag.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Persica
description: Iris persica, the Persian iris, shown in flower with its narrow leaves in a plate from Redoute's Les Liliacees. The work was issued in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816, its plates printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Pratensis
description: Iris pratensis sends up slender hollow stems from a fibrous root, each bearing three or four medium-sized blue flowers; the very narrow grass-like leaves may reach twice the height of the stems. The outer segments are spatulate, with a yellowish claw veined in violet or blue, and the inner segments are a deeper blue-purple. Redouté drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807–1809).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Pseudacorus
description: Iris pseudacorus, the common yellow flag of Europe, with entirely yellow beardless flowers whose inner segments fall short of the stigmas. Its sheathing sword-shaped leaves shorten upward into bracts; Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Scorpioides
description: Plate 211 shows Iris scorpioides, its glossy channelled leaves rising around three successive blue flowers with a long slender perigone tube and very small inner lobes. From the Iridaceae as classified on the sheet (Triandria monogynia in the Linnaean system); the stipple engraving was printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Iris Xyphioides
description: Plate 212 shows Iris xyphioides, an ovoid bulb sending up a stem to four or six decimetres with two large blue flowers tinged violet, some specimens speckled with darker spots. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine; this plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees, 1807.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ixia Plantaginea
description: Ixia plantaginea bears many small deep-blue flowers arranged in two opposite ranks along a compressed, two-edged stem, forming a dense imbricated spike. The broad lower leaf curves like a scythe, while the source text notes that small bulbils sometimes develop in place of flowers between the bracts. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées, dated between 1807 and 1809.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Leucoium Grandiflorum
description: Leucoium grandiflorum, growing from a cherry-sized bulb with narrow grassy leaves and a slender stalk bearing two white nodding flowers, each segment veined and bell-arranged. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); de Candolle's text records that the fruit was never seen.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lilium Bulbiferum
description: Lilium bulbiferum, the orange or fire lily, named for the small dark bulbils that form in its leaf axils. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), one of the true lilies among the many monocot families the work covers. It was printed in colour from a single plate and hand-finished.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Lilium Candidum
description: Lilium candidum, the Madonna lily, with its erect stem, lance-shaped leaves and trumpet-formed white flowers. The plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), a stipple engraving printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand in watercolour, the method used throughout the eight folio volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Madame Saint-Ange Chevrier
description: Beskrivning på inventarieblanketten: Målningen föreställer en kvinna i ett landskap, sittande på en sten intill en trädstam.
credit: Cecilia Heisser / Nationalmuseum

title: Massonia Pustulata
description: Massonia pustulata, a low Cape bulb of the hyacinth family, set with its paired broad ground-hugging leaves and a sessile tufted cluster of flowers emerging between their bases. Redouté drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), the plate printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Mayanthemum Bifolium
description: Maianthemum bifolium, the two-leaved May lily, shown with its paired heart-based leaves and a terminal raceme of small white flowers, alongside a fruiting specimen bearing dark berries. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Mayanthemum Canadense
description: Maianthemum canadense, the Canada May lily, distinguished from its European cousin by near-sessile, more oblong leaves, glabrous on both faces, with sharper reticulated veining. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Muscari Comosum
description: Muscari comosum, the tassel grape hyacinth, drawn with its raceme topped by a distinctive tuft of erect, violet-blue sterile flowers above the horizontal fertile ones. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), illustrated by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Muscari Racemosum
description: Muscari racemosum, growing from an ovoid bulb with several offsets, its slender drooping linear leaves and erect scape carrying a short, tight raceme of deep blue-violet flowers. The whole plant is glabrous, the small bracts borne on roughly horizontal pedicels.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Candidissimus
description: Narcissus candidissimus, the white daffodil, drawn from a bulb of the Narcisse family with strap-shaped leaves and a pale flower above. The plate was issued in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), a stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Narcissus Gouani
description: Narcissus gouani, Gouan's daffodil, a solitary fragrant flower on a sword-shaped compressed scape, its pale-yellow funnel perianth set off by a deeper orange-yellow cup with crenate wavy margins. The plant rises from a tunicate bulb surrounded by close-set tunics, with flat linear leaves shorter than the scape. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées (between 1807 and 1809).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Newark Abbey on the River Wey
description: The ruined Augustinian priory of Newark stands above the still waters of the Wey, framed by trees and scattered cattle. Turner adopts the picturesque vocabulary of the topographical watercolorists, softened by an early painterly attention to reflected light.

title: Ornithogalum Fistulosum
description: Ornithogalum fistulosum, its slender hollow filiform basal leaves rising from a small ovoid bulb, with scattered yellow six-parted flowers on hairy white pedicels. Floral dissection figures at the foot of the sheet enlarge details of the flower and ovary after the botanical convention of the period. Redouté drew this species for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Ornithogalum Pyrenaicum
description: Ornithogalum pyrenaicum, the Pyrenean star-of-Bethlehem, with long drooping strap-shaped leaves and a bare scape rising to a long spike of small whitish-green flowers. Redouté drew this species for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807); the plates were printed by stipple engraving and finished by hand in colour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Pancratium Croceum
description: Pancratium croceum, distinct among the genus for its saffron-yellow flowers rather than white, borne in a nodding umbel from a split three-valved spathe atop a glaucous scape. The stamen filaments are joined by a toothed membrane into a cylindrical cup. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Paris Quadrifolia
description: Paris quadrifolia (herb-paris), a slender stem rising from a creeping rhizome and topped by four whorled ovate leaves and a single greenish flower whose eight narrow segments stand in two ranks above a dark rounded ovary that ripens into a black berry. The plate, from the fourth volume (1807), includes dissection figures showing the open flower, anther, fruit, and seed.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Phalangium Bicolor
description: Phalangium bicolor, its grassy basal leaves below a branched panicle of six-parted flowers that are rose-violet outside and white within. The plate, from the fourth volume (1807), records the woolly-haired filaments and the spherical three-celled capsule. Redoute placed the genus among the asphodels on the Jussieu line.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Phalangium Elatum
description: Phalangium elatum, a member of the asphodel group, showing broad strap-like basal leaves and multiple tall branching stems bearing scattered small white six-parted flowers in a loose panicle. Redouté drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Polygonatum Multiflorum
description: Polygonatum multiflorum, an arching cylindrical stem with alternate clasping leaves and clusters of pendulous white tubular flowers tipped with six short green teeth. The plate, from the fourth volume (1807), notes the pea-sized blue-black berry. Redoute drew it among the asparagus family on the Jussieu line.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Scilla Lilio-Hyacinthus
description: Scilla lilio-hyacinthus, notable for a scaly fleshy bulb resembling that of a true lily, with bright-green oblong leaves and a slender scape ending in five or six soft-blue flowers. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the fruit is a three-angled capsule.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Scilla non Scripta
description: Scilla non-scripta, the English bluebell, with linear basal leaves and an arched scape ending in a short one-sided nodding raceme of fragrant blue bell-shaped flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Scilla Obtusifolia
description: Scilla obtusifolia, a blunt-leaved squill, drawn with its rounded bulb, short broad basal leaves, and two scapes each bearing a raceme of pink flowers. The plate appeared in Les Liliacées (published 1807–1809) by Pierre-Joseph Redouté, and includes small dissection figures at the margins.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Scilla Patula
description: Scilla patula, the spreading squill, with broad leaves lying on the ground and an upright ovoid raceme of blue bell-shaped flowers that nod once fully open, each pedicel set with two awl-shaped blue bracts. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Smilacina Racemosa
description: Smilacina racemosa, its arching stem set with ovate ribbed leaves and tipped by a branched raceme of small white flowers that give way to red-speckled berries. The work places it among the asparagus family of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 4 of Les Liliacees (1807).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Smilacina Stellata
description: Smilacina stellata, an asparagus-family plant whose leafy stem ends in small white star-shaped flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), printed as a stipple engraving in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: The Battle of Trafalgar
description: A close-quarters view of Nelson's flagship Victory at Trafalgar, taken from the mizen-shrouds rather than the more conventional broadside vantage. Turner had boarded Victory on her return to the Medway and used the sketches he made there to anchor the smoke-wreathed scene.

title: The Junction of the Thames and the Medway
description: An estuary scene with merchantmen and a small boat tossed in choppy water where the two rivers meet. Turner builds the squally light from layered glazes, showing his early debt to Dutch marine painters.

title: The Reading of the Bulletin of the Grand...
description: A family gathered around a printed Napoleonic bulletin, tracing the army's progress on a map. Oil on canvas, 44 by 59 cm, in the Saint Louis Art Museum, shown at the Salon of 1808. The scene follows the campaign of the War of the Fourth Coalition against Prussia.

title: The Thames near Windsor
description: A quiet reach of the upper Thames painted from the boat Turner had fitted out as a floating studio. The fluid handling belongs to the Thames oil sketches in which he loosened his manner before the public ever saw it.

title: Tradescantia Erecta
description: Tradescantia erecta, an upright branching plant with sheathing ovate leaves and tight terminal clusters of nodding flowers whose three inner segments are deep blue. The plate appeared in Volume 4 of Les Liliacees (1807), printed as a stipple engraving and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Tree Tops and Sky
description: Most of the panel is given over to evening sky, with foliage massed at the lower edge and Guildford Castle barely indicated. The composition foreshadows Turner's later willingness to let weather dominate topography.

title: Tulipa Oculus-Solis
