description: Carl Joseph Begas assembled his extended family — including his wife, multiple children, and other relatives — in a spacious domestic interior for this large group portrait, painted in 1821. The figures are arranged across the room in animated domestic activity: a woman sews, a young woman plays guitar, children attend to a dog, and the father stands at centre holding a conductor's baton. Visible through an open window at right is a Gothic church tower.
credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"b/begas/carl/family"

title: Rosa Aciphylla
description: Rosa aciphylla, a low shrub under three feet with stiff dark-brown branches and sparse hooked prickles, its small flowers carrying five tiny petals of white faintly tinged with pink. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in three folio volumes; this plate belongs to the 1821 volume.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Alba
description: A form of Rosa alba, the white rose, its pale blooms set among grey-green foliage on an upright shrub. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour, the method used across all three volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Alpina
description: A variegated form of the Alpine rose, Rosa alpina, its smallish petals streaked bright red on a pink ground, the thornless shrub reaching three or four feet. Redoute drew it for Les Roses (1817-1824); this plate is from the 1821 volume.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Alpina Vulgaris
description: The common Alpine rose, Rosa alpina vulgaris, its pink flowers borne on smooth thornless stems above toothed foliage. Les Roses documents species roses and early garden cultivars before the rise of the modern hybrid.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Andegavensis
description: Rosa andegavensis, the Anjou rose, with five-petalled flowers that begin pale pink and turn white, the gland-bristled calyx and stalk shown beneath sharply toothed foliage. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; this plate belongs to the 1821 volume.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Banksiæ
description: Rosa banksiae, the Lady Banks rose, a rampant near-thornless climber bearing small sweetly scented flowers in primrose-like umbels of ten or more on long stalks. The leaflets are glossy on both faces; Redoute drew the rose for the 1821 volume of Les Roses.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Campanulata
description: A white-flowered form of Rosa campanulata, the bell rose, its pale blooms set among toothed foliage. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the most celebrated rose collection of the age, from which Les Roses grew.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Candolleana
description: Rosa candolleana, the Candolle rose, a graceful four- or five-foot shrub with red-brown stems thick with small prickles, its five white petals banded outside with bright-pink stripes. An ovoid red hip ripens after flowering, shown in this 1821 plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Canina
description: Rosa canina, the wild dog rose, with pale-pink single flowers, toothed leaflets, and arching stems set with curved prickles. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, the most famous rose iconography ever made and the record of species roses before the modern hybrid.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: An anemone-flowered cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia anemonoides, its pink corolla in five or six ranks with the short inner petals folded and cupped like an anemone. The variety can be kept only by grafting, then layered to raise own-root plants, per Thory's text.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: A red-flowered cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia in the form called the Cumberland rose, its full double bloom above toothed leaflets and prickled stems. The plate is a stipple engraving printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: A celery-leaved cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia bipinnata, its finely divided leaflets set below a full pink double flower. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the rose collection from which Les Roses grew.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: A crenate-leaved cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia crenata, with rounded leaflets deeply scalloped and heart-shaped at the base, below a many-petalled pink flower whose inner petals are crumpled. Thory records the bloom as scented, though less so than the common cabbage rose.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: A leafy-bracted cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia foliacea, its pink double flower set among enlarged leaf-like bracts at the calyx. Les Roses was issued in three folio volumes between 1817 and 1824, this plate in the second.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Collina
description: A hill rose, Rosa collina fastigiata, nearly scentless pink flowers arranged in an umbel above singly toothed leaflets on a shrub seven or eight feet high. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the flower's parts, a botanical convention of the period.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Damascena
description: Rosa damascena, the damask rose grown as the Rosier de Cels, its pink double flower set above grey-green foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Damascena Aurora
description: Rosa damascena in its Aurora form, a full bloom of six or seven rows of petals in rose tinted toward yellow, clustered in an umbel above five rounded leaflets. The strongly arching petiole sets this variety apart. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Dumetorum
description: Rosa dumetorum, a wild rose of woods and hedges near Paris, its small five-petalled flowers of very pale pink clustered in a short tight corymb. A spherical hip ripens bright red. The shrub rises to six feet, the flower small for its vigour, with hooked prickles paired near the stipules.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica grown as a Provins rose, its rose-purple bloom set above the toothed leaflets of the French rose. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which grew out of Empress Josephine's celebrated rose collection at Malmaison, where he served as her flower painter.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica grown as the Rosier de France, a deep-toned French rose set above its coarsely toothed leaflets. The stipple plate was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica pontiana, the rose of Andre du Pont, a bushy Provins shrub bearing large bright-red flowers of seven or eight petal ranks with a light fragrance. Its leaflets are firm and finely double-toothed on hairy stalks. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica purpurea velutina parva, a low Provins variety with trailing branches and medium flowers of three petal ranks, brilliant purple shading to a velvety violet over golden stamens. It was raised from seed by the nurseryman Van Eeden of Haarlem, who used it to plant the gardens of Malmaison in 1810.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica purpuro-violacea magna, the rose called l'Eveque, an old Provins variety with broad purple-violet petals heart-notched at the tip and gathered around a central tuft of styles. Its leaves carry five firm ovate leaflets, hairless above and downy beneath. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica regalis, the Royal Provins, a semi-double rose of four or five petal ranks in a pink deeper than the common cabbage rose, its blooms often more than three inches across. A few central stamens have turned into small crumpled petals. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Geminata
description: Rosa geminata, the twin-flowered rose, with branches that arch and lie along the ground like the field rose, bearing five large satin-white petals tinged faintly with pink. The calyx tube swells at the middle between the forms of the white and damask roses. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Hudsoniana
description: Rosa hudsoniana scandens, a climbing Hudson rose able to cover arbours, its smooth red-brown branches free of prickles. The solitary or paired flowers carry three or four ranks of soft pink petals and open in May. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plates.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Hudsoniana
description: Rosa hudsoniana subcorymbosa, a Hudson rose of two or three feet with thornless reddish branches and elliptical leaflets, green above and glaucous beneath. Its flowers gather in a loose corymb and show five or six ranks of soft pink petals around a sessile head of stigmas. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica
description: Rosa indica multipetala, a Bengal rose forming a bushy shrub of three or four feet, its green branches armed with strong reddish hooked prickles. The double flowers, deeper pink than the common China rose, open from a bright-red bud, the crumpled central petals nearly hiding the stamens. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica
description: Rosa indica pannosa, the Bengal bichonne, a China cultivar under a foot and a half with concave frizzled petals of purple streaked in paler tones that give a marked cinnamon scent as they open. It was raised from seed about a dozen years earlier by Gauche, a Paris florist-gardener, who introduced it to foreign nurseries.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica
description: Rosa indica in a near-white Bengal form, its pale petals set above glossy leaflets on a slender stem. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica
description: Rosa indica in a crimson-violet form, its nearly full corolla gathered in an umbel at the branch tips above five or seven pointed leaflets edged in colour. The text marks it as a sub-variety of the crimson-flowered Indian rose, set apart by its deep violet-crimson tone.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica Pumila
description: A single-flowered dwarf Bengal rose, its five white petals washed with pink rounded at the tip above small glossy leaflets, with oval pale-red hips. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; the stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Inermis
description: Rosa inermis, the thornless rose, a dense bush four or five feet high with smooth green branches free of prickles and soft-pink double flowers two inches or more across. Thory's text notes it as one of the first roses to flower in the garden each year.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Longifolia
description: Rosa longifolia, the peach-leaved rose, with long acuminate leaflets and ten to twelve uneven soft-pink petals sometimes flecked white, the inner ones crumpled and rolled at the centre, and an oval reddening hip. Thory's text reports it native to the East Indies, where its near-thornless stem grows tall.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Malmun­dariensis
description: Rosa malmundariensis, the Malmedy rose, a bush six or seven feet tall with mixed straight and hooked prickles and five very pale-pink petals notched at the heart, with large rounded red hips. Thory's text records that Dr Le Jeune found it on the mountains near Malmedy.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Mollissima
description: Rosa mollissima, a four-foot rose of the soft-leaved group whose oval leaflets are so downy they feel like fine cloth, bearing flowers of four ranks of petals in a softened carmine and white. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Roses, issued in 1821.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Multiflora
description: Rosa multiflora in a flesh-pink form, its many small flowers clustered along arching canes above toothed leaflets. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Multiflora
description: Rosa multiflora in a broad-leaved purple form, its flowers larger than the pink type and its leaflets three or four times bigger, rounded and broad. Thory's text records that Noisette introduced it to France, having found it near London grown from seed received from Japan.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: rosa nivea
description: Rosa nivea, a thornless shrub barely two feet high with glossy three-part leaves and large, scentless, snow-white flowers about three inches across above pointed white buds. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: rosa noisettiana
description: Rosa noisettiana, a tall shrub bearing clusters of pale rose-washed double flowers that open in succession at the branch tips, set among five to seven leaflets. Named for Philippe Noisette, it carried as many as a hundred and thirty blooms in a single panicle. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: rosa orbessanea
description: Rosa orbessanea, the Rosier d'Orbessan, shown in flower with its foliage on a single folio sheet. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in three volumes between 1817 and 1824; the plate was stipple-engraved, printed in colour, and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Parviflora
description: Rosa parviflora, a low North American shrub reaching about two feet, its double flowers a pretty rose colour paler at the centre than the edge, above five-leaflet foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pimpinellifolia
description: Rosa pimpinellifolia in a white double form, the burnet rose with small leaflets and pale blooms. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Roses (1821); Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the accompanying botanical text.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pimpinellifolia Major
description: A sub-variety of the burnet rose with five large petals irregularly streaked in greyish-white, pale rose, and deeper pink, yellow toward the claw, above leaflets in sevens to elevens. The branches bristle with many fine, nearly straight prickles, and the small hips ripen from red to black. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pomponia
description: A nearly single form of the pompon rose, a slender shrub under two feet with flowers of six or seven petals, less prickly than the double pompon. Its small elongated red hips often abort before ripening. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Roses (1821).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pumila
description: Rosa pumila, a German sub-shrub to about a foot and a half with firm five-part leaves and fragrant flowers of five large petals, whitish outside and light purple within, above pear-shaped hips that turn reddish or orange and persist through winter. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rapa
description: Rosa rapa in a semi-double form, the Rosier Turneps, shown in flower with its foliage. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Roses (1821); the stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rosenbergiana
description: Rosa rosenbergiana, a very bushy shrub to about three feet with yellowish prickles, oval crenate leaflets, and umbel-like clusters of many-petalled white flowers tinged rose at the centre. The turbinate calyx tubes bristle with small prickles like the branches. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubiginosa
description: Rosa rubiginosa in a densely prickled form, its branches bristling with unequal straight spines below seven-leaflet foliage and small pale-pink five-petalled flowers borne in twos and threes. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubiginosa
description: Rosa rubiginosa in its woodland eglantine form, a tall briar with hooked spines, five pale-green leaflets and small soft-pink flowers notched at the petal tips. The ovoid hips ripen red and keep a few of the bristles from the young calyx tube.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubiginosa
description: Rosa rubiginosa, here the form named for Queen Elizabeth, with its glandular sweetbriar foliage and prickled stems. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the rose collection from which Les Roses grew.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubiginosa
description: A semi-double sweetbriar, Rosa rubiginosa, nursery-grown as the small Hesse rose, its tender-pink flowers carrying ten to twenty notched petals above apple-scented leaves. The orange-red hips stay nearly smooth at maturity and persist a long time.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sempervirens
description: Rosa sempervirens in a broad-leaved form, the evergreen climbing rose with its glossy persistent foliage and white flowers. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates throughout Les Roses.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sempervirens
description: Rosa sempervirens, the evergreen climbing rose, its stems reaching fifteen feet to clamber over shrubs and trees, with firm glossy leaflets and fragrant white five-petalled flowers in small clusters. The styles fuse into a short bristled column and the small round hips ripen red into winter.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sepium
description: A near-double form of Rosa sepium, the hedge rose, its small spaced leaflets glandular beneath and four or five ranks of pale-red petals whitening toward the claw. The styles gather almost smooth in a bundle, and the ovoid calyx tube is hairless.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sepium
description: A pink-flowered hedge rose, Rosa sepium, tall and branching with whitish hooked spines and small leaflets glandular beneath. The five petals open soft pink but lose colour and whiten within hours, especially in full sun, above smooth ovoid hips.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Tomentosa
description: A many-petalled form of Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, with its softly haired leaflets and full pink flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Tomentosa
description: Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, its leaflets clothed both sides with soft pressed hairs and its pale-pink flowers above elongated ovoid hips. Josephine Redoute discovered it near Paris in the woods of Meudon in 1817, where it had escaped earlier botanists.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Villosa
description: Rosa villosa in its turpentine-scented form, a bushy shrub bearing small five-petalled flowers that are red above and pale toward the base, set among large oval leaflets edged with sticky glandular hairs. The crushed foliage gives off a strong turpentine odour. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: The Hay Wain
description: A wooden hay cart fords the millpond at Flatford on the Stour, with Willy Lott's cottage to the left and a slow bank of cumulus overhead. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1821, the six-foot canvas was shown at the 1824 Paris Salon, where it won a gold medal and influenced Delacroix and the young Barbizon painters.
credit: National Gallery, London via gallerix.ru

title: The Sisters Zénaïde and Charlotte Bonaparte
description: Joseph Bonaparte's daughters Zénaïde and Charlotte sit together reading a letter from their exiled father, who had fled to New Jersey after Waterloo. David painted the double portrait in Brussels in 1821; it is now at the Getty Museum.

title: Thomas Jefferson
description: Thomas Jefferson in old age, painted by Stuart from earlier sittings taken in 1805 during Jefferson's second presidency. Stuart kept the original Edgehill portrait in his Boston studio for years, working up replicas like this one for collectors and family members.

title: 1280px-Rocky Landscape in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains - Caspar David Friedrich
englishTitle: Rocky Ravine in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains
description: A study of the Neurathen rock formation in Saxon Switzerland, with weathered sandstone pillars rising against a pale sky. Friedrich drew repeatedly from this region near Dresden, translating direct observation into the meditative, vertical compositions characteristic of his mature Romantic landscapes.

title: Dante and Virgil in Hell
description: Dante and Virgil cross the Stygian marsh in Phlegyas's skiff as the damned claw at the gunwale, drawn from the eighth canto of the Inferno. Delacroix's Salon debut in 1822, the picture was bought by the state and now hangs in the Louvre; the dripping water beads on the nude bodies pay direct homage to Rubens.
credit: Transferred from en.wikipedia ; transferred to Commons by User:NuclearWarfare using CommonsHelper . (Original text : WebMuseum, Paris: Delacroix, EugÃ¨ne )

title: Moonrise over the Sea
description: Two women and a man on a rocky shore watch sailing ships approach beneath a rising moon, the sky banded violet and gold. Friedrich repeated the moonlit-sea motif throughout his career as a Rückenfigur meditation on faith, return, and the threshold between visible and unseen.

title: Solitary Tree
description: A weathered oak rises at the centre of a Bohemian valley at dawn, its dead crown set against luminous distant mountains. Friedrich uses the broken tree as a quiet emblem of endurance, paired with the morning panorama as one half of a meditation on the cycle of day and life.

title: The Movings
description: A family hauling its furniture through a Parisian street near the Port-au-Blé, the household goods piled on a handcart. Oil on canvas, 73 by 92 cm, signed and dated 1822, in the Art Institute of Chicago. Boilly exhibited the canvas at the Salon of 1822 in the hope, unrealised, that the state would buy it.

title: View on the Stour near Dedham
description: Barges and bargemen on the Stour at Dedham, with Dedham church tower distant under broken cloud. The third of Constable's six-foot Stour canvases, exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1822 and now at the Huntington in San Marino.

title: Bishop Jean-Louis Anne Magdelaine Lefebvre de Cheverus
description: Jean-Louis Lefebvre de Cheverus, French émigré priest and first Catholic bishop of Boston, is depicted in black episcopal robes with a large gold pectoral cross suspended on a chain. Stuart painted the portrait in 1823, shortly before Cheverus returned to France; the canvas belongs to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, accession 21.9.

title: First Sketch for ‘The Battle of Trafalgar’
description: A loose oil sketch toward the large Trafalgar canvas commissioned by George IV for St James's Palace. Turner stitched together multiple moments of the engagement onto a single mast-cluttered composition. The freedom of brushwork here, intended only as a working study, anticipates his later, looser exhibited manner.

title: Italian morning
description: A young woman bathes her face at a stone fountain in dappled morning light. Bryullov painted the canvas in Rome in 1823 as part of his pensioner programme for the Society for the Encouragement of the Arts, who sent it to Tsar Alexander I; it remains one of his earliest Italian successes.
credit: here / здесь

title: Romeo and Juliet’s last kiss
description: Romeo and Juliet embrace in a farewell kiss within a vaulted church interior, stained glass and a crucifix visible in the background. Hayez painted this large canvas in 1823 — now held by Villa Carlotta in Tremezzo — charging the Shakespearean subject with the emotional intensity that defines his Italian Romantic manner.
credit: liberamentepensando.it [ dead link ]

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds
description: The cathedral's spire rises through the screen of trees on a property owned by the painter's friend Bishop Fisher, who commissioned the picture. Constable renders the verdant grounds with characteristic flecks of white impasto — his 'snow' that animated foliage and water alike.

title: Alte Nationalgalerie-Krüger-Parade auf dem Opernplatz im Jahre 1822 DSC8028
description: Franz Kruger records a military parade held on Berlin's Opernplatz in 1822, with cavalry drawn up before the opera house and a dense crowd of recognisable Berliners given as much attention as the royal party, which includes Frederick William III of Prussia and the future Tsar Nicholas I. Commissioned by Nicholas, then Grand Duke of Russia, the monumental oil on canvas - roughly 2.5 by 3.7 metres - occupied the painter from 1824 to 1830. It entered the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin in 1928.

title: Branch Hill Pond
description: A wide panoramic view across Hampstead Heath, with a sand or gravel excavation in the foreground where horses and workers with a cart are at work, a pond visible in the middle distance, and a vast, cloud-laden sky filling the upper half. Constable rented a house in Hampstead from 1819, and the heath's open terrain supplied him with the expansive sky studies he returned to throughout the 1820s, now held in the Cleveland Museum of Art.

title: Death of Camilla by F. Bruni
description: Horatius stands over the body of his sister Camilla, whom he has just killed for mourning her Curiatii lover, drawn from Livy's account of the early Roman duel. Fyodor Bruni painted the canvas during his Italian pensioner years for the Imperial Academy; it now hangs in the Russian Museum, Saint Petersburg.

title: Mars désarmé par Vénus
description: Venus and the Graces undress Mars on a cloud-borne couch, removing his sword and helmet while Cupid unbuckles his sandal. David's last completed picture, finished in Brussels in 1824 and exhibited the next year to large crowds; it now belongs to the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium.
credit: This illustration was made by Antoine Motte dit Falisse alias M0tty but it is in the public domain because it is a faithful photographic reproduction of an original two-dimensional work of art and the work of art itself is in the public domain . English | français | +/−

title: Rosa Alba Foliacea
description: Rosa alba foliacea, a branching shrub nearly free of prickles, its full white corolla over three inches across with five or six ranks of heart-notched petals above grey-backed leaves. Two of the calyx lobes stay simple while three are leafy, a trait noted in Thory's text.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Andegavensis
description: Rosa andegavensis, the Anjou rose, a tall hedge shrub whose flowers open pale pink and fade to white, carrying a faint scent of strawberry above oval pointed leaflets. The calyx tube and stalk bristle with gland-tipped hairs, a distinguishing trait recorded in Thory's text.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Bifera Pumila
description: Rosa bifera pumila, a dwarf four-seasons rose barely a foot high, its pale-pink double flowers clustered in upright corymbs above small dark-green leaflets. The stalks and funnel-shaped calyx tubes are coated with rose-scented glandular hairs, with red pear-shaped hips at the foot.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Bifera Variegata
description: Rosa bifera variegata, a four-seasons rose whose nearly round leaflets are blotched with irregular yellowish marks, its fragrant near-double flowers gathered in an upright corymb. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; this plate is from the 1824 volume.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Biserrata
description: Rosa biserrata, the mountain rose, a three- or four-foot shrub with curved prickles, doubly toothed leaflets each ending in a gland, and pale-pink solitary flowers. It was found on Mont Valerien near Paris by Dr Merat, whose description Thory reproduced.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Canina Burboniana
description: Rosa canina burboniana, the Bourbon Island dog rose, a vigorous bushy shrub with strong reddish hooked prickles and glossy leaflets, its sweet-scented flowers of three or four petal ranks in brilliant rose. Red ovoid hips ripen at the foot of the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Canina Grandiflora
description: A large-flowered dog rose, Rosa canina grandiflora, its five soft-pink petals paler toward the claw and yellowish at the base, set above glabrous leaflets and hooked prickles. The branching shrub bears nearly round hips that ripen red, drawn for Les Roses (1817-1824).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: Rosa centifolia in its celery-leaved form, the leaflets cut and divided so the foliage resembles celery, with the usual rose-pink double flower of the cabbage rose. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia
description: A cabbage rose that carries two variations on one plant, the leafy-bracted and the proliferous forms, with a pink flower growing through from its own centre. Thory notes the foliage otherwise matches the many centifolias already figured in the work.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Centifolia Minor
description: The Bordeaux rose, a small cabbage rose forming a bush about a foot and a half high, its flowers in fours and sixes with seven or eight ranks of pink petals smaller than the common centifolia. The leaflets are nearly round and woolly beneath, per Thory's description.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Collina
description: Rosa collina in its fastigiate form, soft-pink five-petalled flowers in a loose umbel above ovate-lanceolate leaflets, glossy above and woolly beneath. The strong hooked prickles are broadly swollen at the base, and the styles are free and glabrous.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Collina Monsoniana
description: Lady Monson's rose, Rosa collina monsoniana, with clear-pink five-petalled flowers notched at the tip and slender stems set with strong hooked prickles. The hips ripen to an orange-red, and Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the accompanying text.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Damascena Italica
description: Rosa damascena italica, the autumn-flowering Quatre-Saisons of Italy, its soft pink flowers carried in threes above bright green oval leaflets. An elongated red hip appears at maturity. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Eglanteria Luteola
description: Rosa eglanteria luteola, a smaller many-branched form of the yellow eglantine to about three feet, with seven to eleven small near-round leaflets. The five canary-yellow petals are notched at the apex and the flower carries a disagreeable scent. The stipple plate was printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Eglanteria-Subrubra
description: Rosa eglanteria subrubra, the cherry eglantine, its solitary flowers showing five heart-notched petals pale cherry-red within and canary-yellow without. Seven small glaucous leaflets sit above a nearly thornless flowering branch. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Farinosa
description: Rosa farinosa, a much-branched shrub whose three to seven leaflets are covered both sides with a soft whitish down. Five very pale pink petals form each flower, gathered in a terminal corymb above an egg-shaped hip that ripens dull red. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica in a marbled form, its nearly scentless flowers above three inches wide carrying two or three rows of pale pink petals spotted with a deeper rose that reads as marbling. Numerous stamens surround a sessile half-globular head of stigmas. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica in a giant-flowered Provins form, its lightly scented corolla more than five inches across with several rows of fine rose petals, those at the centre rolled and crumpled over the spent stamens. A large nearly round hip ripens red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica latifolia, the broad-leaved Provins rose, with deep-pink double flowers of five or six petal ranks notched at the tip and unusually large dark-green leaflets. The fruit ripens almost ellipsoid and bright red. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all three folio volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica
description: Rosa gallica stapeliae-flora, a Provins shrub with five large concave petals of fairly deep purple marked with many small tawny-yellow spots set in longitudinal lines. The numerous stamens surround a convex head of styles, and the fruit ripens from reddish to black. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Agatha
description: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica grown as the Enfant de France, its many close-set petals of deep rose folded over one another like a military pompon, hiding the calyx lobes. A pear-shaped hip ripens red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Agatha
description: An Agatha variety of the Provins rose, its very double flower of dark violet-purple packed with tight rolled petals like a ranunculus. The shrub barely reaches a foot and a half, with pear-shaped hips that hold through much of winter. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Agatha
description: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica, a proliferous rose from whose softer-pink flower a second bloom emerges, sometimes a third from the centre of that. The flattened stalk often carries leafy bracts in tiers. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Agatha
description: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica grown as the Agathe Royale, its very double corolla of bright rose petals rolled and crumpled at the centre and wedged between calyx and styles. The flower carries no stamens. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Agatha
description: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica grown as the Agathe Carnee, its many close-set petals a softer pink than the Agathe Prolifere. Firm dark-green leaflets, downy beneath, sit below flowers borne several together at the branch tips, and the hip is rarely seen. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Auelianensis
description: Rosa gallica aurelianensis, the Duchesse d'Orleans, a gallica to four feet whose lightly scented flowers carry five or six rows of deep rose petals, usually borne in threes. Large firm leaflets sit on glandular-bristly stalks, and the hips ripen red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Gueriniana
description: Rosa gallica gueriniana, the Rosier Guerin, a French rose shown in flower above its toothed leaflets. Les Roses documented species roses and early garden cultivars before the rise of the modern hybrid, and Redoute drew this plate for the third volume, published in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Maheka
description: Rosa gallica maheka in a near-single form, a Provins variety carrying broad pink to crimson petals above toothed foliage. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, the most famous rose iconography ever made, which documented species roses and early garden cultivars before the modern hybrid.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Gallica Rosea
description: Rosa gallica rosea in a single form, five rose-pink petals more than three inches across and heart-notched at the tip, above large leaflets downy beneath. The fruit ripens globular and red. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Hispida
description: Rosa hispida argentea, a dense shrub reaching six or seven feet, its branches covered in stiff bristles and scattered straight prickles. The flowers carry six or seven ranks of concave silvery-white petals, and the round fruit is bristly and reddish when ripe. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in three folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica Autumnalis
description: Rosa indica autumnalis, the autumn Bengal rose, a China cultivar bearing rose-pink double flowers above smooth toothed foliage. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which documented species roses and early garden cultivars before the rise of the modern hybrid. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the flower's parts.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica Caryophillea
description: Rosa indica caryophillea, the carnation Bengal, an elegant China rose under twenty inches with eight to ten ranks of deep rose petals, some crossed by a white line, that crimp and ruffle so the open flower resembles a carnation. The fruit is ovoid and smooth. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica Dichotoma
description: Rosa indica dichotoma, a China rose to two feet or more under glass, its forked branches armed with scattered hooked prickles and glossy five to seven leaflets. The scented flowers gather at the branch tips on repeatedly forking peduncles. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica Fragranas
description: Rosa indica fragrans in a single form, the tea-scented rose, with five fairly large heart-notched petals of soft pink that carry a sweet fragrance far. The long stamens fold back over the styles as in all India roses, and the fruit ripens from red to black. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Indica Sertulata
description: Rosa indica sertulata, a bushy Bengal rose carrying five or six flowers together in a kind of bouquet, the petals white at the claw and tender pink at the tip. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: rosa indica stelligera
description: Rosa indica stelligera, a Bengal rose with rose-pink bloom and toothed leaflets on a slender branching stem. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824; Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose Malmaison garden seeded the work.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Lheritieranea
description: Rosa lheritieranea, a climbing rose laden with flowers whose four or five ranks of petals curl back over the stamens, violet-pink and white toward the claw, each often crossed by a pale line. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Mucosa Anemone-Flora
description: An anemone-flowered moss rose, an upright eighteen-inch bush thick with straight prickles, its four or five ranks of deep-pink petals converging toward the centre, some flecked with paler pink. Thory's text records it was raised from seed by M. Lemeunier and named for his town, La Fleche.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Noisettiana Purpurea
description: A rose-flowered Noisette, smaller in every part than the Philippe Noisette type, its bright pink petals deepening rather than fading as they age. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824), the descriptive text supplied by Claude-Antoine Thory.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pinpinellifolia Inermis
description: Rosa pimpinellifolia inermis, a thornless burnet rose to three feet bearing single five-petalled flowers that range from light to deeper red, above leaves of up to eleven rounded leaflets. The young branches carry a few prickles that vanish as they grow. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pomponiana
description: Rosa pomponiana, a fairly bushy sub-shrub under a metre with five oval leaflets and small, usually double flowers of deep purple-red, long confused with the Pompon de Bordeaux. The botanist De Candolle described it in the Flore Francaise, the source Thory reproduced for this plate.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Pomponiana Muscosa
description: A mossy pompon rose under a foot high, its stem crowded with small prickles mixed with glandular hairs and its pedicels and calyx coated in sticky branched growth like moss. The corolla runs to eight or ten rows of petals in the colour of the ordinary pompon. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Reclinata
description: Rosa reclinata in its single-flowered form, a near-thornless climber with seven-leaflet leaves and soft pink, heart-notched petals, the buds bending toward the ground before opening then straightening. Its hips are nearly round and red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Reclinata
description: Rosa reclinata in its near-double form of about twenty petals, otherwise identical to the single Rosier a Boutons Renverses, a tall climber whose buds nod earthward before rising to open. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubifolia
description: Rosa rubifolia, the bramble-leaved rose, to three or four feet with reddish hooked prickles, soft crisped leaflets, and clusters of five-petalled flowers in soft rose that fade to white. Its styles are fused into a smooth column as in Rosa arvensis. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824).
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubiginosa
description: An anemone-flowered sweetbriar, Rosa rubiginosa, its purple flowers tinged with violet and arranged in a corymb above wine-scented leaves, with red hips that darken in autumn cold. Redoute drew it for Volume 3 of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Rubiginosa Vaillantiana
description: A sweetbriar variety, Rosa rubiginosa vaillantiana, its five-petalled flowers opening faintly washed with pink then settling to a pure matt white that lasts until the petals fall. This colour shift sets it apart from the redder roses of the rubiginosa group, which hold their hue to the end.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sempervirens
description: A globose-hipped form of Rosa sempervirens, the evergreen climber, with glossy persistent leaflets and fragrant white flowers whose styles join in a single bristled column. Redoute drew it for Volume 3 of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sempervirens Leschenaultiana
description: A variety of Rosa sempervirens named for the traveller Leschenault, who found it on a high mountain in southern Asia; its violet branches and foliage carry a glaucous bloom like hoarfrost. Large pure-white heart-notched petals surround many stamens and a bristled column of fused styles topped with violet stigmas.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Sepium
description: Rosa sepium in a myrtle-leaved form, its small glossy leaflets recalling myrtle on slender drooping branches armed with strong hooked spines. The five whitish petals soon flush red in sunlight, and the elliptical fruit ripens red then blackens.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Spinulifolia
description: Rosa spinulifolia, a shrub with red-brown branches bearing long straight solitary spines and leaflets set beneath with many small hooked prickles along the veins. The single soft-pink flowers stand at the branch tips on bristly glandular stalks, with the styles free.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Stylosa
description: Rosa stylosa, the field rose, a shrub with twisting greyish branches and serrated glossy leaflets, its soft-pink flowers borne several together and whitening quickly in sun. The styles fuse into a short column, as in Rosa arvensis, and the elliptical hip ripens red.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Ventenatiana
description: Rosa ventenatiana, a low briar with crowded straight prickles whose upper leaves persist around the bud so the open flower seems to rest on a bed of leaves. The fragrant blooms carry four or five ranks of soft-pink petals yellowish toward the claw, above a thimble-shaped calyx tube.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Rosa Villosa Evrathiana
description: A vigorous variety of Rosa villosa reaching ten feet, nearly spineless, with very large dark-green leaflets and flowers hung in a pendent panicle on bristly glandular stalks. The buds open rarely, and those that do show seven or eight ranks of soft-pink petals.
credit: Restoration by Nicholas Rougeux (c82.net), after Pierre-Joseph Redouté

title: Seascape Study with Rain Cloud
description: Constable records a squall over a flat shore in rapid, loaded brushwork, the composition almost entirely given over to sky and driving rain with the horizon reduced to a thin dark band. The small oil sketch, executed between 1824 and 1828, exemplifies the empirical attention to weather that Constable called the chiaroscuro of nature.

title: Self Portrait in a Group of Friend
englishTitle: Self-Portrait in a Group of Friends
description: Hayez places himself at the centre of a close-knit group that includes the painters Giuseppe Molteni and Giovanni Migliara, the sculptor Pelagio Pelagi, and the writer Tommaso Grossi. The five figures are pressed together in a tight cluster, with Hayez looking directly at the viewer from behind round spectacles. Now in the Museo Poldi Pezzoli, Milan, the small canvas records the intimate Lombard circle that shaped Italian Romanticism.

title: The Lock
description: A barge being lowered through the lock at Flatford Mill on the Stour, the lock-keeper leaning on the beam against a clearing sky. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1824 and sold on opening day, the picture was the only one of Constable's six-footers to find a buyer during the artist's lifetime.
credit: allartpainting.com; Christie's , LotFinder: entry 5584815

title: The Massacre at Chios
description: Greek civilians huddle in the foreground as Ottoman cavalry round up survivors after the 1822 massacre on the island of Chios, in which tens of thousands were killed or enslaved. Delacroix exhibited the canvas at the 1824 Salon alongside Constable's Hay Wain; the picture entered the Louvre directly from the state purchase.

provenance.collection: Department of Paintings of the Louvre

title: (Barcelona) Shipping - 1825-30 - William Turner in Tate Britain
description: A loose marine sketch from Turner's mature years, when his oils and watercolours of shipping abandoned topographic detail for weather and mood. Hulls and masts emerge from a smear of sea and sky, the kind of working study that fed his later exhibited storm and harbour pictures.

title: Death on a pale horse
description: An intensely abstracted figure — skeletal and monstrous, its claw-like hand outstretched — emerges from a vortex of dark ochre and deep red pigment against pale, vaporous ground. The near-formless handling makes this one of Turner's most extreme explorations of sublime terror and dissolution of form. Dated to circa 1825, the canvas is held at Tate Britain (National Gallery collection, N05504).
credit: Google Arts & Culture — VAEyZU0R3M3O5Q Tate images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N05504&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

title: Entrée de cimetière
description: A wrought-iron gate opens onto a hushed graveyard, its crosses and weathered stones receding into mist. Friedrich treats the cemetery as a threshold between visible world and the beyond, his characteristic Romantic meditation on mortality rendered in muted earth tones and silvery atmosphere.

title: Gilbert Stuart
description: A miniature portrait of the elderly portraitist Gilbert Stuart, his white hair and white cravat set against a deep green ground. Painted in watercolour on ivory circa 1825 by his pupil Sarah Goodridge, it is among the most intimate likenesses of the celebrated American painter.
credit: This file was derived from: Sarah Goodridge - Gilbert Stuart - Google Art Project.jpg :

title: Jaques-louis david comte
description: A three-quarter-length portrait of an unidentified officer in dark blue military uniform with gold epaulettes and a group of decorations on his chest, set against a warm neutral ground. The painting is signed and dated 1816 on the canvas, placing it in the period of David's Brussels exile, where the artist supported himself portraying fellow expatriates and visiting subjects until his death in 1825; the work is held at the Clark Art Institute.
credit: Clark Art Institute

title: The Duke of Orléans showing his Lover
description: Louis I, Duke of Orléans lifts the bedclothes to display the lower half of his sleeping mistress to her own husband, the chamberlain Albert Le Flamenc, who fails to recognise her in the half-shadow. Painted in 1825-26 and now in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, the small canvas draws on an anecdote from Brantôme's Vie des dames galantes.
credit: Web Gallery of Art Transfered from fr.wikipedia Transfer was stated to be made by User:laurens . Also available at abcgallery , Original uploader was Cyberprout at fr.wikipedia , 2006-09-06 (original upload date); Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid

title: Cologne
description: Cologne's quayside gilds in evening light as a packet boat draws in beneath the unfinished cathedral. The vast canvas, now in the Frick Collection, pushes Rhineland topography toward Venetian-style golden atmosphere.

title: David's Leonidas and Thermoplyae
description: Jean-Nicolas Laugier's calcographic engraving after David's vast Louvre canvas shows the Spartan king standing bare-chested at the centre, helmeted and holding shield and sword, as warriors around him prepare to defend the pass against Xerxes. David worked on the original painting from 1799 to 1814, and this engraving was published in 1826 by the National Gallery of Art. The dedication below the image reads 'Dédié aux Hellènes.'
credit: Department of Image Collections, National Gallery of Art Library, Washington, DC • Catalog: https://library.nga.gov/permalink/01NGA_INST/1p5jkvq/alma991680593804896

title: Parham Mill
description: A working watermill at Gillingham in Dorset, its great wheel turning as water cascades over it into the stream below, with figures wading in the foreground and a stormy sky above. Constable painted the subject around 1826, working from studies made on visits to the area, and exhibited the picture at the Royal Academy that year.

title: Port Ruysdael
description: An invented harbour named in homage to the Dutch marine master Jacob van Ruisdael, with squat fishing craft straining against a grey-green swell. Turner adopts the seventeenth-century tonal vocabulary while loosening the brushwork toward atmospheric haze.

title: Rue Neuve Notre Dame in Paris
description: A view down the Rue Neuve Notre-Dame on the Île de la Cité, the stone façades of tall urban buildings flanking the street as the towers of Notre-Dame loom at the far end. Eduard Gaertner painted this precisely observed cityscape in 1826, capturing pedestrians, riders, and the everyday activity of a Parisian street before the area was substantially altered in later decades.
credit: Zeno.org , ID number 20004023927

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Garden
description: The thirteenth-century spire of Salisbury Cathedral framed between tall trees in the Bishop's garden, cattle grazing at the edge of a sunlit meadow. Signed and dated 1826 and now in the Frick Collection, the picture was repainted by Constable at the request of Bishop John Fisher, who had objected to the dark sky of an earlier version.

title: Schinkel1
description: A bust-length portrait of the Prussian architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel, painted by Carl Joseph Begas in 1826, showing the sitter with curling hair and a white cravat against a dark ground. Schinkel was at this date the leading architect of Berlin, responsible for the Altes Museum and the Schauspielhaus.
credit: Post card scanned by uploader Muesse .

title: Still-Life with Lobster
description: A scarlet lobster, hare, game birds, and a tartan bag are arranged on an open ground with weapons, while mounted hunters appear in the distant landscape behind. The painting was exhibited at the Salon of 1827–28 alongside the Death of Sardanapalus and is now in the Louvre. Delacroix's handling of the lustrous shell and limp game anticipates the chromatic ambitions of his larger Romantic canvases, dated 1826–27.
credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"d/delacroi/2/201delac"

title: The Cornfield
dateCreated: 1826 Original uploader was Arpingstone at en‧wikipedia
description: A boy drinking from a stream beside a flock of sheep on the sunken Fen Lane between East Bergholt and Dedham, a cornfield opening to a church tower in the middle distance. Painted in Constable's London studio in early 1826 and shown at the Royal Academy that summer, the picture was bought by subscription after his death and presented to the National Gallery in 1837.
credit: http://artchive.com/ftp_site.htm Artchive Originally from en‧wikipedia ; description page is/was here .

title: The Harbor of Dieppe
description: A bustling Norman harbour bathed in unnaturally Italianate light, criticised at the Royal Academy for its sun-drenched palette. The painting forms part of Turner's continental port series following his post-war travels to France.

title: (Barcelona) The Lake, Petworth, Sunset; Sample Study - William Turner - Tate Britain
englishTitle: The Lake, Petworth, Sunset; Sample Study
description: A small oil sketch from the series of sample studies Turner produced during his extended stays at Petworth House as guest of the 3rd Earl of Egremont. The lake dissolves into flat horizontal bands of pink, gold and lavender beneath a low sun, anticipating the radical atmospheric freedom of his late visionary landscapes. The study remained in Turner's studio and entered the Turner Bequest at Tate Britain.

title: A Ship Aground
description: A vessel lists at right, its masts steeply raked, against a pale luminous sky with warm yellow light on the horizon. Turner produced this painting between 1827 and 1828 as one of the Yarmouth sample studies intended to demonstrate his manner to engravers. It is held as part of the Turner Bequest, now at Tate.

title: American Avocet (Plate 318)
description: An American Avocet wades on stilt-like blue legs, the upturned bill sweeping water for invertebrates. The cinnamon head and neck mark breeding plumage; the plate uses a low horizon to emphasise the bird's improbable proportions.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Bittern (Plate 337)
description: Plate 337 of Birds of America depicts three American bitterns among marsh reeds, one with neck stretched upward in the species' characteristic freeze posture and two others in lower, active stances. The streaked brown and buff plumage that serves as camouflage in wetland vegetation is rendered in fine tonal gradations across all three figures. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Coot (Plate 239)
description: An American coot strides along a muddy bank before a stand of reeds, the white frontal shield and ivory bill conspicuous against the slate-black plumage. Its large lobed toes are prominently displayed, distinguishing the species from the ducks with which it shares its habitat. Plate 239 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Crossbill (Plate 197)
description: Red crossbills feeding among conifer cones, the unique mandible crossing essential to their seed-extraction technique clearly visible. The composition unites diet, habitat and anatomy in a single life-size study.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Crow (Plate 156)
description: An American Crow perches on a branch among compound foliage and clusters of green round fruits — consistent with black walnut — in Plate 156 of Birds of America. The bird's glossy black plumage fills the lower portion of the composition, its bill directed toward the fruit. Audubon's corvid imagery often records the crow's association with cultivated or woodland food sources while affording the species a dignified formal portrait.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Flamingo (Plate 431)
description: A single flamingo bows its long neck almost to the ground, its body filling the double-elephant sheet vertically so the entire bird could be shown life-size. Audubon studied the species in the Florida Keys in 1832 and the plate is among the most graphically daring of the folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Goldfinch (Plate 33)
description: Goldfinches in summer yellow perch among thistle, the seedhead Audubon repeatedly used to characterise this species' diet. The plate is among the earlier engravings in the series, executed initially by W. H. Lizars before Havell took over production.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Green winged Teal (Plate 228)
description: Drake and hen green-winged teal stand on a rocky bank, the male's chestnut head marked by an iridescent green eye-mask and the speculum displaying its metallic green patch. The hen shows the species' typical brown, finely scalloped plumage. Plate 228 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Magpie (Plate 357)
description: Two American magpies are depicted: one bird in full flight with wings spread wide, displaying striking iridescent green and blue flight feathers, and a second perched below on a small branch showing the long graduated tail. Plate 357 of Audubon's Birds of America renders the corvid's bold black-and-white plumage alongside its brilliant iridescent wing and tail coloration.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Pied-bill Dobchick (Plate 248)
description: A pied-billed grebe sits on calm water, the short dark-banded ivory bill and stub-tailed silhouette giving the species its archaic name. The plate emphasises the lobed feet barely visible below the surface, the same structural feature shared with coots and other grebes.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Redstart (Plate 40)
description: Black-and-orange flycatching warblers spread their tails through a tangled branch, flashing the pigment patches that give the species its name. Audubon shows the male in the fan-tailed display posture used to startle insects from leaves.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Robin (Plate 131)
description: American robins at a nest in a leafy tree, an adult arriving with food while open-mouthed nestlings beg from the cup below. A second adult perches nearby. The plate documents the species across life stages and is Plate 131 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Scoter Duck (Plate 408)
description: A jet-black drake American Scoter with its distinctive orange-knobbed bill rides a low swell in the foreground, a brownish hen visible behind. Plate 408 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the strong sexual dimorphism of this sea duck, a species that winters in rafts along North American coasts.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Snipe (Plate 243)
description: Three American snipe are shown on a muddy bank among reeds, with a riverside landscape visible behind. One bird stands alert with bill raised, while the others crouch low, their cryptic striped-and-barred plumage blending against the vegetation. Plate 243 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Male 1, Female 2, 3 and identified as Scolopax Wilsonii.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Sparrow Hawk (Plate 142)
description: American kestrels — formerly called sparrow hawks — shown in a leafy tree, one male holding prey while others display the distinctive rufous back and slate-blue wing of this small falcon. The plate is Plate 142 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Swift (Plate 158)
description: Two Chimney Swifts are shown in flight against a plain ground, their dark cigar-shaped bodies and swept-back wings captured in different attitudes. Below the aerial figures Audubon includes a detailed study of the species' characteristic nest of twigs and a grass fragment. Plate 158 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Water Ouzel (Plate 370)
description: Plate 370 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two American Dippers perched on rocks beside a rushing cascade, with an open mountain valley behind. The birds show the species' characteristic rufous-brown crown contrasting with slate-grey body plumage. The rushing water in the composition alludes to the dipper's habitat along fast-flowing mountain streams. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American White Pelican (Plate 311)
description: An American White Pelican fills the folio sheet, its vast bill resting along the breast and the breeding-season horn rising from the upper mandible. The compressed pose was Audubon's standard solution for fitting outsized waterbirds within the double-elephant format.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Widgeon (Plate 345)
description: A drake American wigeon displays the white forecrown and green eye-stripe that distinguish it from its Eurasian cousin. The bird is set on still water, with reflections built up by selective biting of the aquatint plate.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: American Woodcock (Plate 268)
description: Three American woodcocks are shown among tall reeds and marsh grasses at the water's edge, with one bird rising in a wing-spread display. Audubon captures the mottled brown-and-buff plumage that provides cryptic cover in wetland vegetation, and the long bill and high-set eyes adapted for probing damp ground. Plate 268 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Arctic Tern (Plate 250)
description: An Arctic tern hovers with deeply forked tail and short red legs trailing, the blood-red bill held downward as it scans for fish. The plate captures the proportions of the famously long-distance migrant, whose annual journey between polar oceans Audubon could only have suspected.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Arctic Yager (Plate 267)
description: A long-tailed jaeger shown over open water, the slender central rectrices streaming behind a sharply patterned body. The plate documents a high-Arctic breeder that follows seabird colonies south, robbing them of their catch in piratical chases.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Auguste Strobl
description: A half-length portrait of Auguste Strobl (later Auguste Hilber), shown turning over her shoulder in a white off-shoulder dress with red ribbons in her dark curly hair and a pearl necklace. Painted by Joseph Karl Stieler in 1827 for King Ludwig I of Bavaria's Gallery of Beauties at Nymphenburg Palace, it exemplifies his characteristic smooth Romantic technique.

title: Autumnal Warbler (Plate 88)
description: What Audubon described as the Autumnal Warbler is now recognized as the non-breeding plumage of the Bay-breasted Warbler, an instructive example of the seasonal variation that confused early American ornithology. Hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Azure Warbler (Plate 48)
description: Two Azure Warblers — now generally identified with the Cerulean Warbler — are shown among red berries and mixed foliage, their vivid blue-and-white plumage contrasting with the seasonal colouring of the branch. Plate 48 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bachman's Warbler (Plate 185)
description: Bachman's warbler depicted on a flowering branch, named after Audubon's friend and collaborator the Rev. John Bachman. Once a southern wetland species, the bird is now feared extinct, lending the plate added documentary weight.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bachmans Finch (Plate 165)
description: A single Bachman's Sparrow — here called Bachman's Finch — perches on a flowering branch bearing pink blossoms and developing buds, its streaked brown back and plain buff underparts described with restrained precision. The species was named in honour of Audubon's friend and co-author the Reverend John Bachman. Plate 165 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Baltimore Oriole (Plate 12)
description: Baltimore orioles — adult male, female, and immature — arranged across flowering branches, their pendulous woven nest at the centre of the composition. Audubon pairs the birds' bold black-and-orange plumage with the pale rose-centred blooms of the host plant in Plate XII of Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Band-tailed Pigeon (Plate 367)
description: Plate 367 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a male and female Band-tailed Pigeon perched on a branch of flowering dogwood, its white blossoms and red berries filling the upper portion of the composition. Both birds display the species' broad dark terminal tail-band and yellow-tipped bill. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838 and is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Barn Owl (Plate 171)
description: Two barn owls occupy a dramatic nocturnal composition, one perched with a small rodent clasped in its talons. Audubon's hand-coloured aquatint highlights the species' distinctive heart-shaped facial disc and softly mottled buff-and-white plumage against a dark, atmospheric sky. The plate is Plate 171 of Birds of America, engraved by Robert Havell Jr. and held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Barn Swallow (Plate 173)
description: A pair of barn swallows tend their mud-and-grass nest in Plate 173 of Birds of America, one arriving with wings spread and the other perched at the nest entrance. The deep rust-orange throat, steel-blue upperparts, and forked tail are precisely rendered. Audubon's focus on the nesting behaviour rather than isolated specimen poses is characteristic of his approach throughout the folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Barnacle Goose (Plate 296)
description: Plate 296 of Birds of America shows two Barnacle Geese on open rocky terrain, each displaying the species' distinctive white face, jet-black neck and breast, and silvery grey barred back. Audubon's text noted the medieval legend that the birds hatched from goose-barnacles, a belief the plate's natural-history framing quietly refutes by grounding the species in its actual coastal and grassland habitat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Barred Owl (Plate 46)
description: A Barred Owl spreads its wings dramatically on a mossy branch, turning its head downward toward a grey squirrel perched below it — Audubon's characteristic predator-and-prey narrative composition. The horizontal barring across the upper breast and vertical streaking below are clearly differentiated, and the squirrel's bushy tail adds counterweight to the composition. Plate 46 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell, credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bartram Sandpiper (Plate 303)
description: Plate 303 of Birds of America depicts two Bartram's Sandpipers in dynamic action — one in mid-air with wings fully spread, bill open as it pursues an insect, and one crouching at the water's edge before a backdrop of flowering tropical vegetation. The species, now called the Upland Sandpiper, was named by Audubon in honour of the Philadelphia naturalist William Bartram, and the plate's energetic composition is among the more animated in the series.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bathsheba
description: Hayez depicts Bathsheba seated nude at the edge of a stone pool, her body turned in three-quarter view as she glances back toward the viewer, a blue turban wound about her head and a white cloth draped across her lap. The cool, smooth modelling and classical clarity of form reflect the Italian Romantic painter's debt to academic tradition; the work dates to around 1827 and was sold at Christie's London in 2024.
credit: Christie's , LotFinder: entry 6510043 (sale 22691, lot 25, London, 3 December 2024)

title: Bay-breasted Warbler (Plate 69)
description: Two bay-breasted warblers move through the foliage of a flowering branch, the male's chestnut throat and crown contrasted with creamy neck patches. The plate captures spring breeding plumage rarely encountered south of the boreal forest.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Belted Kingfisher (Plate 77)
description: Three belted kingfishers — one male and two females, one of the females tossing a fish — are depicted against a richly painted river and mountain landscape in Plate 77 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838). The composition highlights the sexual dimorphism of the species, with the female's diagnostic chestnut breast band clearly rendered alongside the slate-blue and white plumage shared by both sexes.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bemaculated Duck (Plate 338)
description: Plate 338 of Birds of America shows a single bemaculated duck — a mallard-like bird with a green-glossed head, chestnut breast, and yellow feet — standing alert on a grassy bank with reeds behind it. Audubon recorded this bird as a distinct species, though it is now considered a variant or hybrid rather than a full species. The plate was engraved and hand-coloured by R. Havell and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bewick's Wren (Plate 18)
description: A single Bewick's Wren perches on a slender leafy branch in Plate 18 of Birds of America, its cocked, barred tail and pale supercilium clearly delineated. Named for the English engraver Thomas Bewick, the species was closely observed by Audubon across the eastern United States. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell and represents the male.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bird of Washington (Plate 11)
description: Plate 11 presents Audubon's so-called Bird of Washington, a large brown eagle depicted on a rocky perch. Audubon claimed it as a distinct species, but recent scholarship has demonstrated that the image was based on copies of earlier drawings rather than an original specimen, making it one of the more contested plates in Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black (Plate 317)
description: Plate 317 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a male and female Surf Scoter (then called Black or Surf Duck) on a rocky coastal shore. The drake perches on a rock, his largely black plumage offset by white head patches and the species' distinctive multicoloured orange, red, and yellow bill; the darker brown female rests on the sand below beside open clam shells. The plate represents Audubon's interest in coastal sea ducks of the New England shore.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black & White Creeper (Plate 90)
description: A Black-and-white Warbler clings to a black larch branch bearing green cones, the bold zebra striping characteristic of the species clearly rendered. Plate 90 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint demonstrating Audubon's interest in characteristic foraging posture as a diagnostic field mark, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
