credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black & Yellow Warbler (Plate 50)
description: A Black and Yellow Warbler — now identified as the Magnolia Warbler — perches on an oak branch bearing developing acorns, its tail spread to reveal the distinctive white tail-band pattern. Plate 50 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell for the double-elephant folio, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black & Yellow Warblers (Plate 123)
description: A study of magnolia warblers, formerly called black and yellow warblers, arranged on a flowering branch. Audubon's compositional habit of stacking multiple individuals across a single bough allowed him to display plumage variation within a species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black Backed Gull (Plate 241)
description: A great black-backed gull is shown with wings fully spread and bill open wide, its glossy slate-black mantle contrasted with white underparts and a heavy yellow bill marked by a red gonys spot. The dynamic composition — the bird calling or landing on a grassy coastal bank — conveys the formidable scale of the world's largest gull. Plate 241 of John James Audubon's Birds of America; a small overhead view of the bird in flight appears in the upper right.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black Guillemot (Plate 219)
description: Cepphus grylle in breeding plumage, the sooty body relieved by a striking white wing patch and red feet rendered in saturated watercolour. The cliff-perched composition evokes North Atlantic colony habitat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black Skimmer or Shearwater (Plate 323)
description: A Black Skimmer cuts low over rough, wave-tossed water, its outsized lower mandible slicing the surface in the characteristic feeding flight. The asymmetrical bill, longer below than above, is unique among North American birds and is rendered with precision in Plate 323 of Audubon's Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black Tern (Plate 280)
description: Plate 280 pairs an adult black tern in full sooty breeding plumage, perched on a rock, with a pale grey-and-white non-breeding or juvenile bird shown diving overhead. Audubon's composition records both seasonal plumages in a single sheet, documenting the species' distinctive transformation between its dark summer coat and the pale winter dress. From Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black Vulture or Carrion Crow (Plate 106)
description: Plate 106 presents two Black Vultures at a carcass, a subject that gave Audubon the chance to depict carrion-feeding behavior alongside the species' bare gray head and broad wings. The composition fills the double-elephant sheet with its scavenging pair.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black Warrior (Plate 86)
description: Two Black Warrior hawks (Falco harlani, now classified as Harlan's Hawk), male above and female below, are shown in contrasting dark plumages on bare branches. Plate 86 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents this dark-morph raptor, which Audubon treated as a distinct species before it was later subsumed into Buteo jamaicensis.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-bellied Darter (Plate 316)
description: Plate 316 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Anhingas perched on a dead tree above a southern swamp. The upper bird displays its wings fully spread in the drying posture characteristic of the species, showing the silver-white streaking on the dark scapulars and the long serpentine neck; the lower bird, with its rich cinnamon-brown neck, sits with wings folded. Audubon worked the species from southern swamp habitat, capturing its distinctive pose and plumage contrasts.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-bellied Plover (Plate 334)
description: Plate 334 of Birds of America shows three Black-bellied Plovers on rocky coastal ground: an adult male in full breeding plumage with jet-black underparts and silvery-dappled upperparts, a non-breeding adult above it, and a juvenile on the right. The arrangement documents the species' striking seasonal plumage variation.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-billed Cuckoo (Plate 32)
description: Plate 32 of Audubon's Birds of America places two Black-billed Cuckoos among the large white flowers and glossy dark leaves of the Great Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora), one bird perched above and one hovering to the right with wings spread. The cuckoos' long graduated tails and slender bills are set off against the prominent white blooms, with smaller insects visible near the centre. The botanical backgrounds in Audubon's early plates were typically contributed by assistants such as Joseph Mason.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-capped Titmouse (Plate 160)
description: A Black-capped Chickadee hangs from a slender twig, its bold cap and bib reduced to crisp shapes against the understated background. Audubon often illustrated tits and chickadees in acrobatic feeding postures observed at close range.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-headed Gull (Plate 314)
description: Plate 314 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Laughing Gulls (Larus atricilla) standing on a flat surface: a breeding adult with a dark hood, red bill, grey mantle, white underparts, and red legs, accompanied by a smaller immature bird with duller, brownish plumage and a dark-tipped bill. The Laughing Gull is a common North American coastal species, breeding from the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-poll Warbler (Plate 133)
description: Three blackpoll warblers perch on a fruiting branch bearing clusters of small dark berries, the male's black cap and white cheek contrasting with his streaked flanks. The plate is from Audubon's Birds of America (Plate 133) and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-throated Blue Warbler (Plate 155)
description: A male Black-throated Blue Warbler — its slate-blue upperparts, black face and throat, and white underparts rendered in vivid colour — perches on a Canadian columbine plant bearing red pendant flowers in Plate 155 of Birds of America. The composition shows a single bird, and the columbine setting places the warbler in the woodland habitat it frequents during migration. The plate was engraved and hand-coloured in London by the Havell workshop.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-Throated Bunting (Plate 384)
description: A pair of Dickcissels on grain stalks, the male's yellow breast crossed by a black bib reminiscent of a meadowlark in miniature. Audubon set them in cultivated grasses to allude to the species' preference for grain fields and old prairie.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-Throated Diver (Plate 346)
description: The black-throated loon, called diver in British usage, is shown in breeding plumage with its striped neck patch. The vermiculated back pattern is achieved by very fine engraved cross-hatching beneath the aquatint tone.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Black-Winged Hawk (Plate 352)
description: Two black-winged hawks — the white-tailed kite of later nomenclature — are shown against a pale sky: one bird in an open-winged flight pose above, and a second perched on a broken branch below. Plate 352 of Audubon's Birds of America captures the species' grey and white plumage and sharply contrasting dark wing patches.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blackburnian Warbler (Plate 135)
description: A male Blackburnian warbler perches on a stem of pink-flowering phlox, his flame-orange throat vivid against the black-and-white body plumage. The plate is Plate 135 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue Crane or Heron (Plate 307)
description: Plate 307 of Birds of America depicts a Little Blue Heron in adult spring plumage, standing tall and alert on a muddy bank with reeds and a broad marshland backdrop. The slate-blue body and darker bluish head and neck are precisely rendered, with the long wispy crest feathers visible behind the crown and a small white egret visible in the far background. The plate's caption identifies the subjects as adult in spring plumage and a young bird, reflecting the species' striking seasonal and age-related variation.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue Grosbeak (Plate 122)
description: Male, female, and immature Blue Grosbeaks in the branches of a leafy dogwood, a nest visible at the centre of the composition. The deep cobalt male contrasts with the warm amber-brown female in Plate CXXII of Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue Jay (Plate 102)
description: Plate 102 of Birds of America depicts three Blue Jays — labelled male, female, and a third — gathered on a leafy branch bearing tubular red and orange flowers. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell from Audubon's watercolour, the composition shows the vivid blue-and-white plumage and crested head of Cyanocitta cristata.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue Yellow-backed Warbler (Plate 15)
description: The diminutive Northern Parula is shown working through lichen and blossom, its blue-grey back and yellow throat picked out in delicate washes. Audubon's botanical setting reflects the bird's preference for Spanish-moss-laden southern woodlands.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue-bird (Plate 113)
description: Plate 113 shows the Eastern Bluebird (Sialia sialis) in three figures: a male in mid-flight above, and a male and female on a leafy branch below, the female appearing to pass food to her mate. The vibrant blue plumage, achieved through hand-colouring over the aquatint, made this plate from Birds of America a perennial favourite.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue-green Warbler (Plate 49)
description: A single Blue-green Warbler perches among the large leaves and rounded pink-and-red berry clusters of a tall fruiting plant, its blue-grey and greenish plumage matched to the species' name. Plate 49 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, drawn life-size in the double-elephant folio format and engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell, credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue-Grey Fly-catcher (Plate 84)
description: Two Blue-grey Gnatcatchers perch on branches of a black walnut, their slender forms and long tails characteristic of the species. Plate 84 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue-headed Pigeon (Plate 172)
description: Three Blue-headed Pigeons (Columba cyanocephala) are shown on rocky ground amid low grasses, the male's iridescent blue cap and white throat-stripe contrasting with the chestnut body. Native to Cuba and the Caribbean, the species is depicted here in the sparse, open setting Audubon often reserved for ground-dwelling birds. This is Plate 172 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue-Winged Teal (Plate 313)
description: Plate 313 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a pair of Blue-winged Teal in flight, the large powder-blue forewing patch that names the species prominently displayed on both birds. The drake below presents his blue-grey head with its white facial crescent and richly spotted cinnamon breast; the hen above shows the more cryptic brown plumage typical of the species. A coastal landscape with water and distant hills forms the background.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Blue-winged Yellow Warbler (Plate 20)
description: Two Blue-winged Yellow Warblers are arranged on the stems and blooms of a rose mallow (Hibiscus grandiflorus), the large pale-pink flowers providing a bold counterpoint to the birds' yellow underparts and dark wings. The pose, with one bird clinging to a stem and the other perched below, reflects Audubon's practice of wiring fresh specimens into lifelike attitudes. Plate 20 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Boat-tailed Grackle (Plate 187)
description: Boat-tailed grackles shown in male and female plumage on a live oak branch bearing acorns and trails of Spanish moss — the plate's own caption names the tree Quercus virens. The iridescent blue-black male and the smaller, warm-brown female are contrasted in size and colouring in Plate 187 of Audubon's Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bohemian Chatterer (Plate 363)
description: A pair of Bohemian Waxwings perched on a fruiting branch, their silky cinnamon plumage punctuated by red sealing-wax tips on the secondaries. The aquatint tone captures the smooth, almost powdered quality of waxwing feathers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bonaparte's Flycatcher (Plate 5)
description: A small flycatcher named for the ornithologist Charles Lucien Bonaparte perches among slender branches. The bird is no longer recognised as a distinct species and is generally considered a misidentified or aberrant specimen, surviving only in this plate.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Bonapartian Gull (Plate 324)
description: Plate 324 of Birds of America depicts three Bonaparte's Gulls: an adult in breeding plumage with its distinctive dark brown hood, a second adult in flight shown from behind, and a juvenile with mottled grey-brown wings. Audubon named the species for the ornithologist Charles Lucien Bonaparte, and the plate captures the bird across plumage stages.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Booby Gannet (Plate 207)
description: Sula leucogaster perched in profile, the wedge-shaped bill and dark mantle contrasted against pale underparts. The composition reflects observations from Audubon's Florida and Gulf coast voyages aboard the Marion in the 1830s.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brant Goose (Plate 391)
description: Two brant geese face one another in a tense display on rocky ground, one spreading its wings upward while the other lunges forward with bill open, both showing the species' dark head and neck and pale barred flanks. Plate 391 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts the male and female engaged in territorial behaviour, engraved and coloured by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brasilian Caracara Eagle (Plate 161)
description: Two Crested Caracaras face each other in a confrontational posture, their bare red facial skin, dark crests, and barred breast plumage carefully rendered against a plain ground. One bird is shown from above with wings partially spread, emphasising the bold patterning of the tail and flight feathers. Plate 161 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Broad-winged Hawk (Plate 91)
description: An adult and juvenile Broad-winged Hawk perch together on a branch, paired to show the contrasting plumages of the small forest raptor known for its enormous autumnal kettling migrations. Hand-coloured aquatint engraving from the double-elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brown headed Worm eating Warbler (Plate 198)
description: A worm-eating warbler perched on slender vegetation, the bold dark head-stripes that identify the species precisely registered. The plate shows the typical aquatint-and-watercolour layering of the Havell-engraved double elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brown Pelican (Plate 251)
description: A brown pelican perches on a mangrove branch, its huge gular pouch slack and the chestnut-and-cream nape of breeding plumage clearly registered. Audubon studied the species at close range during his 1832 Florida voyage, allowing the life-size composition to bend the bird into a natural resting posture.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brown Pelican (Plate 421)
description: A Brown Pelican stands on a rocky coastal ledge with its long bill held wide open and the pouch fully extended, its chestnut-brown plumage rendered at near life size against a coastal waterway background. Plate 421 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brown Titlark (Plate 10)
description: Plate 10 of Birds of America depicts two Brown Titlarks, now known as the American Pipit, shown among dark ground cover and mushrooms. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell from Audubon's watercolour, the plate records the male and female of the species with characteristic attention to plumage detail.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Brown-headed Nuthatch (Plate 125)
description: A southern pine specialist shown clinging head-down to bark in the species' typical pose. The plate captures the small nuthatch's sharp bill and stubby tail, characters Audubon emphasised through tight, descriptive line work.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Buff breasted Sandpiper (Plate 265)
description: Two buff-breasted sandpipers appear in Plate 265, one walking on a sandy shore and one perched on a rock with wings partly raised. Both show the soft ochre tones, plain dove-like face, and yellow-orange legs that typify the species. Audubon's hand-coloured plate presents male and female, the upright bearing and open-country habitat well conveyed.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Buffel-headed Duck (Plate 325)
description: A Bufflehead drake displays the puffy white-and-iridescent head pattern that gives the species its old name. Audubon paired the small diver with a more sober female to document the strong sexual dimorphism.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Burgomaster Gull (Plate 396)
description: An adult Burgomaster Gull in pale grey-and-white plumage stands alongside a mottled brown immature bird on a rocky shore, the adult's yellow bill conspicuous against the dark coastal background. Plate 396 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts this large gull — now classified as the glaucous gull — in two age-plumages, engraved and coloured by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cabot's Tern (Plate 279)
description: A Cabot's tern with shaggy black crest and yellow bill tip, rendered in clean profile against the page. The aquatint marks this American population of what was long considered a Sandwich tern, whose taxonomic status has shifted between subspecies and full species over time.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: California Partridge (Plate 413)
description: A male California Partridge stands upright on an open hillside, its forward-curling black topknot and blue-and-chestnut flanks conspicuous, while a female crouches below in a foraging posture. Plate 413 of Audubon's Birds of America introduces one of the West Coast's most distinctive game birds to the folio, set against a broad valley landscape.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Californian Vulture (Plate 426)
description: A California Condor perches on a weathered log, its bare brownish-orange head and blue neck patch contrasting with jet-black body plumage and a bold white stripe along the underwing coverts. Plate 426 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838 from skins rather than a living specimen, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Canada Goose (Plate 201)
description: A large Canada Goose fills the sheet in a near-vertical composition, its black neck extended and bill open, set against marsh reeds and willow foliage. A second bird is partially visible in the lower foreground. The crisply rendered black head and neck, white chinstrap, and soft brown body plumage are characteristic of Audubon's treatment of large waterfowl. Plate 201 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Canada Jay (Plate 107)
description: Plate 107 depicts two Canada Jays among the lobed leaves of a White Oak (Quercus alba), one bird tending a nest at the lower centre of the composition. The soft gray and white plumage is conveyed through selective hand-colouring over the aquatint, and the plate labels the tree as White Oak (Quercus alba).
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Canada Warbler (Plate 103)
description: Plate 103 shows the Canada Warbler among the foliage of a flowering plant, the yellow breast and necklace of streaks rendered with diagnostic precision. Audubon's habit of pairing each species with botanically accurate vegetation is on full display.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Canadian Titmouse (Plate 194)
description: Boreal chickadees, then called Canadian titmice, are shown clinging to deciduous berry-bearing branches in various active postures. Plate 194 of John James Audubon's Birds of America records the species' distinctive brown cap — which distinguishes it from the black-capped chickadee — across male, female, and young plumages.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Canvas backed Duck (Plate 301)
description: Plate 301 of Birds of America depicts three Canvas-backed Ducks — two males with their rich chestnut heads, black breasts, and pale grey backs, and one brown female — arranged at the water's edge with a distant harbour and city skyline in the background, generally identified as Baltimore on the Chesapeake Bay. Audubon's plate documents the species whose taste for wild celery made it highly prized by nineteenth-century market hunters.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Carbonated Warbler (Plate 60)
description: Two male Carbonated Warblers — a species known only from Audubon's single reported encounter and now considered of uncertain identity — perch on a branch of a fruiting may-bush in Plate 60 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. Their greenish-yellow plumage is marked with dark streaking on the crown and back. The plate stands as the sole pictorial record of a bird that has never been confirmed by another observer.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cardinal Grosbeak (Plate 159)
description: A pair of Northern Cardinals are arranged on a fruiting branch, the male's vermilion plumage carried by a saturated red wash applied over the engraved ground. The plate's vivid colouring relies on the brilliant cochineal- and madder-based reds available to the Havell workshop.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Carolina Parrot (Plate 26)
description: Carolina parakeets clustered on a cocklebur branch, their green bodies and yellow-and-orange heads brilliantly hand-coloured. Audubon's plate is now bittersweet documentation of the only parrot native to the eastern United States, driven to extinction by the early twentieth century.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Carolina Turtle Dove (Plate 17)
description: Carolina (mourning) doves grouped on a flowering branch, their pinkish-buff plumage set against delicate blossoms. The composition uses overlapping figures to create the multi-bird tableaux Audubon favoured for sociable species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cat Bird (Plate 128)
description: A pair of grey catbirds among bramble, named for their mewing call. Audubon situates the birds within thorny undergrowth typical of their breeding habitat, a recurring strategy for grounding species in ecological context.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cayenne Tern (Plate 273)
description: A Cayenne tern stands on a sandy shore beside a large pink crab, its shaggy black crest and distinctive orange-red bill rendered in careful profile. The species — now treated as a subspecies of the Sandwich tern — is shown in adult breeding plumage with pale grey upperparts and white underparts. Plate 273 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cedar Bird (Plate 43)
description: Two Cedar Waxwings perch on a branch of eastern red cedar laden with blue-grey berries, their silky fawn plumage, black masks, and red wing-tip wax drops rendered with close attention to texture. Plate 43 of Audubon's Birds of America, published by Robert Havell, London, credited to the University of Pittsburgh collection.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Chestnut-sided Warbler (Plate 59)
description: Two warblers move through a flowering shrub, their yellow crowns and chestnut flanks picked out against fresh green leaves. The aquatint records a species that became more common as nineteenth-century clearing created the second-growth scrub it favours.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Children's Warbler (Plate 35)
description: A small wood-warbler named after John George Children of the British Museum, now considered a juvenile yellow warbler rather than a distinct species. The plate is a record of the taxonomic uncertainty that surrounded many small migrants in Audubon's day.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Chipping Sparrow (Plate 104)
description: Plate 104 depicts the Chipping Sparrow perched on a flowering branch, its rufous crown and clean breast carefully delineated. The aquatint preserves the soft gradations of the small songbird's plumage achieved in Audubon's original watercolor.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Chuck-will's Widow (Plate 52)
description: Two Chuck-will's-widows confront a vividly banded coral snake draped across a branch of a flowering vine in Plate 52 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. The cryptic brown-mottled plumage of both birds is rendered with fine tonal gradations, set against the vine's tubular red flowers. Audubon's preference for staging behavioural encounters rather than isolating specimens against blank grounds is fully evident here.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cock of the Plains (Plate 371)
description: A male Greater Sage-Grouse in lek display, air sacs inflated over a white ruff while the spike-tailed female crouches nearby. The plate documents a sagebrush species Audubon never saw alive, drawn from Townsend specimens.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Columbia Jay (Plate 96)
description: A male and female Columbia Jay (Corvus bullockii) display their rich blue plumage and long, graduated tail feathers as they perch on leafy branches in this striking double-page composition. The birds' prominent crests and elongated tails give the plate an ornamental quality unusual among Audubon's passerine plates. Plate 96 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Columbian Humming Bird (Plate 425)
description: Multiple hummingbirds with iridescent red gorgets and green backs hover around and perch on a tall stem of large pink mallow-type flowers, while a fifth bird sits on a small nest at the base. Plate 425 of Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Columbian Humming Bird and produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Common American Swan (Plate 411)
description: A Common American Swan (Tundra Swan) glides across a still pond bordered by water-lily pads and yellow flowers, the small reddish spot at the base of the dark bill visible in profile. Plate 411 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts the species Audubon distinguished from the Trumpeter Swan by its smaller size and bill markings.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Common Buzzard (Plate 372)
description: Plate 372 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a Common Buzzard diving upon a hare in an open landscape, its dark brown wings spread and talons extended as it descends on the prey. A lighter-breasted second view of the bird appears below, conveying the species' plumage variation. The Eurasian bird was included in the folio on the basis of a single American specimen, a record now generally considered erroneous.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Common Cormorant (Plate 266)
description: Plate 266 depicts a great cormorant nest scene on a cliff ledge: one adult leans over a nest of seaweed to feed two gaping chicks, while a second adult stands upright beside the nest calling with bill agape. The iridescent dark plumage, white facial patch, and yellow gular skin of the adults are finely rendered. Audubon's composition is one of his most animated breeding scenes in Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Common Gallinule (Plate 244)
description: A common gallinule strides across a rocky bank at the water's edge, its bright red frontal shield and yellow-tipped bill catching the eye against dark slate plumage. The long greenish legs and splayed toes that adapt the species to wetland habitats are clearly delineated. Plate 244 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Gallinula chloropus.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Common Gull (Plate 212)
description: Larus canus, as Audubon labelled the species, shown as an adult and a young bird standing on a grassy rise, the adult's soft grey mantle and yellow bill described in muted aquatint washes. A relatively restrained composition typical of plates devoted to widespread coastal species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Connecticut Warbler (Plate 138)
description: Two Connecticut warblers perch among stems bearing large blue flowers, the upper bird showing the olive-green upperparts and the lower displaying yellow underparts typical of the species. The plate is Plate 138 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cow-pen Bird (Plate 99)
description: A male and female Brown-headed Cowbird stand on a mossy, rocky ground surface, the male's glossy dark plumage contrasting with the streaked brown female beside him. Plate 99 of John James Audubon's Birds of America depicts the species — then known as the Cow-pen Bird — in a ground-level setting, from the double-elephant folio held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Crested Grebe (Plate 292)
description: Two Crested Grebes ride choppy waves, one calling with bill raised and chestnut-and-black head plumes fanned in display, the other holding a lower posture with neck curved. A careful study of the lobed foot is inset in the upper right corner. Plate 292 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Crested Titmouse (Plate 39)
description: A pair of tufted titmice work over a white pine branch hung with elongated cones, their upright crests and dark eye-patches giving each a sharp, inquisitive profile. Plate 39 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell, captures the species in its preferred eastern conifer habitat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Cuvier's Regulus (Plate 55)
description: A tiny crested kinglet sits on a leafy branch, its identity now considered a probable hybrid or unrepeatable observation. The plate honours Georges Cuvier and exemplifies the speculative species occasionally included from single field encounters.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Double-crested Cormorant (Plate 257)
description: A double-crested cormorant perched on a rocky coastal outcrop, its two wispy nuptial tufts fanned above a glossy green-black head. The bird faces left against a background of cliffs and distant water. Plate 257 of Birds of America presents the male in adult spring plumage, the iridescent dark plumage and long hooked bill clearly articulated.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Downy Woodpecker (Plate 112)
description: Plate 112 depicts a male and female Downy Woodpecker on a branch covered with a flowering vine bearing red buds and yellow blossoms. The crisp black-and-white plumage and the male's small red nape patch are precisely rendered, and the plate title notes both sexes from Audubon's Birds of America, engraved by Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Dusky Albatros (Plate 407)
description: A uniformly dark-brown Dusky Albatros stands on a rocky coastal ledge, the sea and breaking waves visible behind it. Plate 407 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts this sooty-plumaged seabird in a perched pose, its pale-yellow feet and hooked bill carefully rendered.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Dusky Duck (Plate 302)
description: Plate 302 of Birds of America shows two Dusky Ducks on a grassy bank beside open water, one standing and one with wings raised and spread. Both birds display the species' uniformly dark brown mottled plumage, yellow-green bills, and a flash of iridescent blue-purple on the secondaries — the features Audubon used to distinguish what is now called the American Black Duck from the closely related Mallard.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Dusky Petrel (Plate 299)
description: Plate 299 of Birds of America depicts a Dusky Petrel in low flight above open ocean, the bird's dark upperparts and pale underparts silhouetted against a coastal headland backdrop. The slender wings are held straight and the tail is fanned, capturing the effortless gliding posture characteristic of petrels in flight. Audubon included the species in the double-elephant folio as part of his effort to document the full range of North American seabirds.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Eared Grebe (Plate 404)
description: Two Eared Grebes are shown on a muddy bank beside open water, one in full breeding dress with the species' distinctive golden ear-tufts and red eye, the other in plain grey-and-white winter plumage. Plate 404 of Audubon's Birds of America presents the striking seasonal contrast between the two plumages of the same species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Eider Duck (Plate 246)
description: Several common eiders are grouped on land among dense reeds: drakes display bold black-and-white plumage with the pale green nape characteristic of the species, while a brown hen is visible among them. Plate 246 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Male 1, Female 2 and identified as Fuligula Mollissima.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Esquimaux Curlew (Plate 208)
description: Numenius borealis shown probing tundra ground, the slender decurved bill carefully traced. The species was already in steep decline during Audubon's lifetime and is now likely extinct, lending the plate documentary value.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ferruginous Thrush (Plate 116)
description: Plate 116 depicts three Ferruginous Thrushes (now Brown Thrasher) in a dramatic defensive scene around a nest with eggs, while a black snake coils through the oak-leafed branches toward them. The long tail and rich rusty back of the species are clearly rendered, and the multi-figure composition is among the most narratively charged in Audubon's Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Field Sparrow (Plate 139)
description: A field sparrow rests on a mossy rock amid a low composition of wildflowers and berry-bearing stems, the bird's pale pink bill and warm-toned crown characteristic of the species. The plate is Plate 139 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fish Crow (Plate 146)
description: Two Fish Crows are shown perched among the feathery compound foliage and hanging seed pods of what appears to be a mimosa tree in Plate 146 of Birds of America. The glossy black plumage is rendered through the layered tonal work characteristic of Audubon's engraved plates. Audubon distinguished this species from the larger American Crow chiefly by voice and habitat, as he documented in his Ornithological Biography.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fish Hawk or Osprey (Plate 81)
description: An Osprey grips a large silvery fish in its talons as it rises above a coastal waterway, wings dramatically spread across the composition. Plate 81 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Florida Cormorant (Plate 252)
description: A Florida cormorant perches on a broken stump above open water, its neck arched and bright orange gular pouch fully exposed in an alert, calling pose. The dark iridescent plumage and hooked bill are precisely rendered, with a flock of cormorants visible on the water in the distance. Plate 252 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Carbo Floridanus in spring plumage.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Florida Jay (Plate 87)
description: A pair of Florida Jays (Florida Scrub-Jays) perches on a persimmon branch laden with golden fruits, the vivid blue-and-white plumage rendered against the autumnal foliage. Plate 87 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint engraved by Robert Havell Jr., held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Foolish Guillemot (Plate 218)
description: Common murre, Uria aalge, shown in profile with the pointed bill and dark upperparts of breeding plumage. The plate reflects observations from Audubon's Labrador voyage among dense seabird cliffs.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fork-tail Petrel (Plate 260)
description: Two fork-tailed petrels are shown banking over breaking ocean waves in Plate 260, their dark brown plumage contrasting with white rump patches and pale underwings. The forked tail of the upper bird is clearly visible as it crests a wave. The Birds of America plate — engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr. — conveys the stormy pelagic conditions this small storm-petrel inhabits.

title: Fork-tailed Flycatcher (Plate 168)
description: A Fork-tailed Flycatcher perches on a flowering branch — bearing large white blossoms — its two greatly elongated central tail feathers hanging straight downward in a striking vertical line. The grey upperparts, black cap, and rufous crown patch are crisply rendered. Plate 168 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, depicting a species then known as a rare vagrant to the eastern United States.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fork-tailed Gull (Plate 285)
description: A Fork-tailed Gull with a dark grey hood and forked tail perches on a rock, while a smaller shorebird forages on the sandy ground nearby. The gull's pale grey mantle, white underparts, and distinctive tail are faithfully rendered against a calm riverine background. Plate 285 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fox-coloured Sparrow (Plate 108)
description: Plate 108 shows two Fox-coloured Sparrows among mossy ground cover with ferns, berries, and low vegetation. The rich rufous tail and heavily spotted breast of the species are carefully rendered, set against the dense groundscape typical of Audubon's life-history compositions from Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fresh Water Marsh Hen (Plate 203)
description: King rail, Rallus elegans, drawn skulking among reeds with neck extended in characteristic cautious gait. Fine etched lines build the barred flank pattern, while aquatint shading establishes the dim, vegetated marsh interior.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Frigate Pelican (Plate 271)
description: A male magnificent frigatebird fills the plate in Audubon's characteristic close-up style, its deeply forked tail and angular wings spread wide against a plain ground. The long, hooked bill and iridescent black plumage are recorded in detail, with two isolated feet depicted as anatomical references at the top of the sheet. Plate 271 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Fulmar Petrel (Plate 264)
description: A fulmar perched on a moss-covered rock in Plate 264, its white head and underparts contrasting with pale grey wings against a stormy sky and choppy sea. The bird's yellow tube-nosed bill is clearly shown in profile. Audubon's plate of Fulmarus glacialis presents the male in adult summer plumage, capturing the stocky, gull-like form of this North Atlantic seabird.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Gadwall Duck (Plate 348)
description: Plate 348 of Birds of America shows a pair of gadwall standing on coastal rocks above open water. The drake, on the right, displays the subtly vermiculated grey flanks and black tail coverts that distinguish the species from other dabbling ducks, while the brown-patterned female stands beside him. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Gannet (Plate 326)
description: Plate 326 of Birds of America depicts two Northern Gannets: a standing adult with its characteristic buff-yellow head and vivid blue eye-ring, and a large brown-and-white immature beside it on a rocky shore with open sea behind. Audubon visited breeding colonies on the Gulf of St Lawrence and drew the species across age classes.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Glossy Ibis (Plate 387)
description: A Glossy Ibis probes a wetland margin, the curved bill and mahogany body washed with green-bronze iridescence rendered through layered aquatint and watercolour. Audubon based the figure on a Florida specimen of this then-uncommon coastal wader.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Golden Plover (Plate 300)
description: Plate 300 of Birds of America presents three American Golden Plovers in different plumages and attitudes — one standing bird in mottled transitional plumage, one in crouching summer dress with dark belly patches, and one bird in flight overhead showing the spangled gold-and-black upperparts. Audubon documented this long-distance migrant whose vast autumn flocks were heavily hunted throughout the nineteenth century, and the multi-pose composition conveys both seasonal variation and the species' dynamic behaviour.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Golden-crowned Thrush (Plate 143)
description: Two ovenbirds — depicted under their older name, the Golden-crowned Thrush — are shown near a mossy log beside water, one perching on a branch with red berries above. Audubon renders the olive back and streaked underparts of this ground-dwelling warbler with characteristic precision. The plate is Plate 143 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Golden-Eye Duck (Plate 342)
description: Plate 342 of Birds of America shows a drake and hen common goldeneye in flight, wings fully spread against a grey sky. The drake's bottle-green head, white cheek spot, and bold black-and-white wing pattern are rendered at full scale, while the brown-headed female is shown banking above him. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Golden-eye Duck (Plate 403)
description: A single drake common goldeneye rides open water, its iridescent purple-green head and circular white cheek-patch rendered with close attention to gloss and form. Plate 403 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the male in breeding plumage, the orange-yellow feet and black-and-white flanks clearly delineated beneath the surface.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Golden-winged Woodpecker (Plate 37)
description: Plate 37 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two male and two female Northern Flickers — then called Golden-winged Woodpeckers — around a large weathered tree stump. The bright yellow wing and tail-shaft feathers, visible on the bird shown in flight with spread wings, give the species its Audubon-era common name. The composition appeared early in the double elephant folio, published from 1827 onwards.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Goldon Eagle (Plate 181)
description: A female adult Golden Eagle grips a white Northern Hare in its talons, wings fanned wide against a stormy mountainous backdrop, in Plate 181 of Birds of America. The plate label reads 'female adult — Northern Hare,' and the composition focuses on the close confrontation between predator and prey at ledge level rather than a mid-air stoop. Audubon's treatment of large raptors favoured dramatic scale, and the plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Goldon-crested-Wren (Plate 183)
description: Two Golden-crested Wrens (kinglets) perch on the stems of a broad-leaved plant bearing grey flowering spikes and large paddle-shaped leaves in Plate 183 of Birds of America. The vivid orange and yellow crown stripes of the male and female are sharply rendered against the birds' olive-green plumage. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. for Audubon's double elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Goosander (Plate 331)
description: Plate 331 of Birds of America shows a Common Merganser drake standing on a riverbank before a sweeping waterfall, its glossy dark green head and white flanks contrasting with a female swimming in the foreground with her rusty-brown crested head. The serrated bill, adapted for gripping slippery fish, is clearly rendered on both birds.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Grass Finch or Bay-winged Bunting (Plate 94)
description: A single Vesper Sparrow (Grass Finch or Bay-winged Bunting) stands on a rocky surface before a blooming prickly pear cactus, its streaked brown plumage blending with the warm tones of the stone. Plate 94 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, from the double-elephant folio held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Gray Tyrant (Plate 170)
description: A Gray Kingbird perches alertly on a slender stem, its pale grey upperparts and stout black bill rendered with restrained tonal washes. Audubon associated the species with the Florida coast, where it occupies the same exposed perches as its more northerly relative the Eastern Kingbird.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great American Shrike or Butcher Bird (Plate 192)
description: Four northern shrikes are arranged on a hawthorn branch bearing clusters of red berries, their grey, black, and white plumage precisely recorded across different postures. Plate 192 of John James Audubon's Birds of America presents multiple individuals of the species known as the Butcher Bird, combining naturalistic observation with the compositional drama Audubon favoured for larger passerines.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Auk (Plate 341)
description: Plate 341 of Birds of America depicts two great auks — one swimming in choppy coastal waters and one standing upright on a rock — rendered at full scale against a dramatic backdrop of sea cliffs. The flightless North Atlantic bird was already declining when Audubon's plate was published and went extinct in 1844, making this one of its most widely reproduced likenesses. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great blue Heron (Plate 211)
description: Ardea herodias rendered at full life size by bending the long neck and legs to fit the double-elephant folio sheet. Aquatint and watercolour build the slate-grey body and shaggy plumes, with marshland horizon barely indicated.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Carolina Wren (Plate 78)
description: Two Carolina Wrens — male above, female below — perch on the flowering stem of a Dwarf Buckeye (Aesculus parva), the warm cinnamon plumage and prominent white supercilium characteristic of the species clearly rendered. Plate 78 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) presents the birds at life size on the double-elephant folio sheet, with careful botanical detail devoted to the plant's clustered tubular flowers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Cinereous Owl (Plate 351)
description: A great grey owl perches on a broken branch, the concentric facial discs rendered through circular sweeps of aquatint tone. The plate captures the disproportion between the species' enormous head and its relatively slight body.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Crested Flycatcher (Plate 129)
description: The great crested flycatcher poised on a forked branch, its rufous tail and lemon belly delicately laid in. Audubon notes the species' habit of weaving shed snake skins into its nest, an ethological detail typical of his accompanying writings.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Esquimaux Curlew (Plate 237)
description: An Eskimo curlew stands on open ground amid coastal grasses, its slender decurved bill raised, the streaked buff-and-brown plumage rendered at life-size. The plate is a significant record of a species that was abundant in Audubon's day and is now feared extinct. Plate 237 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Horned Owl (Plate 61)
description: A pair of great horned owls perches on a lichen-covered branch in Plate 61 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, their prominent ear tufts erect and yellow eyes directed toward the viewer. The warm brown and buff barring of their plumage is finely graduated against a pale ground, showing the Havell workshop's control of tonal colour printing. The plate is one of the larger raptors in the series and presents both birds nearly face-on to emphasise the species' intense, forward-facing gaze.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Marbled Godwit (Plate 238)
description: Two marbled godwits stand among coastal grasses, their long slightly upturned bicoloured bills and rich cinnamon plumage with barred upperparts clearly shown. Audubon's composition presents both birds against a backdrop of reeds and low vegetation. Plate 238 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Northern Diver or Loon (Plate 306)
description: Plate 306 of Birds of America depicts two Common Loons: a large adult in full breeding plumage — iridescent dark green head, white-spotted black back, and striped neck — standing upright among reeds with bill open, and a smaller winter-plumaged or immature bird floating on the water in the left background. The life-size rendering of the two birds across the double-elephant folio sheet conveys both the adult's dramatic patterning and the contrast with the greyer immature plumage.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great Tern (Plate 309)
description: Plate 309 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a single tern — labelled Great Tern but corresponding to what is now the Common Tern (Sterna hirundo) — in a dramatic near-vertical diving posture against a grey ground. The black cap, red bill, red feet, and white body are rendered with sharp detail; the deeply forked tail is spread at the apex of the plunge. Audubon favoured these dynamic flight studies for seabirds, composing them from freshly shot specimens wired into lifelike attitudes.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great White Heron (Plate 281)
description: A towering all-white heron with a heavy yellow bill grasps a fish on a sandy bank, with water and a distant shoreline behind it. Audubon treated the Great White Heron as a species distinct from the Great Blue Heron, and the bird's dramatically arched neck — required to fit the double-elephant folio sheet at near life size — gives the plate its striking silhouette. Plate 281 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Great-footed Hawk (Plate 16)
description: A male and female Peregrine Falcon — here called the Great-footed Hawk — contend over freshly killed waterfowl identified on the plate as Green-winged Teal and Gadwall, blood-flecked feathers scattered around them. The two raptors face each other with wings spread, making this one of the most dynamically charged predator compositions in Birds of America. Plate 16 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Green Black-capt Flycatcher (Plate 124)
description: The Wilson's warbler, here under an obsolete name, perched on a slender stem. The black-capped male and plainer female demonstrate the sexual dimorphism Audubon was careful to record.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Green Heron (Plate 333)
description: Plate 333 of Birds of America depicts two Green Herons amid lush vegetation — one bird in a dramatic bill-raised posture and a second in a calmer stance — against a backdrop of broad-leaved tropical plants rather than open reedy water. Audubon's composition captures the species' hunched, cryptic shape and the rich chestnut-and-green plumage.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Greenshank (Plate 269)
description: A greenshank standing tall on its namesake olive-green legs, slightly upturned bill held alert. The aquatint records a Eurasian wader that occasionally appears on American shores, with the soft grey-and-white winter plumage carefully picked out.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ground Dove (Plate 182)
description: Five Common Ground-Doves (Columbina passerina) — two males, a female, and young — are arranged across a leafy branch bearing round green fruits in Plate 182 of Birds of America. The species' small scale, spotted breast, and rufous wing-flashes are accurately recorded across the different plumage stages. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Harlequin Duck (Plate 297)
description: Plate 297 of Birds of America presents three Harlequin Ducks — a brilliantly marked adult male in full breeding plumage, a second male in duller eclipse dress, and a soberly mottled brown female — arranged on a rocky shore with a coastal cliff visible beyond. The adult male's slate-blue, chestnut, and white markings are rendered with characteristic precision, illustrating the sexual dimorphism of a species associated with turbulent mountain streams and surf-washed coastlines.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hawk Owl (Plate 378)
description: Two Hawk Owls appear on a bare tree stub: one perches upright at the top, displaying the barred underparts and long tail that give the species its falcon-like silhouette, while a second bird below spreads its wings wide. Plate 378 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hemlock Warbler (Plate 134)
description: Two warblers — now considered synonymous with the Blackburnian warbler — perch among the broad lobed leaves of a deciduous shrub bearing small hanging flowers. The plate reflects the unsettled state of warbler taxonomy in the early nineteenth century and is Plate 134 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Henslow's Bunting (Plate 70)
description: Henslow's sparrow — placed among the buntings in Audubon's classification — is shown at ground level among rocks and flowering plants, the streaked brown plumage blending naturally with the low-growing vegetation. Plate 70 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) honours the Cambridge professor John Stevens Henslow, for whom the species was named.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hermit Thrush (Plate 58)
description: Two hermit thrushes perch on the wiry branches of a berry-laden shrub in Plate 58 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, their warm rufous tails and spotted breasts rendered against clusters of small orange-red fruit. The pair composition — labelled Male and Female in the plate text — allows comparison of the species' characteristic spotted underparts and contrasting tail colour. The open branch setting gives full prominence to the birds' clean silhouettes.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Herring Gull (Plate 291)
description: An adult Herring Gull with grey mantle and yellow bill soars overhead while a mottled immature bird stands on a rocky shore below, its brown-streaked plumage contrasting with the adult's clean grey and white. The composition illustrating multiple age plumages in a single plate is a recurring feature of Audubon's gull sequences. Plate 291 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hooded Merganser (Plate 232)
description: A drake hooded merganser raises his fan-shaped black-and-white crest while the hen stands alongside on a rocky bank, her shaggy rust-coloured tuft erect. The plate emphasises the saw-edged bill and the bold pied pattern of the breeding male. Plate 232 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hooded Warbler (Plate 110)
description: Plate 110 shows the Hooded Warbler, the male's black hood framing a vivid yellow face. Audubon places the bird among the foliage of an understory plant, in keeping with the species' preference for shady eastern woodlands.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hooping Crane (Plate 226)
description: A whooping crane bows its long neck to seize a young alligator from a marshy Louisiana shoreline, with additional hatchlings scattering through the grass. Composed in stages between 1821 and 1822, the plate combines on-the-spot field study with a later background, and depicts the bird at full life-size by twisting its neck downward.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hooping Crane (Plate 261)
description: A young whooping crane stands on open grassland in Plate 261, its grey-brown plumage and red forehead patch identifying it as an immature bird; white adults are visible in the distant marsh background. The bird's great height fills the double-elephant sheet, bill open and neck arched. Audubon chose to depict the juvenile plumage, a species already declining during his lifetime and now the subject of intensive conservation efforts.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Horned Grebe (Plate 259)
description: Two horned grebes appear side by side in Plate 259: the left bird in vivid breeding plumage with golden ear tufts, chestnut neck, and dark cap, the right in sober winter dress of dark grey above and white below. Both birds are shown at the water's edge against a backdrop of reeds. Audubon's treatment of the species captures the dramatic seasonal transformation in a single plate.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: House Wren (Plate 83)
description: Two House Wrens animate an old hat repurposed as a nesting cavity, a domestic vignette underscoring the species' readiness to nest in human-made objects. Plate 83 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint engraved by Robert Havell Jr., held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hudsonian Godwit (Plate 258)
description: Two Hudsonian godwits share the plate: the left bird in rich cinnamon breeding plumage with wings raised, the right in plainer brownish non-breeding dress. The slightly upturned bill characteristic of the species is evident on both. Audubon's Plate 258 of Birds of America records male, female, and seasonal plumage in a single composition, set against a bare tidal flat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Hutchins's Barnacle Goose (Plate 277)
description: A small Canada goose form, then named for naval officer Thomas Hutchins, depicted standing alert on tundra ground. The plate captures the compact body and short neck that distinguish this northern subspecies, now generally treated as a cackling goose by ornithologists.
credit: This file comes from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , and is available online at biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40392741 .

title: Hyperborean phalarope (Plate 215)
description: Phalaropus hyperboreus (red-necked phalarope) shown in three individuals: one in flight with wings spread and rufous neck markings visible, one swimming among marsh debris, and one wading in shallower water. The plate illustrates both sexes and the species' aquatic habits, with the needle-thin bill prominent in each pose. Plate 215 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. American Ptarmigan - 2. White-tailed Grous (Plate 418)
description: Two high-latitude grouse are posed on a rocky alpine slope against a mountain sky: the American Ptarmigan (left) shown in transitional plumage with mottled brown-and-white markings, wings partially spread, and the White-tailed Grouse (right) in near-complete white winter dress with a red eye-comb. Plate 418 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Arkansaw Flycatcher - 2. Swallow-Tailed Flycatcher - 3. Says Flycatcher (Plate 359)
description: Five tyrant flycatcher figures are distributed across multiple branches: Arkansaw flycatchers (western kingbird) at top, scissor-tailed flycatchers with their distinctive elongated outer tail feathers in the middle register, and a Say's flycatcher at lower right. Plate 359 of Audubon's Birds of America groups three western species in a comparative arrangement, with butterflies included as compositional elements.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Arkansaw Siskin - 2. Mealy Red-poll - 3. Louisiana Tanager - 4.Townsend's Finch - 5. Buff-breasted Finch (Plate 400)
englishTitle: Arkansaw Siskin, Louisiana Tanager and Other Finches (Plate 400)
description: Five birds are arranged across bare twigs and a grassy bank: the yellow-green Arkansaw Siskin at upper left, the streaked red-crowned Mealy Red-poll above, a yellow-green Louisiana Tanager at centre, and two finches — the boldly patterned Townsend's Finch and a Buff-breasted Finch — at the base. Plate 400 of Audubon's Birds of America marks the folio's four-hundredth number and was compiled largely from western study skins.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Audubon's Warbler - 2. Hermit Warbler - 3. Black-throated gray Warbler (Plate 395)
description: Three western wood-warblers perch across a deciduous branch hung with round red berries: Audubon's Warbler with its yellow crown patch, the Hermit Warbler, and the boldly patterned Black-throated Gray Warbler at the base. Plate 395 of Audubon's Birds of America introduced these Pacific species to subscribers, drawn from specimens collected during Townsend and Nuttall's western expedition.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Bank Swallow - 2. Violet-green Swallow (Plate 385)
description: A Bank Swallow at a sandy burrow entrance is paired with the western Violet-green Swallow, contrasting brown plumage against iridescent green and purple. The grouping aligns nesting habit with geographical range across one sheet.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Black-throated green Warbler - 2. Blackburnian - 3. Mourning Warbler (Plate 399)
description: Five warblers are arranged along a deciduous branch bearing broad leaves and pendant acorns: two Black-throated Green Warblers at the top, the warm-throated Blackburnian in the middle, and two Mourning Warblers below. Plate 399 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Havell, groups these eastern wood-warblers in a single composition for the folio's closing numbers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Black-throated Guillemot - 2. Nobbed-billed Auk - 3. Curled-crested Auk - 4. Horned-billed Guillemot (Plate 402)
description: Four North Pacific alcids — Black-throated Guillemot, Nobbed-billed Auk, Curled-crested Auk, and Horned-billed Guillemot — are arranged against an arctic seascape of ice floes and distant snow-capped mountains. Plate 402 of Audubon's Birds of America brings together species collected on the Northwest Coast and largely unknown to Atlantic subscribers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Brown Creeper - 2. Californian Nuthatch (Plate 415)
description: A Brown Creeper fans its wings in mid-flight to the left while two Californian Nuthatches cling to a lichen-covered tree trunk in their characteristic head-up and head-down poses. Plate 415 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., contrasts two bark-foraging species of the western forests.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Bullock's Oriole - 2. Baltimore Oriole - 3. Mexican Goldfinch - 4. Varied Thrush - 5. Common Water Thrush (Plate 433)
englishTitle: 433 Orioles, Mexican Goldfinch, Varied Thrush and Water Thrush
description: An assortment of bright passerines crowds a leafy branch: two oriole species, a Lesser Goldfinch, a Varied Thrush and a Northern Waterthrush. Such mixed plates were a practical way to publish western specimens that reached Audubon late in the project.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Burrowing Owl - 2. Large-headed Burrowing Owl - 3. Little night Owl - 4. Columbian Owl - 5. Short-eared Owl (Plate 432)
englishTitle: 432 Burrowing Owl, Little Night Owl, Columbian Owl and Short-eared Owl
description: Five small owls are arranged across a grassy open landscape: the Burrowing Owl and Large-headed Burrowing Owl perch on branches at left, while the Little Night Owl and Columbian Owl share a central branch, and the large Short-eared Owl crouches on the ground at centre-bottom. Plate 432 of John James Audubon's Birds of America presents a comparative study of head shape, leg length, and wing form across these related species, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Chesnut-backed Titmouse - 2. Black-capt Titmouse - 3. Chesnut-crowned Titmouse (Plate 353)
description: Multiple chestnut-backed, black-capped, and chestnut-crowned titmice are arranged around a large hanging moss nest suspended from leafy branches, with additional birds perched on lower stems. Plate 353 of Audubon's Birds of America presents a nest-building scene that allows comparison of the three closely related western and boreal forms.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Chestnut-coloured Finch - 2. Black-headed Siskin - 3. Black crown Bunting - 4. Arctic Ground Finch (Plate 394)
englishTitle: Chestnut-coloured Finch, Black-headed Siskin and Other Finches (Plate 394)
description: Four small seed-eaters are arranged across twigs and grassy ground: the bright yellow Chestnut-coloured Finch with black head, a streaked finch catching an insect near a pink flower, a rufous-breasted bird at mid-ground, and a dark, rufous-sided Arctic Ground Finch at the base. Plate 394 of Audubon's Birds of America groups newly described western species that reached Audubon as study skins during the later phases of the folio's production.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Columbian Water Ouzel - 2. Arctic Water Ouzel (Plate 435)
description: Two Water Ouzels (American Dippers) are depicted on rocky cliff ledges above a rushing waterfall, one leaning forward as though about to descend toward the water below. Plate 435 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents the Columbian and Arctic Water Ouzel, western specimens associated with Townsend's Pacific collecting expeditions, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Evening Grosbeak - 2. Spotted Grosbeak (Plate 373)
description: Plate 373 of Audubon's Birds of America shows Evening Grosbeaks and Spotted (Black-headed) Grosbeaks perched on bare grey branches. The male Evening Grosbeak at the top displays its bold yellow body and black-and-white wings, while the Black-headed Grosbeak below shows the species' black hood and deep cinnamon-orange breast. The contrasting massive seed-cracking bills of both species are a visual focus of the composition.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Golden-winged Warbler - 2. Cape May Warbler (Plate 414)
description: Several Golden-winged and Cape May Warblers perch among leafy branches, the Golden-winged individuals showing their black throat patch and bold yellow wing bars, the Cape May birds displaying the warm chestnut-orange cheek patches and streaked yellow underparts. Plate 414 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., presents multiple specimens of each species for comparative study.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Goshawk - 2. Stanley Hawk (Plate 141)
description: Three raptors occupy a single composition: an immature goshawk perched atop a stump, a dark-mantled adult goshawk below, and the Stanley hawk — now identified as the Cooper's hawk — shown at right. The plate allowed Audubon to document multiple plumage stages of these accipiters and is Plate 141 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Hairy Woodpecker - 2. Red-bellied Woodpecker - 3. Red-shafted Woodpecker - 4. Lewis' Woodpecker - 5. Red-breasted Woodpecker (Plate 416)
englishTitle: Hairy, Red-bellied, Red-shafted, Lewis's, Red-breasted Woodpeckers (Plate 416)
description: A composite study of five woodpecker species posed on dead snags, comparing crown patterns, barred backs and tail bracing across eastern and western North America. Such grouped plates appeared in the later supplementary numbers of the folio, accommodating species Audubon received from western expeditions.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Havell's Tern - 2. Trudeau's Tern (Plate 409)
description: Havell's Tern and Trudeau's Tern perch together on a rocky, grass-covered coastal headland, a wide estuary and distant shore stretching behind them. Plate 409 of Audubon's Birds of America features two tern species named by Audubon, distinguishable by bill colour and cap pattern, with scattered shells arranged at their feet.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Lark Finch - 2. Prairie Finch - 3. Brown Song Sparrow (Plate 390)
description: Three birds of the Great Plains are arranged on twigs and grassy ground: the Lark Finch with its rufous-marked head perches above, the dark Prairie Finch clings to a twig mid-plate, and a pair of Brown Song Sparrows forage at the base. Plate 390 of Audubon's Birds of America, published by Havell between 1827 and 1838, gathers species representative of the interior grassland and Pacific slope.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Lazuli Finch - 2. Clay-coloured Finch - 3. Oregon Snow Finch (Plate 398)
description: Three western finches share a branch of pink-flowering shrub: the Lazuli Finch above with its blue head and orange breast, the plain Clay-coloured Finch at centre, and the darker Oregon Snow Finch below. Plate 398 of Audubon's Birds of America groups these birds of the western interior, assembled from study skins for the folio's later numbers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Lazuli Finch - 2. Crimson-necked Bull-Finch - 3. Gray-crowned Linnet - 4. Cow-pen Bird - 5. Evening Grosbeak - 6. Brown Longspur (Plate 424)
englishTitle: Lazuli Finch, Evening Grosbeak and Other Finches (Plate 424)
description: Six finch-like passerines crowd a single branch, ranging from the turquoise Lazuli Bunting to the heavy-billed Evening Grosbeak. Such crowded composite sheets close the folio, making efficient use of the costly copper plates as Audubon hurried to incorporate western discoveries.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Little Tawny Thrush - 2. Ptiliogony's Townsendi - 3. Canada Jay (Plate 419)
description: Three forest birds share a sprig of foliage: the russet Hermit Thrush form, Townsend's Solitaire with its pale eye-ring, and the soft grey Canada Jay. The grouping pulls together species new to science from John Kirk Townsend's Columbia River collections.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Little Tyrant Fly-catcher - 2. Small-headed Fly-catcher - 3. Blue Mountain Warbler - 4. Bartran's Vireo - 5. Short-legged Pewee - 6. Rocky Mountain Fly-catcher (Plate 434)
englishTitle: 434 Flycatchers, Blue Mountain Warbler and Bartram's Vireo
description: Six small insect-eaters share a single twig, several of them species known only from a handful of skins and never reliably observed since. The plate has long fascinated ornithologists as a possible record of birds now extinct or never validly described.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Louisiana Tanager - 2. Scarlet Tanager (Plate 354)
description: Four tanagers occupy leafy branches: two Louisiana tanagers (western tanager) showing the male's red head, yellow body, and black wings alongside a duller individual, a vivid all-red scarlet tanager male in flight, and a greenish female below. Plate 354 of Audubon's Birds of America places these species together as a comparative study of the two most colourful North American tanagers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Maria's Woodpecker - 2. Three-toed Woodpecker - 3. Phillips' Woodpecker - 4. Canadian Woodpecker - 5. Harris's Woodpecker - 6. Audubon's Woodpecker (Plate 417)
description: Six woodpecker forms are stacked on a single trunk, several of them now treated as regional races of the Hairy and American Three-toed Woodpeckers. The plate reflects the taxonomic optimism of 1830s ornithology, when subtle plumage variants were routinely described as full species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Mountain Mocking bird - 2. Varied Thrush (Plate 369)
description: Plate 369 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the Mountain Mockingbird (now Sage Thrasher) with male and female Varied Thrushes on a flowering shrub branch. The thrashers show the plain grey-brown streaked upperparts and faintly spotted breast distinctive of the species, while the Varied Thrush male displays its rich orange breast and black breast-band. The plate was published between 1827 and 1838 as part of the double elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Nuttall's Starling - 2. Yellow-headed Troopial - 3. Bullock's Oriole (Plate 388)
description: Three species share a cascade of bare branches: Nuttall's Starling at the top with its black plumage and scarlet shoulder patch, the Yellow-headed Troopial below with its striking yellow head and chest, and Bullock's Oriole at the bottom showing orange and black. A smaller female or immature figure also appears to the right. Plate 388 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Plumed--Partridge - 2. Thick--legged Partridge (Plate 423)
description: Two western quail are figured together: the Mountain Quail with its long straight head plume, and the Scaled Quail showing its distinctive crescent-edged feathering. The plate draws on specimens from Townsend and Nuttall's overland expedition to the Pacific.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Townsend's Warbler - 2. Arctic Blue-bird - 3. Western Blue-bird (Plate 393)
description: Five western birds representing three recently described species share a branch bearing red blossoms: Townsend's Warbler with its yellow and black head, two vivid blue Arctic Blue-birds, and two Western Blue-birds with blue backs and rusty breasts. Plate 393 of Audubon's Birds of America, published by Havell between 1827 and 1838, drew on Pacific Northwest skins supplied by John Kirk Townsend.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Violet-green Cormorant - 2. Townsend's Cormorant (Plate 412)
description: A Violet-green Cormorant and a Townsend's Cormorant stand on a flat rocky ledge with the open sea behind them, the smaller Violet-green displaying brilliantly iridescent blue-green plumage and a red facial patch, while the larger Townsend's shows a pale buff chest and yellow bill. Plate 412 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two Pacific cormorant species drawn from specimens collected on the West Coast.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. White-legged Oyster-catcher - 2. Slender-billed Oyster-catcher (Plate 427)
description: Two dark-plumaged oystercatchers are shown on a rocky shore: the Slender-billed Oyster-catcher (standing, with a bright red bill and red legs) and the White-legged Oyster-catcher (prostrate, probing among small bivalves with an orange-yellow bill). Both names are now subsumed into the Black Oystercatcher of the Pacific coast. Plate 427 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Winter Wren - 2. Rock Wren (Plate 360)
description: Four wrens are depicted in a naturalistic setting of mossy ground, lichen-covered branches, and low herbage: the Winter Wren figures perch on branches and among ground-level vegetation, while the Rock Wrens appear near rocky elements at right. Plate 360 of Audubon's Birds of America presents the two species with careful attention to the fine barring that marks the plumage of both.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: I. Yellow billed Magpie - 2. Stellers Jay - 3. Ultramarine Jay - 4. Clark's Crow (Plate 362)
englishTitle: Yellow-billed Magpie, Steller's Jay, Ultramarine Jay, Clark's Crow (Plate 362)
description: Plate 362 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts four western corvids — Yellow-billed Magpie, Steller's Jay, Ultramarine Jay, and Clark's Crow — arranged on branches of sweetgum amid palmate leaves and spiky seed-balls. The California-endemic Yellow-billed Magpie occupies the lower left, its yellow bill and grey-and-black-green plumage distinct from the deeply blue Steller's Jay above. Published between 1827 and 1838, the plate is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Iceland or Jer Falcon (Plate 366)
description: Plate 366 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two Iceland or Gyrfalcons, both in the pale white morph, against a dark teal background. One bird is shown in mid-flight with wings spread wide, its white plumage marked with dark barring, while the other perches below. The composition emphasises the circumpolar raptor's impressive wingspan and the near-white colouration characteristic of its northern populations.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Indigo Bird (Plate 74)
description: Three indigo buntings — two full-blue males and a brownish female — are shown on a climbing vine with pendant small flowers and berries, the males' saturated blue plumage capturing one of the most vivid colours in North American ornithology. Plate 74 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) employs the common name 'Indigo Bird' current before the species was reclassified among the cardinal-grosbeak family.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Italian Midday
description: A young Italian woman reaches into a sun-shot vine to pluck a heavy cluster of grapes, her white blouse loosened in the midday heat. Painted in 1827 during Bryullov's residency in Italy on a stipend from the Society for the Encouragement of Artists, the picture now belongs to the State Russian Museum.

title: Ivory Gull (Plate 287)
description: Two Ivory Gulls — an adult in pure white plumage and a juvenile with dark spotting — stand on rocky, lichen-covered ground beside scattered shells, against a grey overcast sky.
