The adult's black legs and yellow bill are clearly rendered, with the lobed feet of the juvenile also visible. Plate 287 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ivory-billed Woodpecker (Plate 66)
description: Four ivory-billed woodpeckers — male, female, and two immatures — are shown clinging to a lichen-covered dead trunk, the male's vivid red crest and both sexes' distinctive ivory bills rendered at life size. Plate 66 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), it stands as one of the most celebrated images of a species now widely regarded as extinct, last reliably documented in the old-growth bottomland forests of the American South.
credit: University of Pittsburgh, Audubon's Birds of America, Darlington Digital Library , Image

title: Jager (Plate 253)
description: A jaeger perched on a grassy coastal mound, an open oyster shell beside it and icy peaks visible in the distant background. The bird's dark brown upperparts and pale streaked breast are rendered with characteristic precision. Plate 253 of Audubon's Birds of America documents this pelagic seabird, known for its habit of pursuing other birds to steal their catches.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Kentucky Warbler (Plate 38)
description: Two olive-and-yellow warblers with bold black sideburns perch on a flowering magnolia branch. The composition pairs an eastern songbird with a southern bloom, a habit Audubon used to compress habitat and season into one engraved sheet.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Key-west Dove (Plate 167)
description: A pair of Key West Doves face each other in a billing posture on a fallen log, their rich rufous-brown plumage and iridescent eye-rings rendered against a backdrop of morning glories and low coastal vegetation. The ground-level composition emphasises the species' terrestrial habits. Plate 167 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Kildeer Plover (Plate 225)
description: Charadrius vociferus shown in two figures on a rocky shore: one standing upright and alert, the second in a spread-wing distraction display that exposes the vivid russet rump. The double black breast bands are clearly depicted on both individuals. Plate 225 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: King Duck (Plate 276)
description: Audubon pairs a male king eider — slate-blue crown, vivid green cheek patches, and bulbous orange-pink forehead shield — with a soberly barred brown female against an Arctic coastal backdrop. The dramatic sexual dimorphism of the species is the plate's central subject, with the male standing tall on a rock and the female resting at the water's edge. Plate 276 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Kittiwake Gull (Plate 224)
description: Rissa tridactyla rendered with the species' clean grey mantle and black wingtips, perched on rocks suggestive of ocean cliffs. The plate's restrained palette emphasises the kittiwake's pelagic, colony-nesting life.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Labrador Falcon (Plate 196)
description: Two Labrador falcons — a dark morph of the gyrfalcon — are shown on bare branches, one perched compactly from above and one with wings partially spread looking upward, both rendered in very dark grey-black plumage. Plate 196 of John James Audubon's Birds of America shows male and female adults and reflects observations Audubon made during his 1833 Labrador expedition.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Lapland Long-spur (Plate 365)
description: Plate 365 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts Lapland Longspurs on bare ground before a lake and mountain backdrop. Three birds are shown: a breeding male with a black face and chestnut nape stands prominently, while two more streaked, sparrow-like individuals illustrate alternate plumages. The plate appeared in the double elephant folio published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Large billed Puffin (Plate 293)
description: A Large-billed Puffin stands on a low flat rock at the water's edge while a second bird floats on the sea behind it, with a mountain headland visible in the distance. The species' deep, ridged orange-and-yellow bill and black-and-white plumage are rendered in detail. Plate 293 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Le Petit Caporal (Plate 75)
description: Le Petit Caporal — labelled in the plate as Falco temerarius — is shown as a single small hawk perched on a dead stump entwined with ivy, the banded tail and body shape suggesting an accipiter type. Plate 75 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) preserves a vernacular French name used in Louisiana that never entered standard ornithological nomenclature.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Least Bittern (Plate 210)
description: Three Least Bitterns are shown in marsh reeds: one adult to the left in a low horizontal stance, and two central birds adopting the species' characteristic alarm posture with bills pointed skyward and streaked buff plumage blending into the surrounding stems. The composition illustrates both typical foraging and concealment behaviours. Plate 210 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Least Stormy-Petrel (Plate 340)
description: A tiny pelagic petrel skims a wave trough, wings raised in the fluttering flight that earned the family its name. Audubon shows the species over open ocean, a setting rare in the folio and demanding extensive aquatint tone for the swell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Least Water-hen (Plate 349)
description: Two least water-hens stand at a marshy shoreline, one rufous-backed and one dark-plumaged, with reeds rising behind them. Plate 349 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts Rallus jamaicensis against a low-lying coastal marsh landscape with clouded sky.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Lesser Red-Poll (Plate 375)
description: Plate 375 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Lesser Redpolls (Common Redpolls) perched on a flowering shrub bearing small white blossoms and pale berries. Both birds display the species' distinctive red forecrown, and the male shows a rosy-pink flush on the breast. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838 and is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Lesser Tern (Plate 319)
description: Plate 319 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Lesser Terns (now Least Tern, Sternula antillarum) in flight against a dark sky. The adult below displays the black cap, yellow bill, and white forked-tail form of the breeding bird; the upper figure, in speckled brownish plumage, represents an immature or autumn bird. The Least Tern remains one of the smallest terns in the Americas, nesting colonially on sandy beaches and riverbanks.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Lincoln Finch (Plate 193)
description: Lincoln's sparrow depicted on a flowering branch, named for Audubon's young Labrador-expedition companion Thomas Lincoln. Subtly streaked plumage and a buff malar stripe distinguish the species from related sparrows.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Little Auk (Plate 339)
description: Plate 339 of Birds of America shows two little auks (dovekies): one swimming at the surface with a small fish in its bill, and one standing on a coastal rock in bold black-and-white breeding plumage. The compact, stub-billed auk is depicted against a backdrop of open sea and distant cliffs. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Little Owl (Plate 199)
description: Two owls are depicted: one perched on a bare branch in three-quarter view, and a second shown on a rocky outcrop with wings spread wide, securing a small mammal in its talons. The plate is labelled Plate CXCIX of Birds of America by John James Audubon, with the Latin Strix acadica identifying the North American species Audubon called the Little Owl, now the Northern Saw-whet Owl. Hand-applied colour over aquatint models the warm brown upperparts and streaked white underparts characteristic of the species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Little Sandpiper (Plate 320)
description: Plate 320 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Least Sandpipers on the rocks of a rushing stream, one with bill tilted upward and one leaning forward near the water's edge. The species' warm brown-and-buff spotted upperparts and pale underparts are carefully rendered, and the yellowish legs that distinguish it from the otherwise similar Semipalmated Sandpiper are visible on the foreground bird. Plate 320 of the Birds of America is credited to the University of Pittsburgh collection.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Little Screech Owl (Plate 97)
description: Three Eastern Screech-Owls illustrate the species' striking colour polymorphism, with red-morph and grey-morph individuals shown together on a single branch. Hand-coloured aquatint engraved by Robert Havell Jr., emphasizing the small owl's prominent ear tufts and yellow eyes.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Loggerhead Shrike (Plate 57)
description: A pair of shrikes occupies the spiny branches of a green-briar, the predatory songbird's hooked bill and black mask carefully delineated. The botanical setting accurately records a thicket habitat where shrikes impale prey on thorns.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Long-billed Curlew (Plate 231)
description: Two long-billed curlews stand among tall marsh reeds, their enormous decurved bills and cinnamon-buff plumage rendered at close range against a distant view of Charleston harbour. Audubon's use of a recognisable city skyline as backdrop is unusual for the series. Plate 231 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Long-eared Owl (Plate 383)
description: A Long-eared Owl perches on a single bare gray branch against an open background, its elongated ear tufts and orange-tinted facial disc clearly visible as it turns its head to one side. The mottled brown, buff, and cream plumage is rendered in detail. Plate 383 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Long-legged Avocet (Plate 328)
description: The Black-necked Stilt, here depicted under the older name Long-legged Avocet, stands on rocks against an open coastal horizon, its sharply contrasting black-and-white plumage supported by improbably long reddish-pink legs. Plate 328 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a single bird, and the near-vertical composition emphasises the slender, stilted form.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Long-legged Sandpiper (Plate 344)
description: Plate 344 of Birds of America shows two long-legged sandpipers — now identified as the stilt sandpiper — standing on rocky ground above a coastal shoreline. Both birds display a pinkish-rufous wash on the neck and breast consistent with breeding plumage, and the patterned upper parts are rendered with careful tonal gradation. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Long-tailed Duck (Plate 312)
description: Long-tailed Ducks, then called Old-squaws, are shown in winter pied plumage with the drake's slender tail trailing behind. Audubon studied them on the Atlantic coast where they wintered in noisy rafts.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Long-tailed or Dusky Grous (Plate 361)
description: A dark male and a brown-barred female dusky grouse stand on open mountain terrain with rocky peaks and a distant valley visible behind them. Plate 361 of Audubon's Birds of America captures the species' sexual dimorphism, with the male's dark plumage and reddish eye-comb contrasting against the female's cryptic patterning.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Louisiana Hawk (Plate 392)
description: A Louisiana Hawk — now known as Harris's Hawk — perches alert on a broken stump, its dark plumage contrasting with the rich chestnut shoulder patches that distinguish the species. Plate 392 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by J. Smyth from Audubon's drawing, presents the bird in the composed lateral profile typical of his raptor studies.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Louisiana Heron (Plate 217)
description: Tricolored heron, Egretta tricolor, captured in a sinuous wading pose with white belly stripe set against slate body. The dynamic curve of the neck typifies Audubon's preference for active, narrative postures over static specimen views.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Louisiana Water Thrush (Plate 19)
description: Parkesia motacilla shown probing along a streamside branch, rendered with the characteristic streaked underparts and bold supercilium. Engraved by Robert Havell Jr. from Audubon's double-elephant folio watercolour, with delicate aquatint tonal washes evoking damp woodland habitat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: MacGillivray's Finch (Plate 355)
description: Two small streaked sparrows perch among upright salt-marsh reeds, with two pale butterflies included in the composition above them. Plate 355 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts MacGillivray's Finch — now considered a seaside sparrow — named by Audubon for the Scottish naturalist William MacGillivray, his collaborator on the Ornithological Biography.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Mallard Duck (Plate 221)
description: Anas platyrhynchos shown in a group of males and females amid tall marsh vegetation, the drakes' bottle-green heads and chestnut breasts contrasting with the streaked brown plumage of the hens. A blue speculum is visible on the foreground female. Plate 221 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Mangrove Cuckoo (Plate 169)
description: The Mangrove Cuckoo perches in dense coastal foliage, its buff underparts and black ear-patch picked out against tropical leaves. Audubon recorded the species during his Florida Keys expedition, where he distinguished it from the more familiar Yellow-billed Cuckoo.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Mangrove Humming Bird (Plate 184)
description: A mangrove hummingbird hovering at tropical blossoms, its iridescence captured through the layered aquatint process. The plate reflects the broader nineteenth-century fascination with the dazzling plumage of New World hummingbirds.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Manks Shearwater (Plate 295)
description: Plate 295 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a Manks Shearwater perched on the sea surface, dark brown-black above and white below, with a rocky coastal headland visible in the background. The species — a transatlantic pelagic seabird — is rendered in profile, its pale underparts contrasting sharply with the deep colouring of the back and wings.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Marsh Hawk (Plate 356)
description: Three marsh hawks are presented: a large brown bird perched prominently at top, a grey male on a branch below it, and a third bird at the bottom feeding on prey amid marsh grasses near water. Plate 356 of Audubon's Birds of America captures multiple plumages of the northern harrier, known for the white rump patch visible in the grey male.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Marsh Tern (Plate 410)
description: A Marsh Tern plunges steeply downward against a pale blue sky, wings raised and bill angled sharply toward a small insect below. Plate 410 of Audubon's Birds of America — labelled Sterna anglica on the plate — depicts the bird in a dramatic diving attitude, rendered in summer plumage with a full black cap.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Marsh Wren (Plate 100)
description: Plate 100 of The Birds of America shows the Marsh Wren clinging among reedy stems of its nesting habitat. Engraved and aquatinted by Robert Havell Jr. from Audubon's watercolor, the life-size composition pairs species portrait with carefully observed wetland setting.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Meadow Lark (Plate 136)
description: Eastern meadowlarks posed in tall prairie grass, the yellow breast and black V boldly displayed. The composition links the species firmly to the open agricultural country in which Audubon most often observed it.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Mississippi Kite (Plate 117)
description: Two Mississippi Kites perched on lichen- and moss-draped branches, the male above with wings partially spread and the female below. The slate-grey plumage and pointed wings characteristic of the species are carefully rendered in Audubon's Plate CXVII from Birds of America (1827–1838), credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Mocking Bird (Plate 21)
description: Mimus polyglottos engaged with a coiled rattlesnake amid yellow jessamine vines, one of Audubon's most narrative compositions. The dramatic encounter drew scientific criticism over snake-climbing accuracy but established the plate's enduring fame.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Mortlake Terrace
description: A Thames-side terrace bathed in the dissolving glare of low evening sun, with a small black dog famously cut out and pasted onto the foreground lawn. The picture is among Turner's most radical experiments in painting directly into the light source.

title: Nashville Warbler (Plate 89)
description: Two Nashville Warblers move among the leaves and red berries of a leafy branch, their olive-green upperparts and yellow underparts shown in active foraging poses. Plate 89 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint engraved by Robert Havell Jr., held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Night Hawk (Plate 147)
description: Nighthawks wheel and rest in this composition, their long pointed wings and cryptic mottled plumage shown in multiple attitudes. Audubon characteristically combined several individuals on a single sheet to display sex differences and flight posture in one image.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Night Heron or Qua bird (Plate 236)
description: An adult and an immature black-crowned night heron stand side by side in dense marsh vegetation, the sleek slate-and-white adult leaning toward the water and the streaky brown juvenile standing upright nearby. The plate presents the species' dramatic age-related plumage change in a single composition. Plate 236 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Noddy Tern (Plate 275)
description: A brown noddy with its sooty body and pale cap, perched on a tropical branch. The plate reflects the species' colonial nesting on warm-water islands, where birds build flat platforms in low trees rather than scraping in the sand like most terns.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Nuttall's lesser-marsh Wren (Plate 175)
description: Marsh wrens perched among reedy stalks, named here for the naturalist Thomas Nuttall. The plate places the small passerines within a habitat vignette, a hallmark of Audubon's life-size approach to ornithological portraiture.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Olive sided Flycatcher (Plate 174)
description: Two olive-sided flycatchers — male above, female below — are shown on a conifer branch bearing blue-grey cones in Plate 174 of Birds of America. The species' characteristic large-headed silhouette, dark flanks, and pale central breast are carefully recorded. The aquatint, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., reflects Audubon's standard practice of depicting both sexes on the same plate.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Orange-crowned Warbler (Plate 178)
description: Two orange-crowned warblers cling to the slender stems of a flowering shrub bearing small pink-white blossoms in Plate 178 of Birds of America. The species' uniform olive-green plumage and inconspicuous head-stripe are characteristic, the hidden orange crown patch not prominently displayed. The plate was engraved, etched, and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. for Audubon's double elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Orchard Oriole (Plate 42)
description: Several Orchard Orioles — including a yellow-green female and a brick-red adult male — animate a thorny locust branch bearing compound foliage and a suspended woven nest. Plate 42 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Painted Finch (Plate 53)
description: The painted bunting, called the Nonpareil for its blue, green and crimson plumage, is shown with several individuals on a sprig of wild almond. The plate demonstrates the colourists' ability to register multiple unmixed pigments through the aquatint ground without muddying the saturated hues.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Palm Warbler (Plate 163)
description: Palm Warblers are placed among low foliage with their characteristic tail-pumping posture suggested by the bird's downward-curved attitude. The plate reflects Audubon's habit of incorporating diagnostic behaviour into otherwise still compositions.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Passenger Pigeon (Plate 62)
description: A male and female passenger pigeon are shown in an allofeeding interaction on a branch in Plate 62 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the male's slate-blue head and rich rufous breast contrasting with the olive-brown upperparts of the female above. The intimate pose documents a social behaviour of a species then numbering in the billions but driven to extinction by 1914. Audubon's composition captures both the beauty and the vitality of a bird whose loss he could not have foreseen.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pectoral Sandpiper (Plate 294)
description: Two Pectoral Sandpipers stand on a sandy, shell-strewn coastal shore with water and low hills behind them, the male slightly larger than the female. The species' sharply demarcated streaked breast band and warm brown-and-chestnut upperparts are clearly depicted. Plate 294 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pewit Flycatcher (Plate 120)
description: Two Eastern Phoebes — here under their older name Pewit Flycatcher — perched on the stems of a cotton plant in full boll. One bird is alert with open bill, the other below with wings spread. Plate CXX from Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pied Duck (Plate 332)
description: The Labrador Duck, extinct since around 1878, appears here in piebald drake plumage and brown female dress. Audubon's plate is now a historical document of one of the first North American birds lost to human pressure.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pied oyster-catcher (Plate 223)
description: Haematopus palliatus depicted in active running pose along a surf-washed shoreline, the long vivid-red bill, black hood, and white underparts rendered with bold tonal contrast. Waves and a sandy beach constitute the entire background, placing the bird firmly in its coastal habitat. Plate 223 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pigeon Hawk (Plate 92)
description: A male and female Merlin (Pigeon Hawk) perch on a leafy branch, shown in the plate Audubon labelled Falco columbarius. The darker, brown-backed male sits above the streaked, buff-breasted female, wings partially fanned. Plate 92 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pigmy Curlew (Plate 263)
description: A pygmy curlew, today known as the curlew sandpiper, depicted with its decurved bill probing at the tide line. Audubon's aquatint records a Eurasian visitor to North American shores, in transitional plumage between the rufous breeding dress and pale winter coat.

title: Pileated Woodpecker (Plate 111)
description: Plate 111 fills the double-elephant sheet with four Pileated Woodpeckers on a tree trunk entwined with grape vine. The birds' flaming red crests are a vivid accent against the dark plumage and bark, and the composition showcases Audubon's signature pairing of life-size scale with active, behaviour-driven groupings.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pin tailed Duck (Plate 227)
description: A drake northern pintail and his mate are paired against a watery margin, the male's chocolate head and slender tail-spike contrasted with the hen's softer scalloping. The aquatint records the species' elegant body line and the fine vermiculation across the flanks that Audubon studied closely from skinned specimens.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pine Creeping Warbler (Plate 140)
description: Pine warblers, under an older common name, posed on a pine bough heavy with cones. Audubon ties the species inseparably to its host tree, reflecting the strict habitat fidelity that gives the warbler its name.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pine Finch (Plate 180)
description: Pine finches (now pine siskins) perched among conifer foliage, with streaked plumage and yellow wing-flashes precisely registered. The plate exemplifies Audubon's dual interest in scientific accuracy and decorative botanical setting.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pine Grosbeak (Plate 358)
description: Three pine grosbeaks are arranged on pine branches: a crimson-red male at lower left, a grey-brown bird at centre right, and an olive-green individual at top. Plate 358 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts the species' marked sexual dimorphism, with the heavy bill characteristic of these large boreal finches clearly visible across all three figures.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pine Swamp Warbler (Plate 148)
description: Two Pine Swamp Warblers are shown among the broad leaves and ripe red berry clusters of a deciduous shrub in this plate from the Havell edition of Birds of America. The birds' greenish and grey-blue plumage is set off against the warm reddish-brown berries and large linden-like leaves. The plate was etched and hand-coloured in London by Robert Havell Jr. after Audubon's original watercolour studies.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Pinnated Grous (Plate 186)
description: Pinnated grouse (greater prairie chicken) depicted in a lively group: a male in full display with neck-sacs inflated and pinnae raised, alongside females and a chick, set against an open prairie landscape with yellow lilies. Plate 186 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents the species' courtship behaviour and prairie habitat across male, female, and young plumages.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Piping Plover (Plate 220)
description: Charadrius melodus on pale sand, the bird's sandy-buff back and partial neck band described with minimal etched line. The sparse beach setting reflects the species' preference for open Atlantic shoreline.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Prairie Starling (Plate 420)
description: Two birds perch on a slender budding branch: a male with jet-black plumage and a prominent red-orange shoulder patch, consistent with Audubon's Prairie Starling (now identified as the Red-winged Blackbird), and above it a smaller streaked brownish female. Plate 420 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Prairie Titlark (Plate 80)
description: A single Prairie Titlark (American Pipit) stands on the ground among low vegetation with pink blooms, reflecting the species' terrestrial habits. Plate 80 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Prairie Warbler (Plate 14)
description: Two prairie warblers perch among flowering branches, their yellow underparts and side streaking carefully delineated. The plate is typical of the early Havell numbers, in which Audubon paired songbirds with the specific vegetation in which he had observed them feeding.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Prothonotary Warbler restored (Plate 3)
description: Brilliant golden-yellow warblers move through a tangle of cane and creeper at the edge of a southern swamp. Audubon drew the species in the bottomland habitat where it nests in flooded tree cavities, a detail he stressed in the accompanying Ornithological Biography.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Puffin (Plate 213)
description: Atlantic puffin, Fratercula arctica, shown with breeding-season bill ornament and orange feet. The plate likely draws on observations from Audubon's 1833 expedition to Labrador, where he studied seabird colonies first-hand.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Purple Finch (Plate 4)
description: Two raspberry-red males and a streaked brown female Purple Finch cling to a pine branch hung with small cones, the males' rich crimson heads set against the sparse needles. Plate 4 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the species' marked sexual dimorphism and was among the earliest plates engraved and published by Havell from 1827 onwards.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Purple Gallinule (Plate 305)
description: Plate 305 of Birds of America presents a single adult Purple Gallinule striding along an open bank with a river and distant marsh vegetation behind it. The bird's iridescent blue-violet plumage, green-tinged back, red-and-yellow bill with a pale blue frontal shield, and long yellow-green toes are rendered with precision in the hand-coloured aquatint. Audubon depicted the species in adult spring plumage, as noted in the plate's caption.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Purple Grakle or Common Crow Blackbird (Plate 7)
description: Common Grackles cluster on a maize stalk, ears split open to expose the kernels they raid. The composition links the species directly to its reputation as an agricultural pest, with iridescent plumage rendered through layered hand-colouring over an aquatint base.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Purple Heron (Plate 256)
description: Two herons fill Plate 256: an adult in dark breeding plumage with a striking rust-orange neck and shaggy crest, and a white-plumaged bird standing beside lush tropical foliage. The dark bird's vivid blue legs and upright, alert stance contrast with the quieter posture of its companion. Audubon based the plate on Ardea refescens, the reddish egret, recording both colour morphs of the species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Purple Martin (Plate 22)
description: Several purple martins gather around a hollow gourd nest, the glossy blue-black males and duller females shown in the cooperative groupings typical of the colony-nesting swallow. The plate documents an early form of artificial nest box used by southern planters, embedding ethnography within ornithological observation.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Purple Sandpiper (Plate 284)
description: Three Purple Sandpipers in varying plumage are shown on rocky outcrops by the water's edge, their dark, mottled backs and yellowish-orange legs clearly depicted against the pale stone. The species favours wave-washed rocky shores along North Atlantic coasts, and Audubon's composition captures several individuals in close proximity on such a habitat. Plate 284 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rathbone Warbler (Plate 65)
description: A small warbler named in honour of the Rathbone family of Liverpool, patrons during the artist's English subscription drive. Now considered an immature or variant yellow warbler rather than a distinct species, the plate preserves a name otherwise lost from ornithology.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Raven (Plate 101)
description: Plate 101 presents the Common Raven at full life size, perched on a branch laden with hickory nuts, its beak open. Glossy black plumage is rendered through Havell's hand-coloured aquatint, and the male is labelled on the plate as Corvus corax.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Razor Bill (Plate 214)
description: Alca torda depicted in two figures — male and female — swimming on choppy water before a cliff coastline, with the species' characteristic laterally flattened bill and white vertical stripe faithfully rendered. The dark upperparts and clean white underparts show the sharp tonal contrast of breeding plumage. Plate 214 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red backed Sandpiper (Plate 290)
description: Two Red-backed Sandpipers are shown on a rocky shore: a winter-plumaged bird in grey on the left and a breeding-plumaged bird with brick-red upperparts and a black belly patch on the right. The pairing to show both seasonal plumages was a characteristic device in the later plates of Birds of America. Plate 290, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red headed Woodpecker (Plate 27)
description: Plate 27 depicts adult red-headed woodpeckers — crimson head, white belly, and ink-black wings with bold white secondaries — attending young birds at a nest cavity in a weathered dead tree. Audubon records both flying adults and nestlings at different stages, documenting the species across its life cycle. The plate is from Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red Phalarope (Plate 255)
description: Red phalaropes depicted in their rust-coloured summer dress, slender bills probing at the water's edge. Hand-coloured aquatint by Robert Havell Jr. brings out the contrast between the rich plumage and the muted tones of the Arctic-tinged habitat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-breasted Merganser (Plate 401)
description: A female Red-breasted Merganser flies overhead with wings fully spread while the drake swims below, his ragged green crest, white collar, and rust-washed breast contrasting with the female's brown head and white chin. Plate 401 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the sexes in action against a wetland setting of pitcher plants and reeds, engraved and coloured by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-breasted Nuthatch (Plate 105)
description: Plate 105 depicts two Red-breasted Nuthatches on a broken dead tree trunk, one bird in its characteristic head-down posture. The slate-blue back, rust-orange underparts, and bold black-and-white facial striping are rendered at life size in this plate from Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-breasted Sandpiper (Plate 315)
description: The Red Knot, here under its older common name, is shown in the rust-coloured breeding plumage that earns the species its alternative title. Audubon paired it with a winter-plumaged bird to record the dramatic seasonal change.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-breasted Snipe (Plate 335)
description: Long-billed dowitchers, then known as red-breasted snipe, probe a shoreline in postures observed during Audubon's wetland field studies. The plate uses Robert Havell Jr.'s aquatint and engraving to render the streaked, cinnamon-toned breeding dress.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-Cockaded Woodpecker (Plate 389)
description: Three Red-cockaded Woodpeckers cling to a single smooth-barked trunk: one bird near a cavity at the top, another mid-trunk with the male's tiny red cockade visible behind the eye, and a third lower on the tree. The bold black-and-white ladder pattern of the back and the white cheek patch are the key marks rendered at life size in the double elephant folio format. Plate 389 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-eyed Vireo (Plate 150)
description: A Red-eyed Vireo perches on a bare branch above a spray of compound foliage in Plate 150 of Birds of America, with a large spider suspended from its web prominently depicted in the upper left of the composition. The bird's olive-green back, white eyebrow stripe, and diagnostic eye are carefully rendered by the Havell workshop colourists. Audubon's inclusion of the spider reflects his broader interest in recording the natural relationships of his subjects.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-headed Duck (Plate 322)
description: A Redhead drake and female stand on a bank, the drake's deep chestnut head and pale grey back clearly distinct from the closely related Canvasback. Plate 322 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the two sexes to document the species' strong plumage contrast.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-necked Grebe (Plate 298)
description: Plate 298 of Birds of America depicts two Red-necked Grebes on a grassy bank with a landscape of cliffs and water behind them. The left-hand bird is in rich breeding plumage — a deep chestnut neck and dark cap with small reddish eye — while the right-hand bird shows the greyer winter dress, its yellow-tipped bill clearly rendered. The contrast between the two seasonal plumages is the plate's central ornithological subject.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-shouldered Hawk (Plate 56)
dateCreated: 1827-1838 (publication; from painting made in Louisiana c. 1826)
description: Two red-shouldered hawks — male above, female below — perch on lichen-draped oak branches draped with Spanish moss in Plate 56 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. The male's strongly barred rufous breast and boldly banded tail are carefully differentiated from the broader, browner female. Spanish moss festooning the branches grounds the composition in the Louisiana lowland habitat where Audubon first observed the species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-tailed Hawk (Plate 51)
description: Two hawks grapple over a hare in a dramatic mid-air struggle, talons interlocked and wings braced against one another. The double-elephant folio's full sheet is exploited to show the raptors at life size, a scale unprecedented in ornithological publishing of the period.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-Throated Diver (Plate 202)
description: Four Red-throated Divers in different plumages are depicted: a large standing bird in spotted winter dress beside marsh plants including pitcher plants, two swimming birds showing summer breeding plumage with the distinctive rust-red throat patch, and a fourth turning away. The arrangement across breeding and non-breeding plumages makes Plate 202 of Birds of America by John James Audubon a comprehensive reference for the species, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Red-winged Starling or Marsh Blackbird (Plate 67)
description: Red-winged blackbirds in graded plumages — adult male, young male, and female — are shown on a blossoming branch bearing small pink flowers, the male's scarlet-and-yellow epaulet conspicuous in display. Plate 67 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) uses the older common names 'Red-winged Starling' and 'Marsh Blackbird' current before the species was universally grouped among American blackbirds.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Republican or Cliff Swallow (Plate 68)
description: Cliff swallows are shown alongside their gourd-shaped mud nests built under a rocky overhang, several birds entering and leaving the colony. The plate documents the colonial nesting biology that earned the bird its alternative name of Republican Swallow.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rice Bird (Plate 54)
description: A breeding male bobolink in his striking inverted black, white, and buff plumage perches at the top of a red-maple branch, while a streaked olive-brown female occupies a lower spray of the same tree in Plate 54 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. The plate documents the species under the agricultural name 'Rice Bird,' reflecting the damage migrating flocks caused to Carolina grain fields. The red-maple setting, labelled in the plate text, gives the composition its warm autumnal tones.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Richardson's Jager (Plate 272)
description: A parasitic jaeger, here under its older name honouring the Arctic naturalist Sir John Richardson, shown as a pale-bellied adult alongside a barred young bird in September plumage. The plate captures the falcon-like wings and pointed central tail feathers used in agile aerial pursuits of terns and small gulls.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ring Plover (Plate 330)
description: Plate 330 of Birds of America depicts two Semipalmated Plovers on rocky ground beside water: an adult in breeding plumage with its distinctive black breast-band in a distraction display, and a juvenile in plain brownish-grey plumage. The sourceDescription confirms the species as Charadrius semipalmatus, long grouped with the Eurasian Ringed Plover.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rock Grous (Plate 368)
description: Plate 368 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Rock Ptarmigan in an alpine landscape: a male in white winter plumage stands upright at right, its red eye-comb prominent against a snowy mountain backdrop, while a second bird in brown mottled summer plumage crouches at lower left. The contrasting seasonal coats on a single plate illustrate the species' dramatic moult cycle. The plate appeared in the double elephant folio published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rocky Coast
description: An unpeopled stretch of cliff and surf treated as a study in elemental force. The thinly brushed sea and broken light show Turner's late shorthand for shoreline weather.

title: Rocky Mountain Plover (Plate 350)
description: A mountain plover forages on a rocky alpine slope against a backdrop of craggy peaks. Plate 350 of Audubon's Birds of America captures the pale, unmarked underparts and the bird's characteristic posture, placing it in the mountain terrain for which it was named.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Roscoe's Yellow-throat (Plate 24)
description: A small yellow-throated warbler perches on a slender twig, the throat and breast a saturated lemon yellow against an olive back. The name Roscoe's Yellow-throat reflects nineteenth-century nomenclatural confusion that ornithology later resolved by folding the bird into established species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rose-breasted Grosbeak (Plate 127)
description: Multiple Rose-breasted Grosbeaks — adult male, female, and birds in autumn plumage — arranged across spruce branches bearing small red berries. The adult male's vivid crimson bib and bold black-and-white wings anchor the composition in Plate CXXVII of Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Roseate Spoonbill (Plate 321)
description: A Roseate Spoonbill bends its spatulate bill to feed, the deep pink wing coverts and orange tail set against a Florida backwater. The plate is among the most flamboyant in Birds of America and helped fix the species in the public imagination.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Roseate Tern (Plate 240)
description: A roseate tern plunges in a steep dive against a blue-grey ground, its deeply forked tail and long wings spread wide. The pale grey mantle and faintly pink-flushed underparts distinguish it from related species, while the orange-red bill — tipped dark — is clearly rendered in Audubon's hand-coloured aquatint. Plate 240 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by R. Havell, London.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rough-legged Falcon (Plate 166)
description: A single male Rough-legged Falcon clings to the top of a weathered stump, bending forward to grip a small dark bird in its talons, its wings raised in a sweeping arc above. The feathered tarsi that give the species its name are visible against the pale buff and dark-streaked plumage. Plate 166 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rough-legged Falcon (Plate 422)
description: Two Rough-legged Hawks — a dark morph and a light morph — perch on a forked branch facing each other, their feathered tarsi and barred underparts clearly displayed against a plain ground. Plate 422 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ruby crowned Wren (Plate 195)
description: Ruby-crowned kinglets shown among slender sprigs, the male displaying the scarlet crown-patch usually concealed beneath olive feathers. The miniature scale required especially fine aquatint work in the Havell engraving.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ruby-throated Humming Bird (Plate 47)
description: Multiple Ruby-throated Hummingbirds hover and perch around trumpet-creeper blossoms, the iridescent throats catching light at different angles. Audubon used the plate to advertise the species' status as the only hummingbird breeding east of the Mississippi.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ruddy Duck (Plate 343)
description: Plate 343 of Birds of America presents four ruddy ducks in different plumages: a breeding male standing tall on a rock with chestnut body, black cap, and bright blue bill; a female; and two birds in intermediate or non-breeding dress. The stiff-tailed posture of the breeding male, with bill tilted upward, is characteristic of the species' courtship display. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ruddy Plover (Plate 230)
description: Two sanderlings, here called Ruddy Plover, are shown on a rocky coastal slope in pale transitional plumage, with islands visible across the water behind them. Audubon rendered the species' compact form and scalloped upperparts against a broad shoreline setting. Plate 230 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ruff-necked Humming-bird (Plate 379)
description: Several Ruff-necked (Rufous) Hummingbirds surround a tall flowering plant, the males' copper-and-flame gorgets catching the light as they hover near the blooms; a fourth bird tends a small lichen-covered nest lower on the stem. The plate gathers multiple postures and sexes to document the species' plumage variation. Plate 379 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Ruffed Grouse (Plate 41)
description: Two male Ruffed Grouse fan their black-banded tails and erect their dark neck ruffs in courtship display while a female stands nearby amid dense foliage with large broad leaves and clusters of dark berries. Plate 41 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the species' dramatic sexual display within the leafy undergrowth of the eastern hardwood forest.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Rusty Grakle (Plate 157)
description: Four Rusty Grakles are shown in autumn plumage among bare branches bearing clusters of dark blue berries and yellow-turning leaves in Plate 157 of Birds of America. Three dark males and one warm-brown female are arranged across the composition, the brownish edging to their feathers giving the group the rufous cast for which the species was named. The Havell workshop colourists captured the subtle contrast between the female's warm brown tones and the iridescent black of the males.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Salt Water Marsh Hen (Plate 204)
description: Rallus crepitans set within tidal cordgrass, the long bill and laterally compressed body conveying its furtive habits in salt marshes. Subtle tonal aquatint distinguishes the muted ochre and grey plumage suited to coastal camouflage.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Savannah Finch (Plate 109)
description: Plate 109 depicts two Savannah Finches (Savannah Sparrows) perched on branches and slender stems among grasses and flowering plants including red tubular blooms. Audubon's composition captures the species' open-country habitat, and the streaked brown plumage is rendered with characteristic precision in this plate from Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Scarlet Ibis (Plate 397)
description: A vivid scarlet adult ibis stands beside a brown, immature individual on a muddy coastal bank, both birds showing the species' long decurved bill against a pale open-water sky. Plate 397 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the two plumage stages, published by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Scaup Duck (Plate 229)
description: A drake and hen scaup rest on a bank before marsh grasses, the male's dark iridescent head and finely vermiculated back contrasted with the female's brown plumage and pale facial patch. The blue-grey bill and compact body typical of the species are clearly rendered. Plate 229 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Scene from “The Last of the Mohicans
description: Thomas Cole depicts the scene from Cooper's novel in which Cora Munro kneels before the Delaware chief Tamenund on a rocky outcrop, a crowd of warriors encircling them against a sweeping mountain landscape. Painted in 1827, shortly after the novel's publication, the picture subordinates the narrative figures to a grand Hudson River School wilderness, the human drama rendered small beneath the soaring peaks.

title: Schinz's Sandpiper restored (Plate 278)
description: A small sandpiper attributed to Schinz, with the streaked breast and decurved bill that fit it equally to a dunlin or white-rumped sandpiper. The plate stands at the centre of a long taxonomic confusion stretching from Brehm's 1822 description through Bonaparte and Coues.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Scolopaceus Courlan (Plate 377)
description: A Limpkin strides across an open rocky bank, its straight pointed bill carried forward and its long legs extended mid-step. The brown plumage shows white streaking on the neck and breast. Plate 377 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sea-side Finch (Plate 93)
description: Two Seaside Sparrows perch among rose-like flowering plants and tall reeds, the olive-grey plumage and pale supercilium carefully rendered as diagnostic field marks. The plate, from Audubon's Birds of America, uses the botanical setting to frame both birds in characteristic postures. Plate 93 of the double-elephant folio, credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Selby's Flycatcher (Plate 9)
description: What Audubon named Selby's Flycatcher in honour of British ornithologist Prideaux John Selby is now generally regarded as a Hooded Warbler. Hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, recording one of several taxonomic redeterminations made after the work's initial publication.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Semipalmated Sandpiper (Plate 405)
description: Two Semipalmated Sandpipers forage along a rocky shore littered with small shells, one probing low at the water's edge and the other walking at a higher point. Plate 405 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., shows the streaked brown-and-white plumage of this common Atlantic shorebird in detail.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Semipalmated Snipe (Plate 274)
description: A willet in breeding plumage, the long straight bill and grey-brown body opening to reveal the striking black-and-white wing pattern in flight. Audubon's plate shows both standing and flying postures to record the field marks that emerge only when the wings unfold.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sharp-shinned Hawk (Plate 374)
description: Plate 374 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Sharp-shinned Hawks perched on a curved branch, one of which grips a small prey item in its talons. Both birds show the slate-blue upperparts and rusty-barred underparts of adults, with strongly banded tails. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838 and is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sharp-tailed Finch (Plate 149)
description: Three Sharp-tailed Finches are depicted in a marsh setting of grasses and reeds in Plate 149 of Birds of America: one bird sings from the tip of a bare twig, a second perches in the grass, and a third tends a nest at the base of the composition. The streaked breast and buff face pattern of the species are clearly rendered against the muted greens of the wetland vegetation. Audubon associated the species with the low coastal marshes of eastern North America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sharp-tailed Grous (Plate 382)
description: Two Sharp-tailed Grouse walk across open ground before a mountain and river landscape, the pointed central tail feathers and pale spotted underparts clearly shown. A small berry-bearing shrub appears at lower left. Plate 382 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Shipping off East Cowes Headland
description: Sails crowd the Solent off East Cowes, where Turner stayed with the architect John Nash during the 1827 Royal Yacht Club regatta. The picture belongs to a series of studies generated by that summer visit.

title: Shore Lark (Plate 200)
description: Four Shore Larks in varying plumages—adult male with black facial mask and horns, a winter-plumage adult, and juveniles—are shown in and around a nest set in dense green low vegetation. The composition illustrates the species' life history rather than a single field pose. Plate 200 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Shoveller Duck (Plate 327)
description: A Northern Shoveler drake and female face each other on a rocky bank in a courtship display, both birds upright with bills open to reveal the broad, spatulate shape that gives the species its name. The drake's iridescent dark green head, chestnut flanks, and blue wing patches are vividly rendered in Plate 327 of Audubon's Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sketch for ‘East Cowes Castle
englishTitle: Sketch for 'East Cowes Castle, the Regatta Beating to Windward', No. 1
description: An oil sketch on canvas worked up while Turner was Nash's guest at East Cowes Castle. The yachts beating against the wind would be reorganised into the finished regatta picture exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1828.

title: Sketch for ‘East Cowes Castle
englishTitle: Sketch for 'East Cowes Castle, the Regatta Beating to Windward', No. 2

title: Slender-billed Guillemot (Plate 430)
description: Two Slender-billed Guillemots stand on a rocky coastal ledge, one showing the brownish scalloped upperparts and pale belly of its plumage, the other darker with a contrasting white underside, a grey sea and clouds receding behind them. Plate 430 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Small Green Crested Flycatcher (Plate 144)
description: Two Small Green Crested Flycatchers are shown among leafy branches laden with dark berries in this plate from the Havell edition of Birds of America. One bird is perched in an alert posture while the other is depicted with wings spread, together demonstrating the species' lively character. Audubon's botanical setting is rendered with the careful observation that distinguishes the double-elephant folio from earlier ornithological prints.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Smew or White Nun (Plate 347)
description: Plate 347 of Birds of America depicts two smews against a mountainous coastal background: a drake in flight showing his crisp white plumage with black markings, and a rufous-headed female riding the waves below. The smew is a small Eurasian sawbill that occasionally strays to North America, and the plate records both sexes to illustrate the marked sexual dimorphism of the species. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Snow Bird (Plate 13)
description: Male and female dark-eyed juncos — then called the Snow Bird — perched on leafless winter branches hung with small dark berries. Audubon's spare, uncluttered staging suits the species' winter familiarity in Plate XIII of Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Snow Bunting (Plate 189)
description: Three snow buntings are shown in a coastal or upland setting with hills in the background: one adult in flight displaying bold black-and-white wing pattern, one perched adult in white-and-buff plumage, and one younger, browner bird on the ground. Plate 189 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents adult and immature plumages of this circumpolar species.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Snow Goose (Plate 381)
description: An adult white-morph Snow Goose stands beside a dark-morph (Blue Goose) individual, the latter showing a dark body with white head and neck, together contrasting the two recognised colour forms of the species. The black wingtips of the white bird and the pink bill and feet of both are rendered against a stormy coastal sky. Plate 381 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Snowy Heron or White Egret
description: A snowy egret in full breeding plumage stands on a muddy bank amid marsh vegetation, its golden-yellow feet prominent against dark ground and the long aigrette plumes cascading from back and breast. A distant background shows a plantation landscape with buildings and a river. Plate 242 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Egretta thula and drawn from a South Carolina locality.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Snowy Owl (Plate 121)
description: A pair of Snowy Owls perched on the limbs of a dead tree against a dark, cloud-streaked sky, the more heavily barred individual in the foreground and the paler bird above. Audubon differentiates male and female by the density of their dark markings in Plate CXXI of Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Solitary Flycatcher or Vireo (Plate 28)
description: A small olive-and-white songbird with bold white spectacles, perched among foliage. Now known as the Blue-headed Vireo, the plate captures the deliberate, gleaning movements that distinguish vireos from the more aerial true flycatchers.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Solitary Sandpiper (Plate 289)
description: Two Solitary Sandpipers are shown in a marshy setting among reeds and broad-leaved plants, one with wings raised in display and the other alert on the opposite bank. The species' spotted, dark-backed plumage and white eye-ring are well rendered in Audubon's composition. Plate 289 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Song Sparrow (Plate 25)
description: Song sparrows perched on a flowering branch, their streaked breasts and warm brown backs picked out in fine engraved line. Audubon places the birds in active poses that suggest the territorial singing for which the species is named across North America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sooty Tern (Plate 235)
description: A sooty tern banks in flight, its dark upperparts and white underparts and forehead resolved against a pale clouded sky. The plate captures the species' deeply forked tail and swept-back wings in a spare, aerial composition. Plate 235 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Sora or Rail (Plate 233)
description: Three soras — male, female, and young — are shown on a fallen log amid marsh grasses, the adults displaying the species' yellow bill, dark facial mask, and barred flanks, while the young bird shows plainer buff tones. Audubon used the dense reed setting to suggest the species' preference for dense cover. Plate 233 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Spotted Grous (Plate 176)
description: Four Spotted Grouse (Tetrao canadensis) — three males displaying their vivid red eye-combs and a brown female at left — are grouped among low foliage bearing red berries in Plate 176 of Birds of America. The bold barred and scaled patterning of the males' black-and-white plumage contrasts with the female's streaked brown colouring. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. for Audubon's double elephant folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Spotted Sandpiper (Plate 310)
description: Two Spotted Sandpipers occupy a rocky shoreline, their breeding plumage carrying the heavy round spots that vanish in winter. Audubon often paired adults to compress life history into a single sheet of the Birds of America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Stanley Hawk (Plate 36)
description: A Stanley Hawk in dynamic flight — shown as a young male — sweeps across the composition above a second hawk perched on a weathered post, while a small eastern bluebird appears at upper right. Plate 36 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two plumages of this Cooper's Hawk, known under an older vernacular name, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Stormy Petrel (Plate 270)
description: A storm petrel skimming low over the waves, its small dark form and white rump patch finely engraved. The plate captures the swallow-like flight by which these tiny seabirds patter across the surface, picking at oily morsels in open water.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Summer or Wood Duck (Plate 206)
dateCreated: 1827-1838 (publication; from a painting made in Louisiana in 1821)
description: Aix sponsa shown in arboreal habit suggested by overhanging foliage, the drake's iridescent crest and bold facial striping rendered in saturated hand-applied watercolour over aquatint. A favoured Audubon subject for its colour and behaviour.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Summer Red Bird (Plate 44)
description: Three Summer Tanagers share a fruiting branch bearing dark grapes: the adult male in full scarlet perches at the top, a transitional bird with mixed red and olive-green plumage appears at lower left, and an olive-yellow female occupies the centre. Plate 44 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Swallow-tailed Hawk (Plate 72)
description: A swallow-tailed kite (called Swallow-tailed Hawk by Audubon) banks on long pointed wings against a plain background, a garter snake gripped in its bill — illustrating one of the reptilian prey items the species takes in flight. Plate 72 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) exploits the double-elephant folio's generous format to convey the dramatic wingspan of this raptor of southern North America.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Swamp Sparrow (Plate 64)
description: A swamp sparrow perches on the arching stem of a may-apple in Plate 64 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the bird's rusty cap and streaked back set against the plant's large lobed leaves and single white flower. The plate text identifies the botanical subject as May Apple, Podophyllum peltatum. The single-bird composition keeps the focus on the sparrow's subdued but carefully differentiated plumage.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tawny Thrush (Plate 164)
description: A Veery is shown among understorey foliage, the warm cinnamon back and faintly spotted breast realised through restrained washes. Audubon followed nineteenth-century usage in calling this woodland thrush the Tawny Thrush.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tell-tale Godwit or Snipe (Plate 308)
description: Plate 308 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Greater Yellowlegs — then called Tell-tale Godwit for the alarm calls that warned hunters of an observer's approach. One bird stands alert with wings slightly raised while the other probes the mud below, both showing the bright yellow legs that give the species its modern name. A background of coastal marsh with distant buildings situates the birds in their tidal habitat.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tengmalm's Owl (Plate 380)
description: Two Tengmalm's (Boreal) Owls share a plain composition: one perches on a bare stub facing away, showing the spotted back and rounded facial disc, while a second bird spreads its wings below in a contrasting posture. The background is plain paper with no foliage. Plate 380 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tennessee Warbler (Plate 154)
description: A Tennessee Warbler perches among slender twigs, its olive-and-grey palette modelled by selectively applied aquatint. The species was named by Alexander Wilson from a migrant collected on the Cumberland River, and Audubon retained the regional epithet.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: The Apotheosis of Homer
description: Commissioned for a ceiling in the Louvre, this strictly symmetrical tableau enthrones the blind poet beneath a winged Victory while artists and writers from antiquity to the modern age gather as witnesses. Ingres treats the canvas almost as a bas-relief, marshalling Neoclassical contour and frieze-like balance to assert Homer's status as the wellspring of Western art.
credit: photo Shonagon 2025-03-29

provenance.collection: Department of Paintings of the Louvre

title: The Death of Sardanapalus
description: Victorious Central Asian troops stand among severed heads and abandoned weapons after the action, the celebration unsettling rather than triumphant. Paired with 'After a failure', the picture insists that battlefield outcomes share a single moral landscape of slaughter.
credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"d/delacroi/2/204delac"

title: Thick-billed Murre (Plate 245)
description: A thick-billed murre is shown in low flight over an open sea, its black-and-white plumage and stout bill captured mid-wingbeat above choppy water. The horizontal flight pose was a compositional choice that emphasises the species' powerful, rapid flight over northern oceans. Plate 245 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Uria Brunnichii.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Three-toed Woodpecker (Plate 132)
description: Three woodpeckers cling to a deciduous tree trunk, each displaying the yellow crown patch that distinguishes the three-toed species. The plate groups male and female birds of differing plumages and is Plate 132 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Towhe Bunting (Plate 29)
description: A male Towhe Bunting with a black hood, rufous flanks, and white belly perches on a thorny branch above a brown-hooded female in a tangle of brambles and flowering shrubs. The plate corresponds to the Eastern Towhee, and Audubon's two-bird composition shows the strong sexual plumage dimorphism of the species. Plate 29 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Townsend's Sandpiper (Plate 428)
description: Two Townsend's Sandpipers are shown in flight above a misty waterway, their wing patterns and underparts displayed in dorsal and ventral views. First described from a single specimen collected by John Kirk Townsend, the taxon is now regarded by modern ornithologists as aberrant or hybrid rather than a valid species. Plate 428 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Traill's Flycatcher (Plate 45)
description: A small olive-brown Empidonax flycatcher named after the Edinburgh naturalist Thomas Stewart Traill perches alertly on a sprig. Modern taxonomy splits the original Traill's into the Alder and Willow Flycatchers, two near-identical species separable mainly by song.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tree Sparrow (Plate 188)
description: Two American tree sparrows perch on fruiting branches hung with small red berries, their rufous caps and characteristic breast-spots carefully rendered. Plate 188 of John James Audubon's Birds of America shows both birds in characteristic poses, foregrounding the plumage study that defines the series.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tropic Bird (Plate 262)
description: A tropicbird rendered with elongated tail streamers trailing behind a stout white body. The plate evokes the species' offshore wanderings across warm seas, where it plunge-dives for squid and flying fish far from any coast.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Trumpeter Swan (Plate 376)
description: An adult Trumpeter Swan arches its neck to drink from a marsh pool, the long body filling almost the full sheet of the double elephant folio. The plate is one of the largest single-bird compositions in the series, exploiting the format for North America's heaviest waterfowl.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Trumpeter Swan (Plate 406)
description: A massive white swan arches its neck along the full height of the double elephant folio sheet, snapping at a small moth. Audubon bent the bird's neck into a tight curl so it could stand at life size on a page just over a metre tall — one of his most-discussed compositional solutions.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tufted Auk (Plate 249)
description: Two birds occupy the plate: a large tufted puffin stands in profile on rocky ground, its white facial plumes, pale eye, and large orange-and-yellow bill clearly rendered; beside it a second, smaller bird is shown face-on. Plate 249 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Tufted Auk and identified as Mormon Cirrhatus, Male 1, Female 2.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tufted Duck (Plate 234)
description: A drake and hen tufted duck stand on low grassy ground, the male's drooping black crest and golden eye contrasted with his bold black-and-white body, while the brown hen rests alongside. Plate 234 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838, depicts this Eurasian diving duck.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Turkey Buzzard (Plate 151)
description: Two Turkey Vultures are shown in Plate 151 of Birds of America: a large individual perches upright on a heavy branch, its bare red head and dark brown plumage dominating the upper composition, while a second bird below holds its wings partially spread. Audubon's observations on this species fed his celebrated dispute with Charles Waterton over whether vultures locate carrion by sight or smell, a controversy he documented in the Ornithological Biography.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Turn-stone (Plate 304)
description: Plate 304 of Birds of America shows two Ruddy Turnstones: one in vigorous flight, wings fully spread to display the striking orange-chestnut, black, and white pattern that distinguishes the species, and one standing on a sandy shore in slightly duller plumage. The hand-coloured aquatint captures the harlequin boldness of the breeding male's markings, making this one of the most visually striking shorebird plates in the folio.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Tyrant Fly-catcher (Plate 79)
description: An Eastern Kingbird is shown defending its territory, the species' aggressive behaviour toward larger raptors having earned it the name Tyrant Fly-catcher. Hand-coloured aquatint engraving by Robert Havell Jr. of London, working from the original watercolour study.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Velvet Duck (Plate 247)
description: A white-winged scoter, here called Velvet Duck, floats on coastal water, the drake's velvety black plumage broken by a white wing patch and a knobbed orange bill. Aquatint reproduces the matte quality of the breeding plumage that gave the species its old name.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Vigor's Warbler (Plate 30)
description: Plate 30 of Birds of America depicts a single Vigor's Warbler — a small, yellowish wood warbler — perched on a broad-leaved plant bearing purple-red blossoms, identified in the plate caption as Virginia spiderwort. Audubon named the species in honour of British zoologist Nicholas Aylward Vigors; the bird is now regarded as a probable hybrid or misidentified specimen, making the plate a notable artefact of early American ornithological taxonomy.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Virginia Rail (Plate 205)
description: Three Virginia Rails are depicted at a marsh edge among reeds: one adult strides forward, a second raises its bill sharply skyward, and a juvenile crouches in the lower right. The plate captures different ages and postures of the species, with the characteristic long reddish bill and barred flanks carefully rendered. Plate 205 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Virginian Partridge (Plate 76)
description: A covey of Virginian (Northern Bobwhite) Partridges scatters in panic as a hawk strikes from above, the dynamic composition exemplifying the dramatic narrative staging that distinguishes Birds of America from earlier ornithological plates. Hand-coloured aquatint after a watercolour drawn from life-size specimens.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Wandering Shearwater (Plate 283)
description: A dark-backed, white-bellied shearwater stands on a low rocky ledge beside calm water, with mountains visible in the distance. The contrast between the bird's dark upperparts and white underparts — a characteristic of the species — is clearly rendered in the plate. Plate 283 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Warbling Flycatcher (Plate 118)
description: A study of the small olive-toned songbird known today as the warbling vireo, perched amid foliage. The plate exemplifies Audubon's habit of pairing each species with a botanical setting drawn from direct field observation.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Western Duck (Plate 429)
description: Two male Steller's Eiders — shown under the name Western Duck — stand on a rocky reed-fringed shore, displaying their white heads with iridescent green patches, black backs, and warm buff-orange underparts. Plate 429 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: Whip-poor-will (Plate 82)
description: Three Eastern Whip-poor-wills are depicted among lobed oak foliage: two roosting on branches and one in flight catching a large moth, its gaping bill and bristled rictus conveying the nocturnal nightjar's hunting behaviour. Plate 82 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White Heron (Plate 386)
description: A Great Egret in breeding plumage stands amid coastal vegetation, long aigrette plumes cascading down its back. The plate documents the species before late nineteenth-century plume hunting nearly drove it to extinction.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White Ibis (Plate 222)
description: Eudocimus albus rendered in two individuals: a white adult with long pink decurved bill, black wingtips, and pink legs, facing a heavily brown-plumaged immature bird with a yellowish bill. A small crayfish at lower left adds habitat context. Plate 222 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White throated Sparrow (Plate 8)
description: Two White-throated Sparrows perch on a flowering dogwood branch bearing white blossoms, the boldly striped head and bright white throat patch of each bird clearly differentiated. Hand-coloured aquatint from Plate 8 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White-bellied Swallow (Plate 98)
description: A male and female White-bellied Swallow are shown in mid-air against a light sky, the male's iridescent blue-green upperparts contrasting with the clean white underparts of both birds. The composition captures the species in characteristic flight, a device Audubon used to portray aerial insectivores in motion. Plate 98 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White-breasted Black-capped Nuthatch (Plate 152)
description: Nuthatches descend a tree trunk head-first in their characteristic posture, the bark texture engraved with fine aquatint grain. The composition records the bird's habitual foraging behaviour rather than presenting it as a static museum specimen.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White-crowned Pigeon (Plate 177)
description: Two White-crowned Pigeons (Columba leucocephala) perch among the dark green foliage and vivid orange trumpet-shaped blossoms of a tropical shrub in Plate 177 of Birds of America. The species' white cap and deep slate-grey body are precisely rendered, with iridescent greenish neck feathers visible on the upper bird. Audubon documented the species from its Caribbean and Floridian range, and the plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White-crowned Sparrow (Plate 114)
description: Plate 114 depicts two White-crowned Sparrows among the broad leaves and dark berry clusters of a grape vine. The boldly black-and-white striped crown and clean gray breast are crisply rendered in this plate from Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
credit: University of Pittsburgh

title: White-eyed Flycatcher or Vireo (Plate 63)
